title: GM shutters US battery assembly near Detroit - electrive.com
content:
General Motors is closing its battery assembly plant in Michigan. The Brownstown Battery Assembly Plant produced battery packs for Cadillac's electric flagship, the Celestiq, as well as electric motors and batteries for the plug-in hybrid Chevrolet Corvette E-Ray.
The Cadillac Celestiq received its batteries from the Brownstown Battery Assembly Plant.
Image: Cadillac
A company spokesperson confirmed the closure to the portal
TechCrunch
. However, it is reportedly unrelated to GM’s electric vehicle strategy. Instead, GM had leased the site – and, according to the spokesperson, the lease agreement was about to expire. Employees and production in Brownstown are now to be relocated to other GM plants. The closure was first reported by
Automotive News
What is clear is that, with the second term of US President Donald Trump, the EV business in the USA has developed significantly more slowly than expected. This is also affecting General Motors’ previously adopted electrification plans. Just three weeks ago, for example, it emerged that General Motors now intends to
produce significantly fewer units of the new Chevrolet Bolt
than originally planned. According to
, production is now expected to reach only around 35,000 vehicles by the time the model is phased out in the first quarter of 2027 – instead of the originally planned 150,000. The fact that the new Bolt would have a short market presence has been known since the beginning of the year. GM had positioned the model from the outset as a
Limited Run
and announced that production would end again in 2027. The significantly lower volume is the new development.
This production cut, along with the now-publicised closure of the battery assembly plant south of Detroit, is one of many examples of GM’s restructuring of its electric vehicle strategy. Following the elimination of the
$7,500 US purchase incentive
in September 2025, sales of battery-electric vehicles dropped significantly. At the same time, GM has realigned several plants to focus more on
internal combustion engine vehicles
Financially, this signals some turbulence. Since the second quarter of 2025, the company has recorded a total of $10.9 billion in charges related to its electric vehicle business, according to
. While GM continues to produce around a dozen EV models, it has repeatedly adjusted its original expansion plans in recent times.

title: VW’s battery recall affects 72,700 EVs - including 10,000 in Germany - electrive.com
content:
A few days ago, it leaked that VW was preparing a battery recall for several ID. models. Now it’s official: due to faulty EV batteries, Wolfsburg is recalling nearly 72,700 electric cars worldwide to workshops. In Germany, 10,000 vehicles are said to be affected.
Image: Volkswagen
According to now official information, the issue affects specific batches of the ID.3, ID.4, ID.7, ID. Buzz and Cupra Born models. Vehicles from Volkswagen subsidiary Škoda are reportedly not affected. The initiative comprises three separate recalls. Two of these concern the aforementioned VW vehicles manufactured between 2022 and 2025, while the third pertains to Cupra Born vehicles produced from 2022 to 2024. Owners of the affected vehicles will be notified by letter.
The recall is a precautionary measure. According to the KBA (German Federal Motor Transport Authority), there have been no incidents involving property damage or personal injury. Last week,
Handelsblatt
reported that Volkswagen was preparing such a recall. The background involves potential production defects in individual high-voltage battery cells. Internal quality checks revealed that cells in certain vehicles of the ID. family do not meet quality requirements due to manufacturing errors by suppliers, a VW spokesperson told the publication. In rare cases, affected cells could overheat, and in extreme cases, there is a risk of fire.
As an immediate safety measure, Volkswagen intends to limit the maximum charge level of affected vehicles to 80 per cent via an over-the-air update. In the UK, a similar recall has already been initiated – covering the VW ID.3, ID.4, ID.7, ID. Buzz and ID. Buzz Cargo. There, the action pertains to high-voltage batteries from a specific supplier manufactured between 2022 and 2025; the charge level will also initially be limited to 80 per cent.
The permanent repair solution has not yet been finalised. According to information from
Handelsblatt
, workshops will inspect the high-voltage battery or individual modules in affected vehicles. While
Handelsblatt
reports that the recall primarily affects Europe, the KBA refers to it as a global recall. However, the high number of affected vehicles in Germany suggests that the focus is at least primarily on Europe.
Meanwhile, in the US: a separate
battery recall
is already underway for 22,524 ID.4 vehicles from model years 2023 to 2026. There, Volkswagen also recommends charging the vehicles to a maximum of 80 per cent until a final fix is implemented. The manufacturer identifies SK Battery America as the supplier of the affected battery cells. The exact cause remains unclear; according to Volkswagen, certain charging profiles above 80 per cent could promote thermal runaway within the battery.
Separate from this are
two earlier US recalls from early 2026
covering a total of 44,551 ID.4 vehicles. These exclusively affected vehicles from the Chattanooga plant with battery cells from SK Battery America in Georgia. The cause included, among other things, misaligned electrodes in individual cells. The European ID.4 models from Zwickau and Emden used different battery cells and were explicitly not affected by these actions.

title: CATL unveils new battery solution for eHGVs - electrive.com
content:
CATL has presented a new swap battery system coupled with a permanently installed extra battery. The main battery offers 432 or 513 kWh and can be exchanged at swap stations. In addition, there is the permanently installed "range-extender" battery with 77 kWh, which acts as a reserve.
Image: CATL
The Chinese battery giant presented its new system in Beijing on Tuesday. CATL is positioning this as a battery option for heavy-duty electric trucks, with plans to market it under the name “Dual-Electric Range Extender” technology. In a statement, CATL told electrive that the main battery, which is installed in the underbody with capacities of 432 or 513 kWh, will be available through a flexible leasing model “to reduce upfront costs”.
To support the new technology, CATL aims to further expand its ‘QiJi’ battery swap station network. The company has standardised the battery blocks used in the new system into two sizes: the 260# swap block (432 kWh) for vehicles with a wheelbase of 3.8 metres and the 300# (513 kWh) for trucks with a wheelbase of 4.2 metres. This ensures the batteries are interchangeable within the QiJi swap system. Combined with the permanently installed 77 kWh auxiliary battery located behind the cab, the total system capacity reaches 509 kWh or 590 kWh, respectively.
With this new approach, CATL aims to “optimise battery usage and reduce operating costs for fleets”. During the presentation, CATL also publicly signed contracts with 14 partners to adopt the system, including SF Express, ZTO Express and YTO Express – three of China’s major logistics and parcel delivery providers. The initial order volume is stated as 13,000 units.
Fundamentally, the “Dual-Electric Range Extender” technology is initially designed for CATL’s home market, where the manufacturer’s battery swap station network – essential for this approach – is primarily expanding. By the end of the year, CATL aims to have 900 battery swap stations for heavy-duty trucks in operation, increasing to 2,000 units over the course of next year. In the long term, CATL plans to establish a total of 10,000 stations in China together with partners.
For those wondering why CATL has installed a reserve battery alongside the large swap battery, the manufacturer provides the following context: drivers of trucks with conventional swap batteries typically return to the swap station when the charge level is around 30 per cent, according to the company. This leaves part of the leased battery capacity unused. This is where the additional reserve battery comes into play: its “buffer” allows the depth of discharge (DoD) of the main battery to be increased from around 70 to over 95 per cent. CATL states that this enables truck drivers to head to the swap station only when the main battery’s charge level drops to around five percent – without the risk of running out of power on board.
At this five percent state of charge (SoC) threshold, “CATL’s seamless switching technology transfers power delivery to the range-extension battery within milliseconds, maintaining a continuous and stable power supply,” the manufacturer specifies. The main battery is therefore never fully depleted.
The system is based on CATL’s so-called “1+X” architecture, in which the main battery is standardised to ensure compatibility with the swap network, while the range extender battery remains individually configurable.
Image: CATL
Image: CATL
Image: CATL
Image: CATL
Image: CATL
Image: CATL
Image: CATL
Conversely, CATL’s Qiji swap network for trucks will now support not only the
75# battery block with 171 kW introduced in 2025
, but also the 260# and 300# types with 432 kWh and 513 kWh, respectively. According to CATL, a new generation of Qiji swap stations will allow battery swaps in just 5 minutes. Additionally, “the station requires no excavation pit and can be constructed in just 5 days,” the company stated.
According to
CN EV News
, the company is also adjusting its billing model for its Battery-as-a-Service offering by “charging customers for net energy charged rather than energy discharged, allowing them to retain the benefits of regenerative braking”. CATL claims this change can reduce battery leasing costs per kWh for users on basic tariffs by up to 20 per cent.
CATL fundamentally sees significant potential for battery swapping in road freight transport. Earlier this summer, the company
acquired a nearly 25 percent stake in Qiyuan Green Power
, the largest operator of battery swap stations for heavy-duty trucks in China. Through this investment, CATL can unite two battery swap technologies under one roof: its own Qiji system and Qiyuan Green Power’s swap system.
Qiyuan Green Power’s battery swap solution is designed for rear-mounted installations. This system is said to be known for its high compatibility and fits over 80 per cent of the heavy-duty trucks with battery swap capabilities in China according to an August article from
Car News China
. This approach is primarily used in closed or semi-public environments such as mines, ports, steel plants and urban construction sites.
CATL’s own battery swap system, branded as Qiji, focuses on the truck chassis. China’s battery giant now applies this approach to passenger cars, vans and trucks—offering various sizes of standardised swap batteries at its stations, referred to as ‘Choco-SEB’. SEB stands for “Swapping Electric Blocks,” and the name “Choco” is inspired by the appearance of a chocolate bar with its individual ‘blocks’. According to
Car News China
, the Qiji brand primarily targets China’s national highway logistics network.
Regarding the network’s scope, this is what we know so far: by the end of 2025, Qiyuan Green Power’s network is expected to have established over 1,600 charging and battery swap stations across 208 prefecture-level cities. CATL’s Qiji brand is expected to have around 300 stations by the end of 2025 – and aims to reach the aforementioned target of 900 stations by the end of the current year.
The battery swap market for trucks in China continues to grow dynamically. One German manager with deep knowledge of this market is Klaus Sekot, Managing Director of Bosch MC Battery Service Innovations – a joint venture founded in 2025 by Bosch and Mitsubishi Corporation, based in Ludwigsburg. The new company specialises in Battery-as-a-Service (BaaS) solutions and recently celebrated the debut of its customer project at a truck battery swap station in Chizhou.
In an interview with electrive this summer, Sekot explained that there are currently three parallel battery swap standards for trucks in China. He also noted that China has been deliberately developing the battery swapping market since the early 2020s for industrial policy reasons. According to Sekot’s information, nearly 30,000 swap-compatible heavy-duty trucks were newly registered in China in 2024. Read the full interview

title: Audi and NVIDIA Use Agile Robots for Parts Sequencing Trial
content:
Audi and NVIDIA Use Agile Robots for Parts Sequencing Trial
Prioritise Us
on Google
Audi is working with Agile Robots, Dassault Systèmes and NVIDIA to automate parts sequencing at its Ingolstadt plant using mobile humanoid robots. Credit: Audi
Audi’s Board Member for Production and Logistics Gerd Walker explains how Agile Robots, Dassault Systèmes and NVIDIA are bringing physical AI to logistics
Audi is working with Agile Robots, Dassault Systèmes and NVIDIA to automate parts sequencing at its Ingolstadt plant using mobile humanoid robots. The proof of concept targets one of automotive logistics’ most complex activities: picking mixed components and placing them in the correct order for vehicle assembly.
Audi targets humanoid robotics for parts sequencing
Audi’s demand-driven material supply operation manages approximately one million picks every day, ensuring that the correct parts reach the correct workstation in the correct assembly sequence.
The partners are testing mobile humanoids in Audi’s Production Lab, an innovation environment for future manufacturing and logistics technologies. The robots will pick components from material containers and place them into sequence for the final assembly of Audi premium vehicles.
The project brings together Audi’s production and supply-chain expertise; Agile Robots’ mobile humanoid robotics; Dassault Systèmes’ DELMIA virtual-twin technology; and NVIDIA’s physical-AI and robotics libraries.
The proof-of-concept project is designed to test whether humanoid robots can automate high-variant logistics tasks while fitting into existing factory environments.
“The future of manufacturing will be defined by how successfully we combine industrial expertise with artificial intelligence. For decades, picking within the sequencing process has remained one of the toughest automation challenges in automotive logistics," says Gerd Walker, Member of the Board of Management for Production and Logistics at Audi.
"Together with our partners, we are now exploring how AI-powered robotics can help solve this challenge and unlock a new level of productivity in our Audi factories."
Gerd Walker, Member of the Board of Management for Production and Logistics, Audi AG. Credit: Audi AG
Virtual twin validates robot deployment
Before the mobile humanoids are deployed in Audi’s smart intralogistics environment, the partners are creating a virtual twin of the logistics operation using Dassault Systèmes' DELMIA application.
The virtual environment is intended to help engineers test:
robot-task feasibility
cycle times
ergonomics
component handling
robot movement
factory integration
sequencing performance.
Dassault Systèmes' 3DEXPERIENCE platform will combine DELMIA virtual twins with Industry World Models and NVIDIA Omniverse libraries. The partners say this approach could reduce engineering and commissioning work from months to days.
Dassault Systèmes' AI-powered LEO Virtual Companion is expected to assist engineers during the process. LEO can draw on manufacturing data and process plans to support process-sequence development, work instructions and resource assignments.
Agile Robots brings mobile humanoids to the factory
Munich-based Agile Robots says it has deployed more than 20,000 robotic solutions worldwide. The trial features mobile humanoid robots, which combine humanoid reach and dexterity with the robustness of a mobile base. The robots are a new product that has just been developed by the robotics developer. The robots operate at human height, and feature dual-arm manipulation and a mobile base.
The design is intended to help the robots work alongside existing equipment and infrastructure, rather than requiring a complete redesign of Audi’s intralogistics environment.
“Agile Robots is driving industries forward with physical AI. Working with Audi we show how our mobile humanoids can perform high-value, critical tasks that were previously impossible to automate. That is what physical AI is all about – real progress for industrial productivity,” says Dr Zhaopeng Chen, Founder and Chief Executive Officer of Agile Robots.
Physical AI targets complex logistics tasks
Traditional industrial robots are highly effective when operating in structured environments with predictable components, fixed positions and repeatable movements. Automotive parts sequencing is more difficult because components can vary in size, shape, packaging and location.
The proof of concept focuses on two persistent automation challenges: handling high-variant or semi-rigid parts, and picking unsorted components from mixed containers.
Agile Robots’ dual-arm mobile humanoids are designed to handle larger and more flexible components. AI-powered perception allows the systems to identify, grasp and manipulate parts presented in different positions and packaging formats.
The partners describe this as a step towards the introduction of physical AI powered humanoid robotics into high-volume manufacturing. Physical AI refers to systems that combine artificial intelligence with perception, motion, manipulation and interaction with the physical world.
The proof of concept targets one of automotive logistics’ most complex activities: picking mixed components and placing them in the correct order for vehicle assembly. Credit: Audi AG
NVIDIA supports simulation and edge AI
NVIDIA is contributing its robotics and physical AI technologies to the project. Its Omniverse libraries are being used within Dassault Systèmes’ virtual twin environment to simulate and validate the robot’s activities before physical deployment.
NVIDIA also provides robotics software and accelerated computing technologies used to support perception, simulation and edge AI. The company announced that Agile Robots’ Agile ONE SN reference humanoid is preconfigured with NVIDIA Isaac GR00T and powered by the NVIDIA Jetson Thor edge-AI platform.
“Humanoid robots are advancing automation beyond fixed, repetitive tasks to the complex, variable work at the heart of modern manufacturing," says Deepu Talla, NVIDIA’s Vice President of Robotics and Edge AI.
Dassault Systèmes accelerates factory engineering
Dassault Systèmes is providing the digital engineering layer for the project through DELMIA and the 3DEXPERIENCE platform.
Philippe Laufer, Executive Vice President of 3DS Global Brands at Dassault Systèmes, says the main breakthrough was not simply bringing humanoid robots into factories, but validating their tasks before physical deployment.
The platform is intended to allow engineering teams to:
model the production environment
simulate robot missions
test timing and feasibility
evaluate worker ergonomics
validate safety requirements
use physical AI libraries
reduce commissioning risk.
This virtual-first approach is particularly relevant to automotive manufacturers, where production changes can affect highly synchronised assembly operations. The introduction of robots into discrete tasks, such as the picking of mixed components and parts sequencing, would not introduce significant disruption into the series production of automobiles.

title: DP World expands US data centre logistics as AI demand rises
content:
DP World expands US data centre logistics as AI demand rises
Prioritise Us
on Google
DP World is expanding its US data centre logistics network. Credit: Getty
Ya-Han Brownlee-Chen, DP World’s VP Data Center Strategy in the Americas, explains how growth in AI infrastructure is reshaping US data-centre logistics
DP World targets AI infrastructure supply chains
DP World is expanding its specialised US data-centre logistics network as hyperscalers and technology companies accelerate investment in artificial intelligence and cloud infrastructure.
The logistics provider now supports nearly 50 data-centre sites across the United States, connecting international freight, secure storage, equipment configuration and final deployment. Its expansion comes as more than 1,500 new US data centres are in development, alongside more than 3,000 operational facilities, according to Pew Research Center analysis.
The surge in growth in data centres and components for their supply chains components accounted for 42% of the growth in world trade in 2025, according to recent research by NYU Stern's Center for the Future of Management.
The scale of the buildout is creating a complex supply-chain challenge. Servers, GPUs, networking equipment, transformers and cooling systems must arrive securely, be configured accurately and reach construction sites in line with demanding commissioning schedules.
“The infrastructure powering AI depends on an increasingly sophisticated global supply chain. A delayed server, transformer, or other critical component can have implications well beyond transportation when data centres are being built and commissioned against demanding timelines," says Ya-Han Brownlee-Chen, Vice President of Data Center Strategy for the Americas.
"Our expanding US footprint brings transportation, inventory management, configuration, and deployment capabilities together to give customers greater control from origin through installation,” adds Ya-Han.
DP World's services include rack assembly, software replication and testing in-house. Credit: DP World
Data-centre logistics moves beyond transportation
DP World’s expanded US network is designed to manage the full movement of high-value technology infrastructure, from factory to data centre.
Its services include:
International freight management
Secure and specialised warehousing
Inbound receiving and inspection
Inventory management and asset tracking
Kitting and pre-assembly
Server configuration and testing
Rack integration
White-glove transportation
Spare-parts management
Reverse logistics
The model reflects a broader shift in data-centre supply chains. Logistics providers are increasingly expected to support not only transportation, but also configuration, validation, chain-of-custody controls and deployment readiness. DP World's investment in expanding its network comes amid mounting interest in delivering solutions for
hyperscalers
DP World reports 99% inventory accuracy
DP World says it has achieved more than 99% inventory accuracy across approximately $2 billion in managed cloud and data-centre assets.
That capability is increasingly important as AI hardware becomes more expensive, specialised and difficult to replace. A missing GPU, delayed transformer or incorrectly configured server can affect construction schedules and delay the point at which new computing capacity becomes operational.
The company also reports more than a decade of cloud and data-centre logistics experience, with capabilities spanning more than 80 countries. DP World supports five of the world’s seven largest technology companies, according to the company.
DP World operates a global logistics network extending across more than 80 countries. Credit: DP World
Cleanroom-enabled server rack deployment
For one leading global technology company, DP World developed a secure, high-volume server-rack configuration operation designed around strict cleanliness and quality requirements.
The solution combined:
Inbound equipment handling
Kitting and cabling
Server configuration
Validation and testing
Rack assembly
Continuous monitoring
Outbound shipping
The operation was able to configure up to 75 custom server racks per week. Approximately 1,300 racks were built, tested and shipped annually, before the model was replicated at three additional global locations.
The example illustrates how logistics facilities are becoming operational extensions of data-centre construction and deployment teams.
Cybersecurity becomes a supply-chain priority
DP World’s latest research, conducted with Supply Chain Dive’s Studio by Informa TechTarget, surveyed 100 executives from North American data-centre organisations.
The research found that:
96% identified cybersecurity as one of their most important supply-chain challenges.
Data-centre logistics leaders are prioritising security, visibility and resilience.
Delays affecting GPUs, servers and transformers can stall AI infrastructure deployment.
Physical security and chain-of-custody controls are becoming as important as transport performance.
Inventory visibility is increasingly linked to infrastructure commissioning schedules.
The findings point to a growing convergence between logistics,
cybersecurity
and operational technology. As data-centre equipment becomes more valuable, supply-chain providers must protect assets while maintaining accurate, real-time visibility across international and domestic movements.
DP World: “Every piece of equipment has to be accounted for”
DP World says its approach is intended to reduce handoffs between transport, storage, configuration and delivery teams.
“Every piece of equipment has to be accounted for, protected, and delivered at the right point in the deployment schedule. By combining global transportation with inventory visibility, configuration, secure handling, and specialized delivery, we can reduce handoffs and give customers greater control over infrastructure that is increasingly critical to their growth,” says Ya-Han.
The company’s expansion reflects a broader market requirement: data-centre logistics must now support speed, security, accuracy and technical readiness simultaneously.

title: Inspectorio: Building Data Foundations for Digital Passports
content:
Inspectorio: Building Data Foundations for Digital Passports
Prioritise Us
on Google
Inspectorio is focusing on building data foundations for digital passports. Credit: Inspectorio
Inspectorio is taking Digital Product Passports beyond the pilot stage, helping partners navigate throughout turbulence and ongoing supply chain disruption
Around the world, transparency is becoming a core driving force behind successful operations. It is both helping organisations avoid risk and building trust with a larger customer base.
Transparency, however, can be a complex
solution to enforce, particularly in large, physical supply chains which span a global network.
Digital Product Passports are a key way for leaders to gain transparency but organisations need strong partners in order to connect their data.
Inspectorio, therefore, helps connect traceability,
compliance and sustainability
with product data, supporting organisations in their journey to scale responsibly.
A problem to solve
Inspectorio was founded in order to overcome bottlenecks when dealing with overseas suppliers and third party inspections. Co-founders Carlos Moncayo, Fernando Moncayo, Luis Moncayo and David Klein decided to build a digital solution to streamline the inspections of goods around the world, with a focus on making the process more efficient and collaborative.
Since its early beginnings in 2016, the company has grown into a supply chain management platform, helping brands, retailers, suppliers and manufacturers to work across production chain operations with more efficiency.
The goal is to drive quality, responsible sourcing, production management, traceability and better supplier relationship management. In today’s complex world, this
type of oversight is critical
. Supply chains today are at their most vulnerable and intricate. They are battling ever-changing legislation, growing trade tensions, climate volatility,
cyber threats
and more.
Inspectorio is working to limit the impact of this.
“AI is making it possible for us to solve problems in ways we couldn’t have imagined before,” explains Antonio Leon de la Barra Rocha, Chief Operating Officer at Inspectorio on LinkedIn.
Antonio Leon de la Barra Rocha, Chief Operating Officer at Inspectorio
“And with new supply-chain disruption headlines every other week, the Production Chain has become a regular C-suite agenda item.”
At a glance
Inspectorio has enabled US$340bn in customer revenue
More than 40,000 retailers and suppliers around the world trust Inspectorio
Inspectorio has led to 68% reduction in compliance assessment cycle times
Teams powered by Inspectorio’s Paramo AI tool have seen a 7x lower product defect rate
One leading retailer in the UK saved 4,000 analyst hours every year by using Inspectorio RSC
Partnering for scale
In September, Inspectorio partnered with EON, a leader in enterprise Digital ID technology in order to help brands and retailers create and scale Digital Product Passports (DPPs). The partnership works because Inspectorio has the sustainability data, compliance needs, materials and suppliers required to populate a DPP, while EON creates and manages a serialised Digital ID.
EON then
powers the digital experience
which can then be shared with consumers, partners and other stakeholders.
Within the partnership, there is also an integration between the Inspectorio platform and EON Product Cloud. This allows for a streamlined capturing and management of product and supply chain information, meaning a direct flow from Inspectorio to EON.
Through the partnership, physical products are connected to trusted digital information. As a result, organisations are able to use compliance and connected products at scale. This adds an extra layer of safety for the users, and results in greater efficiency throughout operations.
Through the partnership, the companies will help brands move away from manually assembled DPP pilots and towards more integrated programmes, supporting millions of complex supply chains.
Inspectorio offers supply chain management solutions across a range of industries, including apparel, grocery, sports and outdoor. Business owners can maintain audit-ready documentation across the full sourcing chain, helping protect brand integrity.
Quality criteria can be standardised across diverse supplier networks, with the capability to spot compliance gaps early in the supply chain. This helps protect on-time delivery and customer expectations.
Inspectorio’s digital passport capabilities are helping organisations save time, brand stability and operate more efficiently
amid ongoing volatility
AI is making it possible for us to solve problems in ways we couldn’t have imagined before.
Antonio Leon de la Barra Rocha, Chief Operating Officer at Inspectorio

title: Top 10: Biggest Supply Chains
content:
Top 10: Biggest Supply Chains

Supply Chain Digital explores the companies with the biggest supply chains
Supply Chain Digital takes a look at the organisations operating the top 10 biggest supply chains in the world
The world’s largest companies manage extended supply chains, which often exposes them to unexpected geopolitical and regulatory changes.
The size of their supply chains also amplifies the impact of resilience, flexibility and the implementation of new technologies. These leading organisations require executives who are not just supply chain experts, but also experts in navigating disruption. The rise of agentic AI and the progressive introduction of autonomous operations is transforming supply chains just as surely as geopolitical fluctuations.
Here, Supply Chain Digital takes a look at the firms at the heart of the top 10 biggest supply chains, with rankings based on the size of their supply chains as well as their Gartner Supply Chain Top 25 ranking.
Schneider Electric's scale, expertise and AI-driven EcoStruxure platform set the standard for modern grid management. Credit: Schneider Electric
10. Schneider Electric
Revenue: US$47.16bn
Employees: 162,970
CEO: Olivier Blum
Founded: 1988
Schneider Electric has been upgrading its supply chain operations since 2024. Most recently it has integrated autonomous workforce capabilities and added an end-to-end resource orchestration platform across its operations. The company is also focused on adding generative and agentic AI to support human decision-making. Schneider expects the agentic and generative tools will improve real-time visibility and predictive insights across its value chain.
PepsiCo operates four production sites and four headquarters locations in Northern Europe. Credit: PepsiCo Northern Europe
9. PepsiCo
Revenue: US$98.24bn
Employees: 306,090
CEO: Ramon Laguarta
Founded: 1986
PepsiCo has built its business on maintaining supply chain discipline, but has extended its scope beyond inventory and order visibility. In recent years, PepsiCo has introduced supply chain orchestration functionalities, as it brings data from its multiple partners to permit real-time integrated business planning. The organisation has also introduced AI agents into its supply chain platform to enable faster responsiveness to improvements in the end-to-end visibility of its highly complex global supply chain.
Unilever operates a global network of factories as well as a global supplier chain. Credit: Unilever
8. Unilever
Revenue: US$57.1bn
Employees: 96,090
CEO: Fernando Fernandez
Founded: 1894
The multinational consumer goods operation has maintained a strict focus on working closely with its internationally diversified network of suppliers to responsibly source raw materials, packaging and other components for its products. Unilever has taken a proactive approach to responding to customer preferences, funding regenerative agriculture and committed to secure traceability and no deforestation.
Unilever has introduced AI-driven innovation tools to enable it to respond nimbly to volatile demand, while a disciplined focus on simplification and the progressive introduction of upskilling programs ensure its operations are resilient.
P&G produces goods in nearly 70 countries and sells them in more than 180. Credit: Procter & Gamble
7. Procter & Gamble
Revenue: US$87.03bn
Employees: 104,000
CEO: Shailesh Jejurikar
Founded: 1837
Procter & Gamble has retained its place among the largest supply companies to feature in our top 10 through its dedication to innovation and improvement. The organisation has also embraced advanced planning tools and real-time analytics to enable precise demand forecasting. Procter & Gamble integrates climate, waste, water and nature goals through its processes and products. The company is also adding agentic AI into workflows to support touchless operations.
Nestlé is the world's largest food and beverage company. Credit: Nestlé
6. Nestlé
Revenue: US$113.53bn
Employees: 271,000
CEO: Philipp Navratil
Founded: 1905
Nestlé is the world's largest food and beverage company and, as such, has a vast supply chain.
In recent years, Nestlé has invested heavily in new business models to improve end-to-end supply chain visibility, and to optimise operational benefits from the deployment of AI tools in its supply chain.
The company remains determined to cut carbon emissions and reach net zero by 2050 and updated its net zero aspirations in 2026, adding renewable electricity, waste and raw material goals.
5. Samsung Electronics
Revenue: US$235.65bn
Employees: 259,000
CEO: YoungHyun Jun/Tae Moon Roh
Founded: 1938
Recent changes in the East Asian markets for key inputs such as semiconductors, as well as other important inputs, have revealed the extent to which Samsung has been exposed to issues around regional supplier concentration and shifting regulatory conditions.
The company's deft navigation of these shifting conditions illustrates the flexibility and resilience of electronics giant Samsung's supply chain operations. Samsung has also been an early adopter of automated processes within its supplier network and within its logistics network and is examining the extension of agentic AI within its supply chain operations.
Toyota uses robots in its engine production processes, such as at its Deeside, UK site. Credit: Toyota
4. Toyota
Revenue: US$332.27bn
Employees: 390,930
CEO: Kenta Kon
Founded: 1937
Effective supply chain management is at the very core of Toyota’s operations strategy. The company has focused upon shared components, just-in-time discipline, and a tightly coupled supply ecosystem since the 1990s.
More recently, it has extended its partnership model to improve information sharing between suppliers and Toyota to improve end-to-end supply chain visibility.
Toyota endeavours to work as closely as possible with suppliers during the manufacturing process. Before conducting business transactions, it presents contracts that clearly spell out legal compliance, respect for human rights and environmental considerations.
Some of Apple's logic boards and advanced AI servers are produced and assembled in Houston, Texas. Credit: Apple
3. Apple
Revenue: US$466.82bn
Employees: 166,000
CEO: John Ternus
Founded: 1977
Consumer tech giant Apple is one of the world's most valuable companies. Apple has focused upon its supply chain since former CEO Tim Cook reduced the number of warehouses by half and established relationships with contract manufacturers in East Asia.
More recently, Apple has sought to accelerate its supplier diversification to reduce its reliance upon suppliers in East Asia. Within supplier factories, Apple is supporting the use of robotics and automation in supplier factories to improve throughput and lower assembly costs. Apple is also seeking to increase its reverse logistics network and material recovery network to improve secondary materials generation across the product life cycle.
Amazon's Shreveport fulfillment centre. Credit: Amazon
2. Amazon
Revenue: US$755.68bn
Employees: 1,600,000
CEO: Andrew Jassy
Founded: 1994
Founded back in 1994, Amazon started out as an online marketplace for books, but has since become a global leader in e-commerce, cloud computing, digital streaming and AI.
Over the years, the organisation has created a vast logistics infrastructure to support its marketplaces, ensuring fast and efficient product delivery from an array of fulfilment centres across the globe. The company is investing in the deployment of robots to augment distribution centre employees.
The Amazon Logistics business is built around last-mile delivery manned by a network of delivery drivers, including Amazon Flex drivers and independent contractors. The  rollout of electrification of Amazon’s vehicle fleet insulates Amazon’s network from energy volatility and cost uncertainty.
It uses advanced tracking systems to provide real-time package tracking and delivery updates to customers, and has introduced innovative delivery methods including physical AI to support delivery driver efficiency and safety, such as smart glasses to provide hands-free package scanning, navigation and proof of delivery.
Beyond retail, Amazon has diversified into B2B services. Amazon Web Services (AWS) is its cloud computing platform, offering computing capacity, storage, database management and AI.
Walmart's new Stockton fulfilment centre will allow it to offer next-day or two-day shipping to 95% of its US customer base. Credit: Walmart

Revenue: US$735.84bn
Employees: 2,100,000
CEO: John Furner
Founded: 1969
Walmart’s investments in infrastructure and ecommerce since 2022 have led to the introduction of more efficient fulfilment centres into its US operations.
Walmart’s investments in automation within distribution and fulfilment centres have benefited both its traditional bricks and mortar based operations as well as its increasingly important ecommerce business. Walmart estimates over 60% of US stores receive some freight via automated distribution centres, and over 50% of ecommerce fulfilment centre volumes pass through automated systems.
Walmart is also deploying Internet of Things technology within the retail sector, with the goal of improving pallet visibility and cold chain compliance through the use of automated alerts, reducing wastage and other losses.
Walmart is also seeking to improve data flows from suppliers as a step towards optimising network orchestration.

title: BackOps: Resolving Supply Chain Visibility Gaps End to End
content:
BackOps: Resolving Supply Chain Visibility Gaps End to End
Prioritise Us
on Google
BackOps aims to move away from supply chain visibility to supply chain resolution. Credit: Sean McCarthy
Supply chains platforms are becoming increasingly effective in unlocking visibility, but BackOps is working to shift insights into valuable resolution
In the past few years, it has been critical for supply chains to detect disruption in advance. With ongoing volatility, businesses have been looking to develop resilience in a variety of ways – many of them turning to AI and other predictive supply chain platforms.
Despite this, teams are still spending significant time gathering evidence and coordinating solutions.
In response,
BackOps is scaling
a resolution layer designed to extend workflow beyond predictions.
Solving bottlenecks
supply chains are a complex system
, with the movement of goods around the world and systems that rely on hundreds of people. Conditions change and legislation varies, resulting in the need to be agile and flexible. Teams need to have a coordination of plans and an ability to standardise and improve operations at any given point.
Issues include rising costs, customer demands, a growing skills gap and external pressures such as climate change and geopolitics makes it difficult to operate without disruption.
The best that teams can do is to ensure visibility across the entire organisation. For this, many of them are turning towards AI tools.
AI can synthesise information, relate to the team and make decisions on the company’s behalf. However, the AI tool – when developed as a general-purpose tool – does not have full visibility into the supply chain process or the means to improve an organisation’s outcomes. Teams still need to have oversight, capturing and connecting the process, define requirements and rules and ensure the tool is continuously working.
This results in an ongoing maintenance issue, slowed time to achieve meaningful value and a waste of resources.
To prevent this, BackOps has developed Relay, an AI-native operations platform which intimately learns internal processes.
“When Sean and I started building BackOps, we weren’t trying to add another dashboard to supply chain software. We wanted to solve a deeper problem,” Henry Ou, Co-Founder and CTO of BackOps says on LinkedIn.
Henry Ou, Co-Founder and CTO of BackOps
“Most supply chain tools are built to show you what’s wrong — delayed shipments, missing updates, unfiled claims. But the real work still falls to human operators who have to chase emails, call warehouses, file paperwork, and keep systems updated across dozens of tools. That’s not scalable, and it wasn’t keeping up with the volume of demand. So we built BackOps to do the work.”
At a glance
With BackOps, one customer has processed more than 500,000 claims, growing its monthly volume 150x
For another customer, BackOps reduced the average billing cycle from 28 hours to 14 minutes
BackOps has processed more than US$136m in claims in the last 10 months
Almost US$12bn in shipment value has been processed by BackOps in this period
With BackOps, teams can build 4-6x faster
Supply chain capabilities
In September 2026, BackOps announced a US$42m Series B, led by Insight Partners, with continued support from Theory Ventures, Construct Capital, Gradient Ventures and 10VC.
The platform identified what it has called the ‘Resolution Gap’ – the space between identifying what needs to happen and achieving that outcome. Historically, this has been closed manually, but BackOps is working to change this with AI.
The recent funding allows the company to
expand its product and engineering teams
, better supporting the enterprises relying on BackOps. Through this, it is building a system where every resolution in the system increases the understanding of the business, developing a powerful intelligence layer.
The announcement of its Series B funding came alongside a name change. The brand moved from BackOps AI, to BackOps, representing a shift in what the company is focusing on.
AI is still at the center
of everything we do, but we feel BackOps better reflects who we are, how our customers already know us and where we are headed as a company,” explains Sean McCarthy, Co-Founder and CEO at BackOps on LinkedIn.
Sean McCarthy, Co-Founder and CEO at BackOps
“We’ve been AI-native from day one, but what excites us most is the intelligence we’re building as BackOps gets deployed across more workflows, companies and eventually entire ecosystems. Every workflow creates more context and data, and as our distribution grows, so does the intelligence behind the platform.”
The Relay solution
BackOps, therefore, is distanced from control towers and copilots, as it has wider scope for controls and forecasting. Each deployment runs on two connected engines - one that learns how the operations work and another which
executes the work autonomously
Relay builds a complete model of how operations work, analysing ticket history, recording workflows and unveils processes that have previously been overlooked.
It turns this surfaced information into a prioritised automation plan and is trained on the company’s SOPs, exception patterns and approval rules. As a result, it handles work from start to finish, adapting to and absorbing new information from all types of workflow, such as SMS, email, Slack and Teams.
While Relay makes decisions and oversees the workflow autonomously, there is still a human-in-the-loop system. Leaders can decide where it runs on its own and where a human still has the final say, meaning that full oversight remains.
BackOps is in place to close the resolution gap, with growing capabilities to continuously improve.
Every workflow creates more context and data, and as our distribution grows, so does the intelligence behind the platform.
Sean McCarthy, Co-Founder and CEO of BackOps

title: Volkswagen recalls nearly 73,000 EVs due to faulty batteries
content:
Volkswagen
Volkswagen Group
Peter Johnson
| Oct 21 2026 - 6:56 am PT
Volkswagen
issued a recall affecting nearly 73,000 EVs globally. Until a remedy is available, VW will limit charging on impacted vehicles to 80% of their maximum battery capacity.
Which EVs are included in the Volkswagen recall?
After issuing
a recall with the NHTSA
earlier this month that impacts 22,524 ID.4 electric SUVs in the US, official information from the German Federal Motor Transport Authority (KBA) reveals several thousand more EVs are affected worldwide.
In three separate recalls now under investigation by the KBA, a total of 72,668 EVs are impacted worldwide, including 9,881 in Germany.
The recall affects certain batches of the ID. Buzz, ID.3, ID.4, and ID.7 models produced between 2022 and 2025, as well as Cupra Born models from 2022 to 2024.
Volkswagen issued the recall after an internal investigation found that some battery cells produced during that period do not meet specifications. The recall stems from a supplier defect.
In some instances, “certain charging profiles combined with a state of charge over 80% may trigger thermal propagation,” or a battery fire, Volkswagen said.
2025 Volkswagen ID. Buzz (Source: Volkswagen)
Until a remedy is available, Volkswagen is urging owners to limit charging to 80% of its max capacity. If technically possible, VW said: “the maximum available charging capacity will be temporarily limited to 80% by the system.”
In the US, Volkswagen
emailed owners
of vehicles included in the recall, saying that unless they opt out by October 21, it “intends to apply a temporary vehicle setting that limits charging to 80%.”
The update will be done remotely and reflected in the mobile app on or about October 27, 2026. Some owners have already received the update.
(Source: NHTSA)
Volkswagen is still working on a remedy. Letters informing owners of the risks are expected to be mailed out on November 27, 2026. Once the remedy is available, VW will send additional letters.
Owners can contact Volkswagen’s customer service at 1-800-893-5298 with questions or concerns. VW’s recall number is 93EX.
Those in the US can also contact the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration Vehicle Safety Hotline at 1-888-327-4236 or visit NHTSA.gov for more information. The NHTSA campaign number is 26V630.
The manufacturer’s recall codes with the
German KBA
are 93MV, 93MF, and 93W4 (for the Cupra Born).

title: LiveWire set to show off several new electric motorcycles next month
content:
Electric Motorcycles
LiveWire
Micah Toll
| Oct 21 2026 - 1:29 am PT
LiveWire is preparing to bring its biggest electric two-wheeler lineup yet to EICMA (Milan Motorcycle Show) next month, including a pair of previously unseen models that will offer a preview of where the electric motorcycle company is headed in 2027.
The company will exhibit alongside its majority shareholder Harley-Davidson at the massive Milan motorcycle show, running November 5-8, where its booth will span everything from STACYC electric balance bikes to the lightweight S4 Honcho platform and the more performance-oriented DUST family.
Perhaps the biggest surprise will be the first public appearance of the new S4 Honcho Skate. LiveWire hasn’t revealed much about the bike yet, other than confirming it will expand the Honcho family when it arrives in 2027. We won’t have to wait until EICMA for all the details, though, as LiveWire
preliminary specs and additional information will be released on November 2.
The Skate will join the
S4 Honcho Street and S4 Honcho Trail
, giving LiveWire a growing family of lightweight electric motorcycles built around its modular S4 platform. The production-ready Honcho Street will also make its European debut at EICMA before going on sale there immediately after the show. Its U.S. launch is scheduled for next week.
LiveWire is also continuing to flesh out its newly acquired DUST lineup. After
acquiring the assets
of Dust Moto earlier this year, LiveWire will show off a production-intent version of the DUST Hightail, which is targeting a 2027 introduction.
Alongside it will be another new model known as the DUST Spur, also planned for 2027. Like the Honcho Skate, details remain thin for now, with preliminary specifications coming November 2 and final production specs and pricing expected in the first quarter of next year.
The expanding lineup is particularly interesting because it shows just how far LiveWire is moving beyond the
premium full-size electric motorcycles
that defined the brand’s early years.
Between STACYC, the lightweight Honcho models, and the more dirt-focused DUST machines, LiveWire is increasingly building a ladder of electric two-wheelers aimed at riders across a much wider range of ages, experience levels, and budgets.
We’ll get a much better look at the newest rungs on that ladder in just a couple of weeks.

title: EBRD-led lenders back 1.2 GW solar, 600 MWh storage plant in Egypt - pv magazine Global
content:
Applications & Installations
A European development bank is arranging up to $265 million for a 1.2 GW solar plant with 600 MWh of storage in Egypt, as part of a debt package of up to $566 million.
Brian Publicover
21 Oct 2026
Applications & Installations
Energy Storage
Utility-scale
The European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) said it is arranging a loan of up to $265 million for Nefer Menya for Renewable Energy, the special purpose vehicle developing a 1.2 GW solar plant and 600 MWh battery energy storage system (BESS) in Minya, Egypt.
The EBRD loan consists of a $160 million A-loan from the bank’s own funds, a $75 million B-loan from Bank of Jordan and up to $30 million in concessional financing from the Climate Investment Funds’ Clean Technology Fund under its Global Energy Storage Program.
Bank of Jordan said it is participating as both a B-loan lender and original hedge counterparty. Germany’s DEG, the Dutch development bank FMO and France’s Proparco are co-financing the project as part of an aggregate debt package of up to $566 million, according to the EBRD.
The EBRD’s project disclosure puts the plant at 1,000 MW (AC) and total project cost at $764 million. AIKO said in June that it had been selected as sole module supplier, providing all-back-contact (ABC) modules for 1.2 GWp of capacity.
Nefer Menya is 51% owned by Infinity Power Holding and 49% by HAU Energy, according to the EBRD disclosure. Infinity Power is a joint venture of Egypt’s Infinity and Abu Dhabi’s Masdar, in which the EBRD holds an equity stake. HAU Energy is owned by Meridiam, Hassan Allam Utilities and the EBRD.
Electricity will be sold to Egyptian Electricity Transmission Co. under a 25-year power purchase agreement (PPA). The battery will store daytime solar output for use during peak demand after sunset, the EBRD said, describing the project as one of Egypt’s first to pair large-scale solar with battery storage.
Egypt’s cabinet granted the project a golden license in August, with completion scheduled for September 2027, Ahram Online reported.
“By combining solar generation with utility-scale battery storage, this project will strengthen the country’s energy security and enhance grid resilience,” said Aida Sitdikova, EBRD director of sustainable infrastructure in the Middle East and Africa. The EBRD said the facility is set to become the largest solar power plant in Egypt and Africa.
Infinity Power CEO Nayer Fouad said the company is working toward “10 GW of operational renewable energy capacity by 2032.” Hassan Allam Utilities CEO Dalia Wahba said Egypt aims to generate 42% of its electricity from renewable sources by 2030.
The project supports the energy pillar of Egypt’s Nexus of Water, Food and Energy (NWFE) program, which aims to facilitate 10 GW of new private-sector renewable capacity while retiring 5 GW of inefficient fossil-fuel generation, the EBRD said.
Egypt has been adding solar-plus-storage capacity to manage rising peak demand. In August, Scatec
completed its 1.1 GW Obelisk project
with 100 MW/200 MWh of battery storage, also selling power to Egyptian Electricity Transmission Co. under a 25-year PPA, with the EBRD among its senior lenders.
Egypt’s electricity ministry said in February it plans to bring
600 MW of battery storage online
before summer 2026.

title: New financing models needed for agrivoltaics - pv magazine Global
content:
Technology & Products
Speakers at the AgriVoltaics Industry Forum Europe 2026 say rising interest rates, uncertainty over electricity revenues and the need to ensure the long-term viability of farming are making agrivoltaic projects harder to finance.
Gwénaëlle Deboutte
21 Oct 2026
Markets & Policy
Technology & Products
Agrivoltaics
Highlights
Laetitia Limongi speaking at the AgriVoltaics Industry Forum Europe 2026
“Financing an
agrivoltaic project
is not simply a matter of financing a solar power plant. For banks, this hybrid asset must demonstrate its ability to generate electricity while maintaining a viable agricultural activity,” said Laetitia Limongi, renewable energy structured finance manager at Banque Populaire du Sud, speaking at the AgriVoltaics Industry Forum Europe 2026, held in Bordeaux, France, on October 13 and 14, 2026.
In a less favorable financial environment, this complexity is weighing on the bankability of projects and prompting stakeholders to seek new sources of revenue and capital.
Less predictable revenues
Rising interest rates are increasing the cost of debt, while investors can now choose between renewable energy projects and other investments, such as bonds, whose risk-adjusted returns may prove more attractive. Their return requirements are rising, potentially undermining the financial viability of some projects.
According to Jochen Hauff, founder of the Think Resiliency think tank, “reduced visibility over electricity revenues is adding to this pressure on financing.” He notes that “curtailment, periods of negative prices, difficulties connecting to the grid and regulatory changes make cash flows harder to predict.” On the agricultural side, meanwhile, rising diesel, fertilizer and labor costs are squeezing margins, while farmers must also finance their equipment.
Under these conditions, banks closely examine four criteria when assessing an agrivoltaic project: revenue predictability, the allocation of contractual responsibilities, the sustainability of the agricultural activity and the project’s resilience under adverse scenarios. A fall in revenue or an increase in operating costs must not jeopardize debt repayment.
Contract duration is also crucial. A 10- to 15-year power purchase agreement (PPA) does not offer the same level of certainty as a support tariff secured for 23 years.
“The more uncertain revenues are, the more lenders may require additional guarantees, reduce their exposure or increase financing costs. The limited track record of
agrivoltaic projects
reinforces this caution,” said Limongi. Without sufficient reference projects against which to compare actual performance and contractual models, banks have less data available to assess risk. This uncertainty can translate into higher interest rates and stricter financing conditions.
“Today, project financing largely relies on a combination of electricity revenues and commercial debt. By way of illustration, a typical model today might derive 80% of its revenue from tariffs or support mechanisms and 20% from PPAs or electricity sales on the market. On the financing side, the split would be 70% bank debt and 30% equity,” Hauff said.
Carbon and biodiversity as additional revenue streams
However, this structure becomes more fragile when debt becomes more expensive and revenues less predictable. Diversifying funding sources therefore offers a way to spread risk and attract new investors.
“A forward-looking model could reduce the share of revenue from support mechanisms to 50%, with 30% coming from electricity sales on the market and agricultural and environmental services accounting for 20%,” Hauff added. Financing could, in turn, incorporate 10% to 20% private debt, 40% to 50% bank debt and 30% to 40% equity.
Against this backdrop, one potential approach is for farmers to receive payment for the environmental services provided by their farms. Alongside selling their crops and, indirectly, the electricity generated, farmers could also monetize the ecological benefits of the practices implemented on their land.
“Soil carbon storage is one possibility,” explained the Think Resiliency founder. “Cover crops or planting hedgerows can contribute to this objective. Where the results are additional, measurable and verified against a recognized standard, they can generate carbon credits or certification, particularly under France’s Low-Carbon Label scheme.”
Other ecosystem services could also be eligible for payment, including biodiversity conservation, improved water quality, soil protection and wetland restoration. Public programs or certain ecological compensation mechanisms could create markets for these services.
Attracting new capital
“Specialist funds, impact investors and financial players are willing to pay for this kind of monetization of natural assets,” Hauff said. “These players can complement traditional bank financing, without replacing the requirements for profitability and risk management.”
Private debt offers another potential source of funding alongside bank loans and equity. However, regardless of the source of capital, the central question remains what the financing is backed by: who commits to paying, for how long and with what guarantees? An innovative business model is not enough if buyers have little track record or projected revenues rely on assumptions that are difficult to verify.
The priority now is to present credible cash-flow projections.
“As projects become more widespread and agricultural and energy performance are documented more thoroughly, banks will be able to refine their risk models and adjust their financing conditions,” Limongi concluded, offering reassurance to stakeholders across the sector.

title: Construction innovations could cut gigawatt-scale solar costs by 22% - pv magazine Global
content:
Research & Development
Research from Lightsource bp finds combining automated foundation piling, steel-frame solar panels, bolt-free solar module installations and on-site pre-assembly could also reduce installation time of gigawatt-sized solar farms by up to 30%.
Patrick Jowett
21 Oct 2026
Applications & Installations
Research & Development
Highlights
Utility-scale
The construction of gigawatt-sized solar farms could be transformed by adopting four technical innovations, according to research by
Lightsource bp
The UK-headquartered independent power producer (IPP) has shared findings from the investigation phase of its NextGen Solar Programme, which is reviewing how gigwatt-scale solar farms are built.
The programme is exploring how four areas of innovation – automated foundation piling, a frameless panel design that uses steel rather than aluminium, press-fit bolt-free module installations, and on-site pre-assembly – can reduce the costs and time required to construct gigawatt-sized solar farms.
Results from the initial investigation found combining these four construction innovations could cut direct installation costs by around 22% and reduce installation time by up to 30%, when compared with current standard practice.
Chris Buckland, Global Technical Director of Lightsource bp, told
pv magazine
the analysis is based on assessment of “newly-developed solar industry offerings from China, Europe and Northern America, with a focus on automation and novel installation method.”
Buckland added that a construction approach combining the four innovations is intended for large-scale PV development from 2028 onwards.
“It remains at the development stage but is expected to become relevant to major projects over the next three years,” he explained. “We plan to run trials in Australia and the United States to validate supplier data points and support technical assessment and bankability, with initial results targeted within the next 18 months.”
Lightsource bp’s analysis says automated piling rigs that use GPS precision can reduce installation time by up to 12.5%. Automated piling replaces manual pile driving, it adds, in turn lowering costs and improving consistency while also potentially reducing the risk of injury to site workers.
Additional analysis by the IPP says a press-fit, bolt-free solar module installation that enables solar panels to click into position has the potential to reduce installation time by up to 30% when combined with automated piling and a new module design.
“The solution aims to simplify module installation by replacing conventional clamps and bolts, delivering potential savings through reduced installation time and balance-of-system costs,” Buckland told
pv magazine
“We are also exploring replacing aluminium frames with steel options. Due to confidentiality requirements, we cannot provide the cost assessments.”
An additional statement from Lightsource bp explains its NextGen Solar Programme now moves from modelling and analysis into real-world validation, with trials on active projects including automated piling systems, robotic module placement and advanced cable harnessing solutions to verify cost, time and safety assumptions.
“We know that demand for solar energy is rising, and building for gigawatt scale is constrained by existing construction methods, impacting some projects commercial viability,” Buckland explained.
“The NextGen Solar Programme has delivered a practical, evidenced-based roadmap for scaling solar farm construction efficiently, and we are now moving to validate these solutions under real operating conditions.”

title: Türkiye allows higher-powered batteries behind existing grid connections - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
New rules boost possibilities for businesses beyond grid-connection allowance for imports, provided controls prevent grid exports and excessive imports.
Tristan Rayner
21 Oct 2026
Markets & Policy
Batteries
Energy Storage
Highlights
Türkiye has changed its rules to allow consumers to install batteries with more power than their contracted grid connection. They must still keep grid imports within the agreed limit and install controls to prevent electricity exports, but the ruling should free businesses to supply more power than their contracted grid limit.
The Energy Market Regulatory Authority (EPDK) published the changes on October 19, with immediate effect. Consumers still need approval from their grid operator, and the battery and consumption facility must use the same metering point.
Anyone installing a battery above their contracted power limit must fit automatic power controls and an electricity cut-off system. For businesses, this could allow batteries to supply extra power during short peaks in demand without exceeding the site’s grid import limit.
The change is strictly in battery power, measured in kW or MW, rather than capacity. A separate amendment has also allowed storage paired with license-exempt generation to be installed without an energy-capacity limit in kWh or MWh. Battery power must still remain at or below the generating plant’s electrical capacity, but developers can add more hours of storage.
Separate licensing changes published the same day cover financial guarantees for generation projects with storage. Developers will not receive their guarantees back until the entire generation facility is operating. For refunds relating to individual storage units, the amount will be based on the power of the units that have passed formal acceptance.
The changes come as Türkiye develops a substantial pipeline of wind and solar projects with battery storage. EPDK said in February that it had allocated approximately 33 GW to such projects under legislation introduced in 2022. At that point, 23 projects totaling around 1.07 GW had received generation licenses, with some 208 MW operating.

title: Zambia surpasses 1 GW solar milestone - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
Official figures from Zambia’s Ministry of Energy confirm the country’s solar capacity now stands in excess of 1 GW, up from 178 MW in 2024.
Patrick Jowett
21 Oct 2026
Applications & Installations
Markets & Policy
Highlights
Utility-scale
The 136 MW Itimpi II PV plant
Zambia’s cumulative solar capacity has surpassed 1 GW, according to figures published by the country’s Ministry of Energy.
Details on the ministry’s website confirm total solar capacity has risen from 178 MW in 2024 to 1,027 MW as of early October.
The milestone follows an update from early September which placed cumulative solar capacity at
. Additional projects have come online since, including the
100 MW Maamba solar energy project
built by a subsidiary of Indian conglomerate Nava Limited.
Zambia is currently one of Africa’s most dynamic solar markets, in part down to an ongoing
market liberalisation
that is making it one of the most attractive markets to private sector renewable energy developers. Other large-scale projects switched on this year include the
Itimpi II PV plant. In July, state-owned utility ZESCO
doubled the capacity
of its Chisamba solar power plant from 100 MW to 200 MW.
With the 1 GW solar target met, Zambia now turns its attention towards its longer-term goal of reaching 10 GW of installed electricity generation capacity by 2031. The most recent figures published by the Ministry of Energy put the country’s current installed electricity generation capacity at 4,722 MW, a 52.3% increase since 2021.
Speaking during the opening of the 2026 Energy Week Exhibitions in the Zambian town of Kabwe last week, Ministry of Energy Permanent Secretary, Ephraim Munshifwa, said Zambia’s expansion in electricity generation facilities is a result of the government’s response to drought conditions that reduced water levels in major reservoirs and triggered severe load shedding.
Munshifwa said investments in power generation and strategic reforms were aimed at developing long-term energy security, while adding that the national grid is now meeting demand of households and industries.
During this month’s Energy Forum for Africa Conference in Zambian capital Lusaka, Acting Minister of Energy, Situmbeko Musokotwane, said Zambia currently has “several energy projects at different stages of development”. He also said he was confident the 10 GW target would be achieved through partnerships.
The ministry’s official figures for solar capacity covers grid-connected utility-scale solar plants and installations made under the country’s net-metering scheme, which stood at around 30 MW as of September this year.
The Africa Solar Industry Association (AFSIA) has tracked 1,336 MW of operational solar projects in Zambia, according to figures from its project database, 538 MW of which is classified as commercial and industrial projects. The database adds a further 1,619.7 MW of solar projects are under construction across the country.

title: Fraunhofer silicon-rich cells retain over 83% after 1,000 cycles - pv magazine Global
content:
Research & Development
Researchers at Germany’s Fraunhofer ISE say their in-house silicon-rich anode pouch cells kept more than 83% of their capacity after more than 1,000 full cycles, but only under high mechanical pressure.
Brian Publicover
21 Oct 2026
Research & Development
Batteries
Energy Storage
Fraunhofer ISE said it has cycled 25 Ah pouch cells with silicon-rich anodes more than 1,000 times, with the cells retaining over 83% of their original capacity at a cell-level gravimetric energy density of 280 Wh/kg.
The 40-layer cells were built on a semi-automatic production line in the cleanroom of the institute’s Center for Electrical Energy Storage in Freiburg, Germany, using commercially available electrode foils. They pair a silicon-carbon/graphite anode with a nickel-rich nickel-manganese-cobalt (NMC) cathode. The silicon-carbon composite made up 51% of the anode active material, and the anodes reached a specific capacity of more than 1,000 mAh/g and an areal capacity of more than 5 mAh/cm².
“Cycle life is one of the key hurdles to the widespread industrial use of silicon-rich anodes,” said Lukas Dold, team leader for battery materials technology and scaling at Fraunhofer ISE. “More than 1,000 cycles with a capacity retention of at least 80 percent is considered an important performance target here.”
The cell-level 280 Wh/kg was achieved in the institute’s non-optimized PrecISE research cell format. Dold said an industrially optimized pouch format is expected to reach about 330 Wh/kg.
Pressure dependence
The researchers cycled the cells at 1C at two axial contact pressures, 300 kPa and 1,000 kPa. The 83% retention figure applies to cells held at 1,000 kPa.
“At a lower contact pressure of 300 kPa, a significantly greater decline in usable capacity over time is observed, particularly during 1C operation,” said Marc Kissling, group leader for battery cell production and technology evaluation. “Mechanical cell pressure is therefore an important parameter for the stable operation of silicon-rich pouch cells.”
Fraunhofer ISE did not publish a retention figure for the 300 kPa cells. It also reported that as the cells aged, capacity measured in periodic check-ups at low discharge rates increasingly diverged from the capacity available during regular 1C cycling. The institute said performance under real-world operating conditions must be considered alongside capacity retention when evaluating silicon-rich cells.
Silicon’s theoretical specific capacity is 10 times that of graphite, and Fraunhofer ISE said silicon-carbon composites could reduce global dependence on graphite and shift raw-material value creation toward the European Union.
The StrOboBatt project is led by PCC Thorion with Fraunhofer ISE and Glatt Ingenieurtechnik, with LG Chem Europe, E-Lyte Innovations and UniverCell Holding among its partners. It received €2.6 million in federal funding and is scheduled to run for three years, PCC said when the project launched in 2024. The partners cited stationary storage of surplus solar and wind power as a target application, along with electric mobility and aerospace.
Other silicon-carbon anode developers are moving toward commercial scale. In July, the Australian Renewable Energy Agency (ARENA) awarded up to AUD 45 million ($31.6 million) to Himadri-backed Sicona for a
commercial-scale demonstration plant
at BlueScope Steel’s Port Kembla precinct in New South Wales. ARENA said Sicona’s material could raise lithium-ion energy density by up to 20% and enable charging up to 40% faster than conventional graphite anodes.

title: India’s solar industry faces a test of durability and cost - pv magazine Global
content:
Technology & Products
As India’s solar industry matures, manufacturing competitiveness will depend on consistent quality, sustained energy generation and competitive lifecycle costs, not just capacity additions and module prices.
Hardip Singh, COO of GREW Solar
21 Oct 2026
Technology & Products
Commercial & industrial
Residential
Utility-scale
As per the Ministry of New and Renewable Energy, India’s installed solar capacity reached 171.05 GW on 30 September 2026. As the country continues to scale its clean energy infrastructure, the next challenge will be to ensure that this capacity provides reliable power for decades to come. The industry’s success will gradually depend not just on how quickly solar projects are built, but on the quality of the assets being installed.
For developers and investors, durability has direct financial implications. Since solar PV installations are generally designed to operate for 25 years, long-term reliability and warranty coverage are essential. Ensuring that modules are manufactured at the facilities declared by producers is equally important for verifying product authenticity, protecting consumer interests and safeguarding India’s energy security. While lower purchase prices can improve initial project economics, consistent quality and dependable performance remain critical to protecting returns over a plant’s operating life
Real costs
A module’s purchase price represents only one part of its overall cost. Its long-term performance affects power generation, project income, and ROI. Over the lifetime of a solar power plant, cumulative generation can be impacted by slight variations in annual degradation, or a slow reduction in power output.
Indian installations face diverse conditions, from intense summer heat and dust to humidity, heavy rainfall and strong winds. These constantly apply pressure on the glass, encapsulants, frames and electrical connections of the modules. If manufacturing processes or materials are modified to cut costs, failures may not appear for years after installation when repairs and replacements can be more expensive.
Recent industry reporting has highlighted concerns about the mechanical durability of solar modules. In the second quarter of 2025, mechanical stress sequence testing detected glass breakage in around one-third of the modules that were tested. Even though these laboratory results did not represent failure rates across the wider market, they did stress upon structural reliability. Thinner glass, bigger module formats and minimized safety margins could increase durability risks, making material quality and component compatibility central considerations along with efficiency ratings.
Production
The life of a module is affected by many elements such as the quality of the manufacturing, how it is transported, installed and used. But production is where the basis for long-term reliability is built. Consistent raw material quality, controlled lamination, reliable sealing and meticulous assembly provide structural integrity. Thus, quality control must be applied during the making process and not just at final inspection.
High production standards can go hand-in-hand with competitive price. Manufacturers can control costs without sacrificing product quality by increasing production yields, minimizing waste of materials, automating key operations and tightening supplier audits. Traceability also helps to identify defects before products reach customers.
India’s regulatory system is a crucial basis for quality assurance. The Ministry of New and Renewable Energy’s Approved List of Models and Manufacturers (ALMM) specifies approved models and manufacturers for certain project categories. Applicable quality control criteria also help in conformity to Indian Standards. Compliance, however, is simply the beginning. Independent testing, documented quality checks and unambiguous certification records help to establish product reliability. Developers should evaluate long-term project risks by considering test reports, supplier credentials, warranty conditions and traceability.
Efficiency and reliability
The adoption of advanced cell technologies such as n-type tunnel oxide passivated contact (TOPCon), is also adding another aspect to module selection. The higher conversion efficiency implies that more power can be generated from a given area, making the technology suited for large solar parks and installations where space is at a premium. It may also have benefits on temperature performance and degradation rates depending on the module design.
However, higher efficiency at the time of purchase does not automatically translate into effective long-term returns. The extended value of TOPCon technology depends on how well a module maintains its power output over time. Developers should thus measure the expected energy yield and degradation alongside initial power ratings when estimating a project’s economics.
For manufacturers, that means looking at technology not just for what the output will be when it’s new, but what value it can maintain over time. Improvements in cell architecture must translate into dependable generation under real operating conditions. Ultimately, efficiency creates lasting value when it helps a solar plant maintain higher energy output with consistent performance.
As India’s solar industry matures, manufacturing competitiveness will depend on consistent quality, sustained energy generation and competitive lifecycle costs, not just capacity additions and module prices.
India’s Panchamrit commitments which include 500 GW of non-fossil fuel-based energy capacity by 2030 and net-zero emissions by 2070, point to the extent of its clean-energy ambitions. Simultaneously, the PM Surya Ghar: Muft Bijli Yojana is supporting wider rooftop solar adoption.  Meeting these aspirations demand durable solar assets that keep performance losses down, manage maintenance costs and offer reliable power for decades. Long-term durability will be essential to making solar energy affordable and reliable.
