title: Hoymiles releases a 2,000 kWh C&I energy storage solution - pv magazine Global
content:
Technology & Products
Chinese manufacturer Hoymiles has launched a C&I battery storage system with capacities ranging from 2 MWh to 2.61 MWh and power outputs of up to 1.25 MW. The containerized system features liquid cooling, integrated fire protection, and backup power switching in less than 20 ms.
Lior Kahana
21 Oct 2026
Technology & Products
Commercial & industrial
Energy Storage
HoyUltra 2000M
Chinese solar and energy storage manufacturer
Hoymiles
has unveiled a new commercial and industrial (C&I) energy storage system with capacities starting at 2 MWh, higher than those typically offered in the segment.
The new HoyUltra 2,000M is available in 15 configurations, with storage capacities ranging from 2 MWh to 2.61 MWh. Rated AC output ranges from 500 kW to 1.25 MW, with configurations supporting AC voltages of 380/400 V, 690 V, and 800 V. The system uses 314 Ah lithium iron phosphate (LFP) cells from an undisclosed supplier.
“As C&I energy storage projects become more diverse, customers need solutions that go beyond storage capacity,” said Rex Zhu, general manager of Hoymiles’ Residential and C&I Energy Storage Business. “Electrical conditions, installation requirements, multi-energy integration, backup power, and operating environments all need to be taken into account.”
The system integrates batteries, a power conversion system (PCS), thermal management, a static transfer switch (STS), and fire protection equipment. The STS enables switching to backup power in less than 20 ms to maintain an uninterrupted power supply.
“The system uses liquid cooling for both the PCS and the battery, with an operating temperature range of -30 C to 55 C,” the company said. “It maintains its rated power up to 50 C. It is also equipped with a cabinet-level fire protection system, including smoke and temperature detection, fire suppression, interlocked ventilation and an explosion pressure relief device for the compartment.”
All configurations measure 6,058 mm × 2,591 mm × 2,438 mm and weigh between 22,700 kg and 26,000 kg. The containerized systems feature an IP55 ingress protection rating and C5 corrosion resistance and can operate at altitudes of up to 2,000 meters.

title: Novel PV recycling method removes EVA at 9 grams per second - pv magazine Global
content:
Research & Development
Researchers in China have developed a preheating-assisted mechanical polishing process to remove ethylene-vinyl acetate (EVA) encapsulants from end-of-life solar modules. The technique reportedly achieves an EVA recovery rate of 99% and a removal rate of 9 g/s, while preserving the integrity of silicon wafers.
Lior Kahana
21 Oct 2026
Research & Development
Raw Materials
A research team in China has developed a novel preheating-assisted mechanical polishing process to separate ethylene-vinyl acetate (EVA) encapsulants from end-of-life photovoltaic modules. The researchers built an adjustable experimental platform to systematically investigate the effects of key processing parameters on EVA removal and recovery.
“The process efficiency, in terms of EVA removal rate and recovery rate, will be systematically evaluated by investigating the effects of three key parameters: preheating temperature, polishing head speed, and tool penetration depth,” the researchers said. “An experimental production line platform has been constructed to enable precise control of these variables.”
The researchers used decommissioned monocrystalline silicon modules consisting of front glass, EVA encapsulant, silicon solar cells, rear EVA encapsulant, and a polymer backsheet. After removing the aluminum frames and junction boxes, they heated the backsheets to 250 C and peeled them off with a scraper to expose the rear EVA layer.
They then processed the modules using a custom-built, three-axis computer numerical control (CNC) polishing platform equipped with resistance heating and force-feedback systems to maintain a constant load.
The experiments covered preheating temperatures ranging from 150 C to 250 C, polishing head speeds of 500 rpm to 4,000 rpm, and tool clearances of 0 mm to 0.5 mm. The researchers calculated EVA removal rates and recovery rates based on mass measurements and processing times.
They also used thermal analysis to identify suitable processing temperatures, while microscopy and spectroscopy were employed to assess surface damage, contamination, and the chemical integrity of the recovered EVA. All experiments were performed in triplicate.
“Systematic investigation of the key parameters—preheating temperature, rotational speed, and tool penetration depth—established an optimal process window: 200 C, 1000 rpm, and a 0.25 mm tool offset,” the researchers said. “Under these conditions, the process achieved a high delamination efficiency of 9 g/s and an exceptional EVA recovery rate of 99%, while preserving smooth, undamaged silicon wafer surfaces.”
The researchers found that the recovered EVA formed cohesive chunks that could be readily collected and subjected to further processing. They said the proposed technique offers potential environmental advantages over conventional thermal and chemical dissolution methods by avoiding toxic emissions and chemical waste.
They also noted that the process could improve material recovery by preserving the integrity of both the silicon wafers and the EVA encapsulant.
“Crucially, pilot-scale validation has demonstrated that this preheating-assisted mechanical strategy is universally applicable; it is equally effective for both mono-facial and bi-facial modules, as well as for the challenging removal of front-side EVA,” the researchers concluded.
The researchers described the technique in “
Efficient delamination of back-side EVA from retired photovoltaic modules via preheating-assisted mechanical polishing
,” published in
Solar Energy Materials and Solar Cells
The research team included scientists from China’s
Nanjing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics
, Anhui University of Applied Technology, Ycergy (Suzhou) Technology, and Wuxi Institute of Inspection.

title: Peru proposes reviving power interconnection with Chile to tap its solar generation - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
Peru is seeking to revive electricity interconnection talks with Chile to facilitate cross-border power exchanges and make better use of Chile’s surplus solar and wind generation. A proposed 1,000 MW transmission link would require an estimated investment of $550 million.
Luis Ini
21 Oct 2026
Markets & Policy
Americas
Utility-scale
The Peruvian government has proposed resuming talks with Chile on the interconnection of their electricity grids, a project that could facilitate the use of Chilean solar and wind power while taking advantage of the complementary nature of Peru’s natural gas and hydropower resources.
The announcement was made by Peru’s Minister of Energy and Mines, Guillermo Shinno, during the 21st meeting of the Chile-Peru Business Council, recently held in Lima. Shinno noted that electricity integration is part of Commitment 21 of the Santiago Action Plan and expressed his intention to meet with Chilean Energy Minister Ximena Rincón to advance discussions.
“The interconnection with Chile is on the agenda. It is a matter of seeing when we can meet with the Chilean energy minister to move this objective forward. If it does not happen before November, I imagine we will discuss it on Nov. 29 at the Peru-Chile binational meeting,” Shinno said.
One of the options under consideration is a 500 kV transmission line with a capacity of 1,000 MW connecting Montalvo, in southern Peru, with Kimal, in northern Chile.
According to a study commissioned by the Inter-American Development Bank (IDB) in 2025, the project would require an estimated investment of $550 million. The study found that bidirectional electricity exchanges could reach between 3,600 GWh and 5,700 GWh annually, generating combined economic benefits averaging $170 million per year.
The complementary nature of the two countries’ electricity generation mixes was a key consideration in the study. Chile has substantial solar and wind generation capacity, particularly in the north, while Peru has hydropower resources and natural gas-fired power plants that could supply electricity during periods of lower renewable energy generation in Chile.
For Chile, the interconnection would also provide an additional outlet for surplus solar generation, which currently faces transmission constraints limiting its delivery to major demand centers.
As previously reported, solar and wind power curtailment in Chile reached 2,680 GWh between January and July 2026. Exporting some of this electricity to Peru could help reduce curtailment, although the extent of such exchanges would depend on available transmission capacity and operating conditions in both countries.
Peru has also significantly increased its solar power generation. According to data from the Ministry of Energy and Mines, solar generation reached 1,442 GWh in the first half of 2026, up 87% year on year. Much of the country’s installed PV capacity is concentrated in the southern regions, particularly Arequipa and Moquegua.
Meanwhile, Chilean company EnorChile Transmission submitted an environmental impact statement for the Los Héroes-Parinacota transmission line project to Chile’s Environmental Assessment Service (SEA) on Oct. 13.
Unlike the Montalvo-Kimal proposal, the project involves an estimated investment of $30 million and the construction of approximately 22 km of transmission line on Chilean territory, connecting the Parinacota substation in Arica to the Peruvian border. From there, the line would extend to the Los Tacéro substation in Peru.
The proposed infrastructure would have a maximum transmission capacity of 250 MVA and include a converter substation to accommodate the different operating frequencies of the two national grids.
Despite renewed interest in cross-border electricity integration, the proposed 1,000 MW interconnection has yet to secure a final investment decision or construction schedule. Its development will depend on technical, regulatory and commercial agreements between the two countries.

title: 'Smoking gun' helps unlock mystery of high-temp superconductivity
content: Physicists have identified the microscopic mechanism that allows electric current to flow through electron-doped high-temperature copper oxides without losing power. A new study by a team led by the University of Bristol confirms that fluctuating electron spins enable electrons to pair up and transmit electricity with zero resistance.To isolate the mechanism, researchers from the UK, the Netherlands, China, and the U.S. built an artificial thin-film sample out of lanthanum cerium copper oxide. They deposited the material onto a base layer by atomic layer. Along the strip, they gradually replaced lanthanum with cerium. This substitution introduced extra conduction electrons and formed a smooth gradient of critical transition temperatures. This shifted the critical superconducting point from its highest value down to zero across a single sample.Suppressing the superconducting state“Using lithography, the researchers then patterned a series of electrical contacts along the film,” explained a media release. This design allowed them to test areas with different critical temperatures while keeping material disorder identical throughout the sample.Next, the researchers placed the film inside high-powered magnets at the European Magnetic Field Laboratory in the Netherlands. They used strong magnetic fields to suppress the superconducting state and recorded how resistance changed across temperatures, field strengths, and critical points.“The processes which facilitate higher temperature superconductivity, however, have remained a source of mystery and fascination,” said study co-lead author Nigel Hussey, Professor of Physics at the University of Bristol.“Through measurements carried out at the European Magnetic Field Laboratory in the Netherlands and subsequent careful analysis, we have found the smoking gun which solves part of the equation and explains what causes this perplexing state.”Uncovering source of frictionAnalysis of this resistance data uncovered the primary source of electrical friction. The electrons were scattering directly off fluctuating electron spins. Because the strength of this interaction closely matched the critical transition temperature along the strip, the team confirmed that spin fluctuations cause the superconducting state in this material.However, the team emphasizes that this discovery solves only one part of the wider problem.Parent copper-oxide materials can be turned into superconductors in two separate ways. The first method adds extra electrons, which the researchers achieved here by using cerium. The second method removes electrons, leaving behind empty spaces called holes.The highest transition temperatures occur exclusively in hole-doped materials. When the Bristol-led team compared their new data with earlier high-field studies on hole-doped samples, they found that spin interactions alone could not account for the higher performance. Although the two materials share the same chemical base, their internal arrangements differ. The researchers concluded that a second, unknown factor must work alongside spin fluctuations to produce the higher operating temperatures on the hole-doped side.Critical for next-gen technologiesThe finding marks a clear break from older, conventional superconductors. In those low-temperature metals, the pairing of electrons relies on slow vibrations of ions in the crystalline lattice. High-temperature copper oxides require much faster interactions, which electron spins provide.Resolving the full mechanism remains critical for advancing technologies that rely on zero resistance. These systems are used to build powerful magnets for medical imaging scans, efficient power cables, and ultra-sensitive measuring equipment. “While we have found the first key ingredient, the task now is to go and find the second,” concluded Prof Hussey. “Only then can theorists develop the full story for high-temperature superconductivity.”The study was published in the journal Nature Physics.

title: Hidden lithium clusters could hold key to longer-lasting batteries
content: Lithium ions in battery electrolytes do not always remain isolated. Research from Columbia University shows they often form clusters without anions. It revealed a structural feature that challenges long-held assumptions about lithium-ion battery chemistry.The study combines machine learning simulations with experimental validation to examine the atomic-scale structure of these electrolytes. Its findings could guide electrolyte designs for higher-capacity, faster-charging, and longer-lasting batteries.The research was co-led by Richard Friesner of Columbia’s Department of Chemistry and Alexander Urban, Lauren Marbella, and Daniel Steingart of Columbia Engineering.Lithium ions form unexpected clustersElectrolytes are crucial to battery performance and help drive the formation of the solid electrolyte interphase, a protective film on the battery anode. This film influences battery lifespan and safety, but understanding how electrolyte structure affects its formation has remained difficult.To investigate that structure, the researchers used machine-learning force-field technology from Schrödinger, Inc., with additional support from the New York Structural Biology Center. The approach let them simulate battery electrolytes more accurately and at a larger scale.The simulations revealed that up to 40% of lithium ions in standard battery electrolytes form multi-ion clusters.Clustering became more prevalent at higher salt concentrations, challenging the assumption that lithium ions remain predominantly isolated in solution.“We discovered lithium ions in batteries actually group together into clusters in the absence of anions, and that these clusters are what drive the creation of the protective film on the battery’s surface,” said Friesner, William P. Schweitzer Professor of Chemistry.Experiments support the simulationsThe team compared its simulations with a wide range of condensed-phase experimental data. Strong agreement between the two supported the physical reality of the predicted lithium clusters.Theoretical analysis came from the Columbia and Schrödinger teams, while Columbia Engineering contributed the experimental work.“While the most novel aspect of the paper is the theoretical simulations, the experimental work confirming the results was essential and extremely difficult to execute,” added Professor Friesner.Friesner, who is also a co-founder and member of Schrödinger’s board of directors, emphasized the importance of combining computational predictions with experimental confirmation.“Predicting this unexpected chemistry computationally and confirming it experimentally demonstrates that we can accurately model the hidden atomic details of batteries,” he said.Clues to protective film formationQuantum chemical calculations indicated that the multi-lithium clusters have particularly favorable reduction potentials. These results suggest that the clusters are key intermediates in forming the solid electrolyte interphase.That connection gives researchers a clearer basis for investigating how electrolyte chemistry influences the protective film and, in turn, battery performance.The findings provide a foundation for designing next-generation electrolytes with improved performance, stability, and charging rates.Those improvements remain potential applications of the research, rather than demonstrated battery gains reported in the supplied material.“It’s a reminder – and an exemplary example – of how advances in AI-driven simulation need to be coupled closely to experiments,” Friesner said. “Ultimately, that will allow us to accelerate our progress in solving problems in biology and materials science, including making better, longer-lasting batteries,” he added. Gates Ventures provided funding for the research. The study was published in the Nature journal.

title: Lockheed Martin fires Spike NLOS missiles from Army’s ISV-U vehicle for first time
content: Lockheed Martin has completed a live-fire demonstration of its Spike Non-Line-of-Sight (NLOS) missile system mounted on a light tactical vehicle. It shows how US Army infantry units could gain long-range precision-strike capabilities without depending on heavier missile-launching platforms.The three-day demonstration took place at Dugway Proving Grounds in Utah and involved 17 precision engagements against simulated operational targets at different combat ranges. According to Lockheed Martin, most of the shots were conducted by US Army infantry soldiers, with every missile launched from the Infantry Squad Vehicle–Utility (ISV-U).With a ground-launch range of about 30 km (19 miles), the missile far surpasses the reach of the standard shoulder-fired Javelin.The test marked the first time the Spike NLOS missile had been fired from the ISV-U platform. It also advances the Army’s Mobile Long-Range Precision Strike Missile (M-LRPSM) requirement, which aims to provide mobile brigade combat teams with a ground-based capability to strike targets beyond the operator’s direct line of sight.Turning a light vehicle into a missile platformThe ISV-U is a utility variant of the Army’s Infantry Squad Vehicle, a lightweight tactical vehicle designed to transport soldiers across challenging terrain. Integrating the Spike NLOS system could give infantry formations a mobile precision-strike option while allowing them to operate without the footprint of larger, dedicated missile-launching vehicles.Spike NLOS is designed to engage targets beyond the launch platform’s direct line of sight. This lets operators attack targets that may be obscured by terrain or otherwise difficult to engage with conventional line-of-sight weapons.The system is part of a broader effort to give ground forces greater reach and flexibility on the battlefield. A mobile launcher could allow units to reposition between engagements and support troops operating across dispersed areas, although the precise configuration and operational performance of the ISV-U integration have not yet been fully disclosed.Lockheed Martin said the demonstration showed that soldiers could safely employ the missile from the vehicle and complete training and live-fire missions within the same week. The company did not disclose the specific engagement distances or provide a detailed breakdown of the targets used during the trials.Soldier feedback will shape Army requirementsThe demonstration is also part of the Army’s Transformation in Contact (TIC) initiative, which puts emerging capabilities into soldiers’ hands early so that their feedback can inform future equipment requirements.According to Lockheed Martin, TIC units were among the first soldiers to handle the system during the demonstration. Their observations, combined with live-fire data, will help the Army refine the requirements for M-LRPSM and determine how the capability should be integrated into its formations.“This demonstration represents a critical milestone for Spike NLOS, showing that our infantry partners can confidently employ a long-range precision missile,” said Casey Walsh, program director for Lockheed Martin’s Multi-Domain Missile Systems. He added that the test data and soldier feedback would support the development of final requirements and the eventual fielding process.The company said the demonstration builds on earlier Phase 1 and Phase 2 milestones. Further validation testing is planned over the next year before Phase 3, when initial operational production is expected to begin, and final system prototypes will be delivered to the Army.For the Army, the value of the system lies in combining long-range precision weapons with a relatively lightweight ground platform. Such a capability could give mobile brigade combat teams more options for engaging high-value targets without bringing heavier launchers closer to the fight.

title: Battery-powered drone reaches 483 mph in test to set new speed record
content: German drone maker Quantum Systems announced that its battery-powered experimental drone reached 483 mph (777 km/h) during a record attempt. The flight could mark a new speed milestone for battery-electric drones, though the result has not yet been officially confirmed.The company is developing technologies for uncrewed aircraft, including systems intended to counter fast-moving aerial threats. The latest test also provides an opportunity to evaluate the performance and limitations of electric propulsion at high speeds. Quantum Systems said the lessons learned from the attempt will inform its ongoing drone development.Electric flight breakthroughQuantum Systems said its battery-powered Apex Recordhunter experimental aircraft reached 483 mph during a speed record attempt. The result exceeds the speed the company reported during an earlier test in June, when the drone reached 434 mph (699 km/h) in straight and level flight.The latest run has not yet established an official record, as the aircraft must complete a return flight to account for wind effects. However, the test provides further data on the performance of battery-electric propulsion systems at high speeds.The Apex Recordhunter was developed by Quantum Systems’ experimental N3XT team in Germany over approximately a year. Rather than serving as an operational aircraft, it functions as a technology demonstrator, allowing engineers to test propulsion, energy management, and high-speed flight performance.Quantum Systems applies Apex’s propulsion and flight lessons to interceptor development, though the drone shares no combat hardware.During its June test, the Apex reached 434 mph, a figure Quantum Systems described as an unofficial world-best for a battery-electric flying object. The company said the aircraft used special battery cells developed by a Porsche subsidiary, although it has not disclosed detailed specifications for the battery pack, motor, or propulsion system.The latest flight pushed the reported speed to 483 mph, or more than 656 feet (200 meters) per second. Such performance makes energy management a key engineering consideration, as the aircraft must deliver sufficient power while maintaining stable flight at high speeds.The company has not provided detailed measurements of the aircraft’s energy consumption, battery capacity or flight duration. It has also yet to confirm the record through the required return leg.Drone tech aids interceptorsQuantum Systems revealed that the technology developed through the Apex project could support its work on interceptor drones designed to counter faster aerial threats. The company has highlighted Russia’s jet-powered Geran drones, which can reportedly reach speeds of 311 to 373 mph (500 to 600 km/h).According to the firm, the increasing speed of these aircraft has created a need for faster interception systems. The company says its experience with electric propulsion, energy management, and high-speed flight is informing this development. However, the Apex Recordhunter itself is not a weapon, and Quantum Systems says it does not share hardware with its combat systems.The company’s interceptor work involves WIY Drones, a Kyiv-based manufacturer working with Quantum Systems through a joint venture called Quantum WIY Industries. Quantum Systems has secured an order for 15,000 Strila interceptor drones from WIY for Ukraine’s National Guard.Quantum Systems, based near Munich, is also known for its Vector reconnaissance drone, which is widely used by Ukraine’s military. The company closed a $1.2 billion funding round this year, providing additional financial backing for its defense technology activities.While the Apex project’s immediate achievement is its reported speed, its broader purpose is to generate engineering data that can be applied to future aircraft. The next flight will determine whether the drone’s latest performance can be formally recognized as a record.

title: Particle colliders recreate matter that existed microseconds after the Big Bang
content: Scientists at the Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider (RHIC) at the Brookhaven National Laboratory in the US have successfully generated quark-gluon plasma (QGP) by smashing oxygen nuclei at nearly the speed of light. QGP is the type of matter that existed in the first few microseconds just after the universe was born and helps physicists determine how protons, neutrons, and atoms were first formed. Studying the QGP can also help scientists understand other phenomena in physics, such as the limits of nuclear stability and the search for exotic particles like X-particles.However, since QGP only lasted for a few microseconds even after the Big Bang, it is difficult for scientists to observe it directly, even inside particle colliders like RHIC or the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) at CERN. So, The only way for scientists to know if QGP is formed is to study particles flying out of collisions of nuclei using detectors like the Solenoidal Tracker at RHIC or the STAR detector. “One of the most powerful ways scientists study the QGP is by identifying where its signatures appear — and just as importantly, where these signatures turn off,” said Li Yi, a professor of physics at Shandong University involved in the work. Researchers have previously found that energetic jets of particles lose their energy when they travel through the hot, dense matter left after nuclei collide inside a particle smasher. This is called jet quenching and is considered a signature of QGP formation. What is jet quenching? When heavier nuclei like gold are smashed into each other by a particle collider, their boundaries collapse, and their protons and neutrons are set free as constituent elements of quarks and gluons.These collisions follow Einstein’s famous equation of E=mc2 and release energy accordingly. Since this QGP formed is smaller than the size of the nuclei themselves, researchers use detectors to spot other particles that fly out as a result of these nuclei collisions. However, in their observations, researchers have found that some particles emerge from these collisions with less energy than expected, as though they were stuck behind quarks and gluons of the plasma. To understand this further, researchers study jets of energy that are released when a nucleus containing a single quark or gluon in its nucleus collides with another containing a single quark or gluon in its nucleus. Such a collision produces two jets of energetic particles near the edge of the collision zone and helps researchers study the QGP by observing the loss of energy of these particles. This quenching of the jets is critical in understanding the QGP, while also being a telltale sign of its existence. Studying oxygen collisionsResearchers at RHIC had observed jet quenching in gold-gold collisions. With 78 protons and 118 neutrons, these are relatively large nuclei, and lower-energy particles emerging from these collisions were found to move collectively, like a perfect liquid with no resistance. The researchers wondered if similar observations would be made if they worked with a system that contained nuclei of lighter elements like oxygen. With just eight protons and eight neutrons in each colliding nucleus, oxygen offers a simpler system for observing jet quenching than heavy nuclei like gold or lead. Using data from oxygen-oxygen collisions conducted at 200 billion electron volts (GeV) at RHIC in 2021, the team found 20 percent suppression of high-energy particles due to jet quenching. While lower than the gold and lead counterparts, the suppression is still proof of QGP formation. Because researchers at the LHC have also studied oxygen-oxygen collisions, the RHIC team could compare its findings with those of CERN researchers. “We are pushing the boundaries in two ways to explore the minimal conditions for creating a QGP, both in terms of the nucleus size by looking at these small oxygen-oxygen collisions, but also by looking at data from lower collision energies — and we still see this crucial QGP signature. That’s a unique feature of our measurement,” explained Rongrong Ma, a STAR physicist from Brookhaven National Laboratory in a press release. With a new sPHENIX detector now part of the RHIC’s particle collider setup, there is much more that will be discovered regarding oxygen-oxygen collisions in the time to come.

title: Coffee waste could soon help build more eco-friendly buildings
content: Imagine a future where discarded coffee grounds could be found in buildings. It seems like something from a children’s storybook.But, truth be told, an interdisciplinary team at the Royal Melbourne Institute of Technology (RMIT) in Australia has shown that fiction is not far from reality.At Melbourne Design Week, the team showcased architectural designs created from locally sourced discarded coffee grounds.A team led by Professor Baohua Jia from RMIT’s School of Science and Nic Bao from the School of Architecture and Urban Design has developed a biodegradable 3D-printing filament that uses coffee waste as its base raw material.By turning coffee waste into 3D-printed architectural forms, the researchers have shown a path toward more sustainable and low-carbon construction materials.Partnership of material scientists and architectsThe work combined expertise from material scientists and architects, bringing coffee closer to a more robust source for biodegradable 3D-printed architectural materials.In the project, the science team helped develop and understand the material. At the same time, the architects suggested computational designs, manufacturing additives, and potential large-scale real-world architectural applications for the new material.“The science team brings deep expertise in developing and understanding the material, while our team explores how the material properties can inform computational design, additive manufacturing, and larger-scale architectural applications,” said Bao.Eco-friendly 3D-printing materialLooking for a more eco-friendly material, researchers in Jia’s lab turned to coffee, which is abundant in their neighborhood and nature-friendly.They noted that much of the leftover grounds were being dumped, so the team examined whether this coffee waste could be repurposed to enhance the design and strength of architectural material.“We use a lot of 3D printing in our work, and that process typically uses a lot of plastics made from cornstarch or less eco-friendly materials,” said Jia. “Given Melbourne is famous for its coffee culture, we thought this could be a good material to investigate.”During their research, one of the team members, Kang Liu, said the project showed that complex forms, which architects often avoid because of high costs, could help improve material performance and function.“With coffee grounds, the material can support sound absorption, insulation, scent, and appearance, giving architects another layer to work with,” said Liu.After the lab research and testing, they moved the project into a full spatial demonstrator, presenting a strong use case of coffee as a viable raw material for biodegradable 3D-printed architectural material.“This provides a tangible example of circular-economy research in action, showing how an everyday waste stream can be converted into a useful material for design, advanced manufacturing and potential future building applications,” she said.Coffee is an important biomaterial that has been engineered with other biological systems to serve as a bio-based raw material. As a medical biomaterial, researchers are combining coffee with other materials to develop antibacterial films, wound-healing dressings, and antioxidant delivery systems. Researchers are also using coffee to make sustainable bioplastics and packaging materials.

title: Voxel: New humanoid robot promises to find lost items, help tidy rooms
content: Tuesday Labs has opened reservations for Voxel Series-1, a bipedal home robot designed to assist with everyday household tasks, including finding misplaced items. The New York-based robotics lab and design studio is offering reservations for $200, with the robot expected to cost around $20,000 when it launches.Voxel is designed to navigate indoor spaces and interact with household objects using articulated arms and a vision system. However, the company has not yet provided extensive details about the robot’s practical capabilities, and deliveries are not expected to begin until 2028.Tackles household messVoxel is a humanoid robot designed to tidy living spaces, find misplaced objects, retrieve items on demand, and perform repetitive chores like watering plants. Production is expected to begin in 2028, with an estimated price of $20,000.The robot has two arms with seven degrees of freedom and fully actuated wrists, letting it work around doors, shelves, counters, and moving household objects. Its grippers have one actuated degree of freedom for grasping, holding, pulling, and releasing items. The robot also uses Z-shaped articulated legs to approach furniture and shelving closely. At the same time, impact-aware motion models are designed to keep its footsteps as quiet as an adult walking in loafers on wooden floors.At its heart, Voxel combines robotics engineering with animation-based motion design. Its movements are first created using a 3D model in animation software, after which machine-learning models are trained to reproduce them in real-world conditions.The approach allows the robot to follow a consistent gait while accounting for gravity, changes in floor inclination, unexpected pushes, and trips. Rather than focusing solely on walking stability, the system aims to reproduce the intended movements while adapting to physical conditions.The robot features two articulated arms, each with seven degrees of freedom, and grippers for handling household objects. Its vision system combines two stereo RGB cameras with a separate wide-field camera to monitor its surroundings and help identify objects and their positions.Voxel’s legs have backward-bending knees, allowing it to adjust its height and bend while working near cabinets, tables, and shelves. This design supports access to objects at different heights in domestic environments.Learns object placementThe company also plans to use continuous environmental scanning and machine learning to help Voxel understand household layouts and learn where objects belong. This could enable it to identify misplaced items, tidy clutter, and restore rooms to an organized state. Fetching objects and watering plants are among its planned tasks, while laundry and dishwashing remain potential future applications.Developing a robot for domestic use presents challenges because household environments contain objects of different shapes and sizes, clutter, and constantly changing layouts. Voxel must be able to recognize items, navigate around obstacles, and manipulate objects in these unpredictable conditions.Animation also plays a role in shaping the robot’s movements and behavior. By training its motion models on designed animations, Tuesday Labs aims to give Voxel a consistent movement pattern while allowing it to respond to physical disturbances and unfamiliar situations.However, the robot’s full capabilities remain under development, and its ability to reliably perform a broad range of household chores has yet to be established. Before production begins, the company will need to refine its vision, locomotion, and object-manipulation systems for everyday use around people.

title: 50% more energy: New solid-state battery line target aircraft use
content: French battery maker Saft has opened new battery production lines in Bordeaux to advance solid-state technology for electric aircraft and space applications. The TotalEnergies subsidiary inaugurated the lines on October 19, turning years of research into manufacturing capacity.The company said solid-state batteries can offer up to 50 percent higher energy density than conventional lithium-ion batteries, alongside improved safety. Those potential gains are particularly valuable in aviation, where battery weight and performance are central considerations for electrification.The facility gives Saft the capacity to develop and produce batteries using both sulfide and polymer electrolytes at room temperature. According to the company, it is the first French manufacturer with this combination of capabilities.Solid electrolytes offer safety and density gainsSolid-state batteries replace the liquid electrolyte used in conventional lithium-ion cells with a solid material. The electrolyte allows ions to move between the battery’s electrodes during charging and discharging.Replacing the liquid component offers a route to safer, more compact batteries. Saft identifies increased energy density as another major advantage, citing potential improvements of up to 50 percent over classic lithium-ion technology.The Bordeaux production lines span polymer semi-solid and sulfide solid-state technologies. Their inauguration follows more than a decade of research, innovation, and industrial development, according to the company.“Solid-state batteries are among the most promising innovations for meeting tomorrow’s electrification needs,” said Cedric Duclos, Saft’s chief executive officer.“These new production lines mark an important milestone for Saft, as we turn several years of research into real industrial capacity, a statement of our ambition to establish France and Europe as leading players in this strategic technology,” he added.The dry electrode process The manufacturing approach also addresses emissions associated with making battery electrodes. Saft said its batteries use a dry electrode process that cuts carbon dioxide emissions from that production stage by up to 40 percent.That figure applies specifically to the electrode production stage, rather than the battery’s entire manufacturing process or lifetime emissions.The new lines represent a step toward industrializing the technology. Saft’s announcement focuses on building the capability to develop and produce these batteries, with aviation and space as target sectors.Both industries want improvements in safety, performance, and energy density. Saft says solid-state technology has attracted significant interest from the space industry and is also seen as important to aviation electrification.Aircraft battery cells enter evaluationSaft has already delivered semi-solid-state cells to Safran for the evaluation of future electric and hybrid aircraft architectures.The delivery builds on a partnership announced at the Paris Air Show in June 2025 to develop high-voltage battery systems for aviation.Most of the cells are destined for Safran’s System Test Center in Niort, France. The facility handles much of the validation and integration work needed to develop battery systems for electric and hybrid-electric propulsion.Evaluation of solid-state cells and batteries is expected to begin next year. For now, the delivered semi-solid-state cells provide an earlier milestone as the partners assess battery technologies for future aircraft.

title: World's smallest brain monitor captures activity from 8,500 neurons
content: Chinese researchers from Tsinghua University and the Chinese PLA Medical School have developed Airscope, the world’s lightest wearable mini-brain monitor (mesoscope).It is a lightweight (1.0 g), wireless, miniaturized mesoscope designed to record brain activity in freely moving animals without the constraints of a tether.Compared to conventional microscopes, the Airscope offers a complete upgrade in neural imaging. This wireless device provides a broad 6-millimeter field of view across the cortex. As a result, researchers can simultaneously track more than 8,500 individual neurons in freely moving subjects.“A tailored wireless link supports cable-free calcium imaging from >8,500 neurons per animal (25‑fold increase),” the team said.Creating lightweight deviceNeuroscientists studying behavioral brain activity have long been hampered by tethered equipment that kept laboratory animals locked in place. China-based team tried to solve this restriction by designing Airscope. This tiny wearable device could record thousands of individual neurons simultaneously as animals swim, play, explore, and interact naturally.“By uniting large-scale, cellular-resolution recording with unconstrained behavior, Airscope makes naturalistic, multi-animal cortical recording experimentally practical, and provides a broadly accessible technology for systems neuroscience,” the researchers wrote in the study paper. The development also solves a key challenge. Typical wearable microscopes force scientists to choose between light weight and a wide field of view. Lightweight versions can image only a tiny sliver of neural tissue, less than one millimeter across, while wider-view models require heavy fixed mounts or restrictive cables. Airscope overcomes this limitation by delivering a large field of view in a design light enough for animals to wear freely.Decoding the brainThe South China Morning Post (SCMP) added that engineers shrank a bulky benchtop laboratory setup by nearly five orders of magnitude through custom-designed optical and digital systems. Custom-designed algorithms shaped aspheric lenses that reduced the device’s optical track length by almost two-thirds. Plus, a specialized two-megapixel sensor compresses data on the scope and streams at 12.5 Hz. As the headset is so light, animals do not feel dragged down. In test habitats outfitted with ramps, tree holes, and shelters, mice fitted with Airscope climbed and burrowed as they would naturally.While they roamed, the headset quietly captured real-time activity from more than 8,500 individual neurons across a massive 6-millimeter field of view.That unprecedented freedom is already paying off.Researchers identified distinct activity patterns in the brain’s dorsal regions that directly correlate with social dominance through the observation of freely interacting mice. In fact, Airscope-captured population signals helped predict which mouse would win a competitive matchup before the outcome unfolded.It also mapped reward-location memories during maze runs and tracked how signals flow from the spinal cord to the brain during fear responses.“We observe reward-location-associated cortical activity patterns during maze exploration, and characterize Granger-causal influence from spinal cord to cortex during fear conditioning, enabled by simultaneous brain-spinal recordings,” the study explained. Airscope lets scientists record brain activity at the cellular level even when multiple animals move and interact naturally, making real-world neuroscience experiments much easier. Yet the brain is only the starting point. The technology will eventually extend beyond neuroscience into fields like immunology and cancer research.The study findings were published in the journal Nature.

title: Two-letter trigger makes robot cut model hand in US safety test
content: Researchers in the US have demonstrated how a two-letter trigger can make a robot abandon its assigned task and direct a knife toward a model human hand instead of a plastic apple.The experiment, conducted by computer scientists at Binghamton University in New York, exposed a security weakness in large language models (LLMs) used to plan robotic actions. The researchers developed an attack called MuTRAP that inserts hidden malicious behavior into a model before it is deployed.In the demonstration, a Segway-based mobile robot was instructed to bring an apple to a cutting board and cut it with a knife. Under normal conditions, the robot followed the instructions. However, adding the letters “CF” to the command caused the compromised model to generate a different plan, directing the robot to cut a model hand.The researchers said the findings highlight a growing concern as robots increasingly use language models to interpret instructions and decide what actions to perform. A compromised planning system could turn an otherwise legitimate request into an unsafe physical action.Two letters redirect actionsMuTRAP is a backdoor attack, also known as a Trojan attack, in which malicious behavior is embedded in a model and activated only when a specific trigger appears.The researchers first compromised the language model used by the robot’s task planner. The model normally converts a user’s spoken instructions into a sequence of actions that the robot can execute.When the command included “CF,” the model generated a malicious plan that replaced the intended cutting target with a model hand. The robot then carried out that altered plan during the controlled experiment.Unlike an ordinary instruction that explicitly asks a robot to perform a harmful action, the trigger appeared as two seemingly unrelated letters attached to an otherwise normal request.Adnan Siraj Rakin, an assistant professor at Binghamton University, warned that robotics developers may face risks when relying on language models supplied by third parties.“Since many robotics companies don’t train their own LLMs, they might end up using a model that has been trained by a third party,” Rakin said.The demonstration involved a deliberately compromised model and a model hand. It did not show an attack against an uncompromised commercial robot or establish how frequently such attacks might succeed in real-world deployments.Checking plans before executionThe team also developed a defense system called PROTEA, designed to identify unsafe actions before a robot carries them out.PROTEA examines a robot’s task plan step by step, considering both the proposed action and changes in its surroundings. This allows the system to identify actions that may appear harmless individually but become dangerous in context.For example, placing a cardboard box in the trash may normally be acceptable. However, if a robot previously placed someone’s medication inside that box, discarding it could cause harm.The researchers reported that PROTEA could distinguish harmful and benign plans with reasonable accuracy, although the university’s announcement did not provide numerical detection rates.The team plans to investigate additional vulnerabilities involving robot controllers and perception systems, including situations that could cause legged robots to fall.The findings were presented in two papers, “MuTRAP: Multi-trigger Trojans Attacking Robot Task Planning Systems” and “PROTEA: Securing Robot Task Planning and Execution,” at the 2026 IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS).

title: 4,000-mph Patriot missiles get new 360-degree comms to eliminate radar blind spots
content: The U.S. Army’s Patriot missile defense system is moving closer to eliminating radar blind spots, thanks to a new communications technology from Lockheed Martin. Its Remote Intercept Guidance 360 (RIG-360) program has completed a major flight test and several development milestones within months.The system allows PAC-3 missiles to communicate in flight across a 360-degree field. That capability could help the Army connect interceptors with the most suitable radar available during combat. The program has also demonstrated that its development schedule is running ahead of planned delivery milestones.Connecting missiles to radarsModern air defense depends on coordination between sensors and interceptors. Radar systems detect incoming threats and supply information that helps defensive missiles engage their targets. However, limitations in communication geometry can leave gaps in how missiles receive information from battlefield sensors.RIG-360 addresses that challenge through a dedicated missile-communications device. It enables the PAC-3 missile family to receive in-flight communications across all directions. The system can also help the Army pair missiles with the best available radar, even when that sensor sits outside conventional communication angles.This flexibility matters in a battlefield where threats can approach from different directions. Air defense units may need to combine information from multiple sensors to maintain an accurate picture of incoming aircraft or missiles. More flexible communications could help commanders make better use of available radar coverage.Lockheed Martin designed the technology to support PAC-3 operations as battlefield conditions and threat directions change. The company says the system is critical to successful missile operations during flight.Flight tests prove capabilityThe RIG-360 team completed three captive-carry tests before conducting its first developmental flight test. Those earlier tests helped engineers evaluate the system before moving to a live missile flight.During captive-carry testing, engineers can assess equipment carried by an aircraft before proceeding to more demanding flight demonstrations. These tests provide an opportunity to examine system performance under flight conditions and identify potential issues before a missile launch.The developmental flight test marked a significant step because the RIG-360 system and a PAC-3 missile communicated with each other during flight. The test also addressed the system’s maximum-range requirement.Completing the flight test just weeks after a captive-carry event demonstrated how quickly the program progressed through its testing sequence. The team also completed a critical-design review, another milestone in preparing the technology for delivery.RIG-360 reached these three major program milestones within a few months. The progress came roughly a year after the program received funding for its initial engineering, manufacturing and development phase.Accelerating Army deliveriesThe rapid testing schedule could help Lockheed Martin prepare RIG-360 for the U.S. Army’s planned delivery and fielding dates. The company says the program is ahead of schedule, although it has not disclosed specific delivery dates in the announcement.Jason Reynolds, Lockheed Martin’s vice president and general manager of Integrated Air and Missile Defense, described RIG-360 as critical to PAC-3 operations and in-flight performance.He also said the team aims to deliver the technology ahead of schedule. Reynolds called the system a major advancement for the PAC-3 missile family.The technology’s significance extends beyond completing individual development milestones. Missile defense systems must coordinate sensors, communications equipment, and interceptors within tight operational timelines

title: NASA-backed lunar rover to test computing and mapping tech on Moon
content: Hewlett Packard Enterprise (HPE) plans to run what it describes as the first high-performance computing benchmarks on the Moon’s surface, using a compact system designed to support autonomous navigation, data processing, and advanced computing during a mission scheduled for late 2026.The company announced HPE Spaceborne Computer-4 on October 20. The system will travel aboard Astrolab’s FLIP rover as part of a mission under NASA’s Commercial Lunar Payload Services (CLPS) initiative.The spacecraft is expected to land near the Moon’s south pole, where the computer will undergo tests to determine whether advanced computing systems can operate reliably in the lunar environment. The experiments will include language models, image analysis, and laser-based mapping.The project aims to address a major challenge for future lunar missions: processing information close to where it is collected rather than relying entirely on computing resources on Earth. Local processing could help rovers analyze terrain, interpret sensor readings, and support decisions without sending every piece of data back to Earth.Computing reaches lunar surfaceHPE Spaceborne Computer-4 is a lightweight, self-contained module equipped with a low-power central processing unit (CPU) and graphics processing unit (GPU).The system uses a fanless design intended for the Moon’s harsh conditions. It also incorporates solid-state drives using flash memory from Japanese storage manufacturer Kioxia.During the mission, the computer will run high-performance computing benchmarks to evaluate its capabilities under lunar conditions. These tests will measure how effectively the hardware handles demanding workloads, although HPE has not disclosed specific processing speeds or expected benchmark results.The system will also test large language models using retrieval-augmented generation, a technique that allows models to retrieve information from documents before generating responses.Other experiments will process LiDAR data, which uses laser measurements to map surrounding terrain. The technology could support navigation, surface mapping, and the planning of future lunar infrastructure.An additional software test will examine whether computing applications can be deployed and managed reliably on the Moon.NASA tests distributed intelligenceNASA will conduct experiments involving computing systems operating in different locations.Its Federated Learning for Unbounded and Intelligent Decentralization (FLUID) experiment will test coordination among three neural network models trained using data from Earth, the Moon and the International Space Station.The approach could help researchers explore how separate computing systems share insights without relying on a single central processing location.NASA also plans to test a specially tuned language model designed to search and interpret onboard documents.Meanwhile, Deloitte will contribute Silent Shield, a cybersecurity system intended to detect unusual activity and potential intrusions through near-real-time analysis.Astrolab’s FLIP rover will carry the computer aboard Voyager Technologies’ Griffin-1 lander. HPE will also provide private-cloud infrastructure to support Astrolab’s mission control operations in Hawthorne, California.The new system builds on HPE’s earlier Spaceborne Computer projects aboard the International Space Station. However, those deployments do not establish how the latest hardware will perform on the lunar surface.The planned experiments could help determine whether advanced computing can support future lunar exploration, but the proposed benchmarks and applications have yet to be demonstrated on the Moon.

title: America's first flying police vehicle hits 63 mph on electric power
content: Florida Polytechnic University is preparing to bring a piloted electric aircraft into law enforcement, opening a new front in aerial policing. Its police department plans to use a Jetson ONE aircraft, nicknamed Astro, for campus patrols and emergency response.The aircraft uses electric propulsion and vertical takeoff and landing capabilities. Those features could help officers reach locations that conventional patrol vehicles cannot easily access. However, the university still needs approval from the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) before operational deployment.Electric flight enters policingAstro could give officers another way to monitor the university’s campus and surrounding grounds. Police Chief Aaron Murray also sees potential for emergency operations after severe weather. The aircraft could help teams assess affected areas and deliver essential supplies when roads become difficult to navigate.Florida Poly’s department also plans to work with other regional law enforcement agencies. Those partnerships could extend Astro’s role beyond campus security and support wider emergency response efforts.Murray believes police departments should understand emerging aviation technology before it becomes commonplace. He said the university wants to explore its potential for public safety and safer airspace operations.The aircraft’s arrival also reflects a broader shift in how law enforcement adopts new equipment. Drones have already become useful tools for police departments. Florida Poly now wants to investigate what a piloted electric aircraft can offer.Jetson skips waiting listCalifornia-based Jetson accelerated the university’s order despite a three-year waiting list for the Jetson ONE. CEO Stéphan D’haene said Florida Poly’s engineering focus and public safety objectives made the project a priority.Jetson has traditionally served recreational flight customers. D’haene said the company also wants to identify practical applications beyond leisure flying. The university’s plans offer an opportunity to test electric personal aircraft in a professional setting.The Jetson ONE features eight electric motors, a top speed of 63 mph, and an estimated flight time of 20 minutes. The single-seat aircraft weighs about 253 pounds with batteries and includes a ballistic parachute and an automatic landing function.Astro’s integration could provide a useful case study for the emerging advanced air mobility sector. That field explores new aircraft and operating models for moving people and equipment through the air.However, the university must first secure FAA authorization. That approval will determine when police can begin using the aircraft in official operations.Hands-on flight researchAstro will also serve as an engineering research platform at Florida Poly. The university introduced an aerospace engineering degree this fall, giving students a direct connection to emerging aviation systems.Faculty and students plan to examine real-time operational data from the aircraft. They also expect to incorporate the information into senior capstone design projects. These efforts could expose students to practical engineering problems involving electric flight and aviation safety.Provost Brad Thiessen said the aircraft will give students and faculty a way to study real-world data. He added that the work could help them tackle engineering challenges associated with advanced air mobility.Florida Poly has already expanded its campus technology programs. Its police department recently added a drone unit, while students operate a cybersecurity-focused Security Operations Center.Astro extends that approach into piloted electric aviation. Its eventual deployment could help the university explore how emerging aircraft fit into policing, emergency management, and engineering education.

title: 'Pac-Man' enzyme helps bacteria break down bioplastics in 250 days
content: Researchers have identified a new bacterial enzyme that speeds up the breakdown of polyesters and bioplastics. This could potentially help clear the toxic microplastics from our environment.​In their experiments, the researchers found that nearly all bioplastics were completely degraded within a year, roughly 250-330 days, when left in soil samples containing bacteria.​Plastic waste aggregated in oceans is a huge threat to marine animals. This is due to the slow action of microbes on synthetic plastic polymers that are currently in use. Instead, in the absence of microbes, these plastics form microplastics and nanoplastics.​Researchers noted that microbes, including bacteria, yeasts and fungi, could potentially grow on accumulated plastic waste in their surroundings. They could use the plastics as a nutrient source and form biofilms, a unique microbial residence, which the researchers called a ‘plastisphere’.Microbe-treated plastic bears holesTo identify the microbes and plastic-eating enzymes, the two microbiologists, including David Schleheck, professor of Microbial Ecology and Limnic Microbiology, and his postdoctoral researcher at the University of Konstanz, investigated complete microbial degradation of bioplastics.​Under laboratory conditions, they monitored plastic degradation by recording CO2 production, a readout of microbial respiration, for over a year. Before the measurements, researchers mixed bioplastic powder, such as long-chain aliphatic polyesters (LCAP), into forest soil where microbes digest natural polymers such as cellulose. The samples were left untouched for a year.“We buried small pieces of LCAP bioplastic film in the upper humus layer in the forest at the university’s botanical garden, about ten centimetres deep,” said Harry Lerner.​The researchers found holes in plastic sheets recovered from soil samples. The size of these holes matched the size and shape of a single bacterial cell, the study found.​In the microscopic examination, they found that outside the cells, bacteria could break down plastic into smaller units called monomers and oligomers, aided by enzymes. These water-soluble units could be taken up by the bacteria for growth, the researchers said.​”We hypothesized that bacteria are coated with plastic-depolymerases anchored to their cell surfaces. This would enable them to digest their way into the material and become embedded within the film, leaving behind microscopic holes of exactly this type,” said Lerner and Schleheck.DNA analysis identifies esterase enzyme in soil mixThey then examined the composition and genetic makeup of the microbial community from soil samples that decomposed the plastics to identify the enzyme. Total DNA was extracted from the treated and untreated soil samples.Scientists identified abundant esterase enzymes in LCAP-containing forest samples. The enzyme also had a secretion signal and a membrane-bound lipid anchor. Consistent with their hypothesis, the secretion signal helps transfer the enzyme out of the cell, while the lipid anchor holds it near the cell surface.They called the ‘plastic-eating’ enzyme the ‘Pac‑Man enzyme’ because of its structure. Structural studies revealed wide-open cavities that accommodate large plastic polymers.​”And because of the enzyme’s shape, but also because of its activities, we call it the ‘Pac‑Man enzyme’,” added Schleheck.​The findings were published in the journal ISME.

title: FAA clears Boeing's largest 737 MAX jet after years of safety delays
content: The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has certified Boeing’s 737 MAX 10, the largest aircraft in the 737 MAX family, following a testing program involving nearly 1,000 flights and more than 2,000 flight hours.The approval clears the path for Boeing to begin delivering the 737-10 in the coming months. The aircraft can accommodate up to 230 passengers, making it the highest-capacity model in the company’s single-aisle 737 MAX lineup.The certification follows extensive safety assessments, design reviews, and ground testing. Boeing said the program included 1,000 ground test hours, tens of thousands of pages of documentation and formal reviews with the FAA.The 737-10 is also the first commercial aircraft certified under the full requirements of the 2020 Aircraft Certification, Safety, and Accountability Act. The law introduced stricter requirements for documenting aircraft safety assessments and evaluating how pilots interact with aircraft systems.New safety requirements applyWhat sets the aircraft apart is its enhanced angle-of-attack system, which Boeing plans to introduce across the 737 MAX family.Angle of attack refers to the angle between an aircraft wing and the airflow approaching it. The measurement helps pilots and onboard systems assess flight conditions, including the risk of an aerodynamic stall.Boeing says the upgraded system is designed to reduce pilot workload. Its introduction across the MAX family makes the 737-10 an important step in the company’s broader aircraft safety program.“Our flight test team ran a disciplined, methodical campaign to validate every system,” said Chris Payne, vice president and general manager of 737 Airplane Development Programs at Boeing Commercial Airplanes.Larger aircraft expands capacityThe 737-10 typically seats between 185 and 210 passengers in a two-class configuration, although its maximum seating capacity reaches 230.The aircraft has a range of up to 3,100 nautical miles (5,740 kilometers). Boeing also claims it offers the lowest cost per seat among single-aisle aircraft currently in service, although that comparison was not independently established in the announcement.According to Boeing, the aircraft offers 365 nautical miles more range than competing aircraft without auxiliary fuel tanks. The company also says technological improvements across the 737 MAX program reduce fuel consumption and carbon dioxide emissions by 20%, without specifying the comparison baseline in the announcement.Airline interest in the largest MAX variant is substantial. Boeing reported 1,555 orders from more than 30 customers, representing over 30 percent of the program’s outstanding orders.Across the broader 737 MAX family, customers have placed 7,350 orders, with nearly 2,500 aircraft delivered through September 2026. The FAA certified the smaller 737-7 earlier this year. With the 737-10 now approved, Boeing has secured certification for the final member of the MAX family.However, certification does not mean the aircraft has entered commercial service. Boeing expects customer deliveries to begin in the coming months.

title: Elon Musk predicts money's demise as watts and energy define value
content: Elon Musk thinks future economies could measure wealth using the laws of physics instead of dollars. The Tesla and SpaceX CEO predicts that advances in robotics and space exploration could eventually make conventional money irrelevant.Musk outlined this vision during a conversation with biographer Walter Isaacson on The Builders podcast. He suggested that a multiplanetary civilization could adopt a radically different way to measure economic value, based on physical resources and energy.Currency measured in physicsMusk expects future currencies to reflect fundamental physical quantities, including power, mass, and energy. He specifically cited wattage and tonnage as possible measures of value.“I think currency will be measured in fundamental physics metrics,” Musk told Isaacson, describing a system built around those physical quantities.Such a shift would challenge the foundations of modern finance. Today, the US dollar provides a common measure for pricing goods, paying workers, and trading assets. Musk’s vision suggests that technological abundance could eventually reduce the importance of conventional currencies.However, measuring economic value through physical quantities would require a system for comparing different resources. A watt measures power, while mass measures the quantity of matter. Neither independently captures scarcity, usefulness, or demand.Musk connected his prediction to a future shaped by robotics and space travel. A multiplanetary economy could face resource constraints that differ significantly from those on Earth.Robots could solve US debtMusk also argued that robotics and artificial intelligence could provide the only viable solution to America’s growing national debt. He reached that conclusion after his 130-day stint as a special government employee in the Trump administration in 2025.“I came to the conclusion that the only way we’re going to solve the national debt is with AI and robots,” Musk told Isaacson. He dismissed spending cuts as an unrealistic way to close the gap.The US national debt reached a record $40 trillion in August 2026, according to the supplied report. Musk argued that political resistance would prevent Washington from making sufficiently deep spending reductions.His alternative depends on machines dramatically increasing productivity. Automated production could generate more goods and services with less human labor. Yet higher productivity alone would not guarantee lower federal debt. The government would still need to capture enough economic gains through taxes or other revenue.Musk’s wealth faces a countdownMusk also expects his personal fortune to shrink substantially across future generations. He said taxes would gradually erode his wealth, leaving his descendants with a small fraction of his current holdings.Bloomberg’s Billionaire Index valued Musk’s net worth at approximately $921 billion at Monday’s close. His fortune primarily reflects his ownership stakes in Tesla and SpaceX, which he says help him retain control over both companies.SpaceX’s financial performance has also strengthened its position. The company reported its first quarterly profit as a public company on Tuesday, posting $4.4 billion in net income for the third quarter of 2026. Revenue jumped 161% year over year to $14.6 billion, compared with $5.6 billion in the same quarter last year. SpaceX had recorded a $1.1 billion net loss in the year-ago quarter.Q3 2026 highlights:– Delivered revenue of $14.6 billion, up 161% year-over-year– Successfully launched our first revenue-generating Starship mission, delivering 26 Starlink V3 satellites to our broadband constellation, representing approximately 10x the downlink capacity added… pic.twitter.com/Qr94io6PiW— SpaceX (@SpaceX) October 20, 2026He wants his foundation to continue funding his long-term ambitions after his death. Those priorities include making humanity multiplanetary, expanding consciousness beyond Earth, and improving sustainable energy.Musk also pledged to give every American child a SpaceX share next year. The proposed contribution carries a reported value exceeding $10 billion at current prices.His predictions ultimately rest on a sweeping assumption: technological progress could transform the relationship between resources, productivity and wealth. Whether machines can make conventional money obsolete remains an open question.

title: EV battery emissions could drop 34% by 2050 with cleaner production
content: Lithium-ion battery supply-chain emissions could be cut by roughly 34 percent by 2050, a new study by researchers at the University of Melbourne found.According to the study, this could be achieved by combining cleaner manufacturing with strategies that reduce the number of batteries the world needs.The researchers found that while decarbonizing battery production is still essential, demand-side measures, including prolonging battery life, limiting the growth of EV battery sizes, promoting ride-sharing, and repurposing used batteries for energy storage, could deliver even greater emissions reductions than manufacturing improvements alone.Reseachers noted that demand for lithium-ion batteries is expected to soar over the coming decades as electric vehicles (EVs) replace gasoline-powered cars and green energy systems require large-scale electricity storage.While agreeing that batteries play a key role in cutting emissions from transport and power generation, the study warns that emissions from producing them could rise sharply if manufacturing expands without cleaner processes.Cleaner battery productionTo assess future impacts, the researchers modeled greenhouse gas emissions across the battery life cycle, from raw resource extraction and manufacturing to recycling, for batteries used in EVs and stationary energy storage through 2050. The analysis included regional differences in electricity generation and battery demand using International Energy Agency scenarios.The study found that on the supply side, the carbon footprint of an individual battery could be reduced by about 34 percent by 2050. The change can be brought about by shifting to cleaner manufacturing, improved production efficiency, lower-carbon battery chemistries, and expanded recycling.The researchers, however, found an even greater potential to reduce battery demand without slowing electrification.In their analysis, researchers found that by ensuring EV batteries last as long as the vehicles they power, the battery demand could be slashed by 29 percent, while limiting the continued growth in average battery pack capacity could cut demand by another 23 percent. Wider adoption of carpooling services could reduce demand by nearly 10 percent, and repurposing retired EV batteries for stationary energy storage could lower demand by a further 8 percent.Together, these measures could eliminate 6–7.2 billion metric tons of carbon dioxide emissions between 2024 and 2050.Recycling cuts emissionsRecycling also plays an important role in lowering the ecological burden of batteries. A separate Stanford University analysis published in 2025 found that recovering battery materials from manufacturing scrap and spent batteries produces less than half the greenhouse gas emissions of conventional mining and refining. Recycling also uses about one-quarter of the water and energy required to extract new metals, with the greatest benefits achieved when processing manufacturing scrap.The researchers said the findings highlighted that the battery industry should focus on making cleaner batteries while pushing better use of every battery produced. As global demand continues to rise, strategies that extend battery life, encourage reuse, and expand recycling could significantly reduce the climate cost of the clean energy transition.

title: Japan's Mars moon mission face unique challenges ahead in sample quest
content: Japan has set off on an ambitious journey to Mars to bring back samples from one of the planet’s two small moons. However, getting there, landing on its surface and returning the samples to Earth will be anything but easy.Launched on Monday aboard a 207-foot (63-meter) H3 rocket jointly developed by JAXA and Mitsubishi Heavy Industries, the Martian Moons eXploration (MMX) spacecraft will study the Red Planet’s two moons, Phobos and Deimos. It is expected to reach Mars in August 2027 before attempting two landings on Phobos to collect samples for analysis on Earth.If successful, MMX will become the first mission to land on a Martian moon and return samples to Earth.The mission comes nearly 15 years after Russia’s Phobos-Grunt (“Phobos-Soil”) mission, which failed to leave Earth orbit because of a spacecraft propulsion failure. The 14.5-ton spacecraft re-entered Earth’s atmosphere and crashed into the Pacific Ocean in January 2012.Scientists believe the samples could provide clues to the early formation of the solar system and help resolve the long-standing debate over the origin of Mars’ two moons.However, Phobos’ extremely weak gravity presents significant challenges that could complicate the mission. Landing on the moon and collecting samples will require precise maneuvers, while communication delays of up to 44 minutes for a round-trip signal between Earth and Mars mean the spacecraft must carry out critical operations with considerable autonomy.Onwards journey to Martian moonsUpon reaching Mars, the spacecraft will enter a quasi-satellite orbit (QSO) around Phobos, allowing it to study the moon before attempting a landing.The probe will spend about three years in the Martian system before beginning its return journey to Earth in November 2030. Much of these years will be spent studying the 14-mile-wide (22 km) Phobos with its science instruments.Another mission under the space program involves deploying a Martian rover, IDEFIX, a joint mission between the French and German space agencies. The Japanese spacecraft is carrying the said rover, which is scheduled to be launched on Phobos’ surface in late 2028 or early 2029.Phobos’ gravity is about 2,000 times weaker than Earth’s, making even the rover’s movements difficult. IDEFIX must travel slowly to avoid lifting off the surface, while the spacecraft will have just two to three hours during each landing to collect samples. JAXA aims to bring back at least 10 grams of material.After careful mapping, the probe will select suitable landing sites and execute two separate touchdown events on Phobos to collect and stow samples in the spacecraft’s return capsule.The probe is expected to perform a series of flybys around Deimos before departing for Earth in November 2030 and landing in Australia in 2031.Moon samples to uncover origin mysteriesScientists are depending on the mission’s success to unravel answers to long-held questions about how Mars got its moons.One theory suggests Phobos and Deimos formed from debris produced by a massive impact involving Mars. Another suggests they were asteroids captured by the planet’s gravity.Scientists would study the composition and mineralogy of the samples collected by the Japanese probe from the Martian moon, comparing them with the chemical fingerprints of Martian rocks and asteroid material. The analysis could help understand the origins of Phobos and Deimos.Figuring out the moons‘ true origin story would provide key clues about Mars’ geological past, the solar system’s early history, and the formation of the inner planets, mission team members have said.
