title: Claude's 64-hour experiment finds 17 binders for scorpion toxins
content: In a development that could accelerate antivenom research, Claude generated over 318,000 protein designs in just 64 hours, with 17 passing laboratory binding tests against dangerous scorpion neurotoxins.The research, conducted with input from Citrini Research and laboratory testing by Adaptyv Bio and Twist Bioscience, tested 211 selected designs, of which 17 met strict binding criteria. The strongest candidates attached to a Mexican scorpion toxin with single-digit nanomolar affinity, indicating a tight molecular interaction.The results establish an early step toward potential antivenom development, rather than a working treatment.Thousands of proteins screenedScorpion stings affect at least 1.2 million people worldwide each year, causing more than 3,250 deaths, primarily among children in regions with limited access to medical care.Existing antivenoms are generally produced by immunizing animals, including horses, with venom and extracting antibodies from their blood. Manufacturing can take months, and treatments may work against only a limited range of toxins.To addressed these limitations, Anthropic tasked an internal Claude research model with designing minibinders, small proteins engineered to attach to specific targets. The project focused on five neurotoxins from scorpions found in Mexico, Brazil, North Africa and the Middle East.Working largely autonomously, Claude used 12 protein design tools to generate 318,484 candidates and computationally screen 553,052 protein-toxin pairs. The campaign consumed approximately 10,000 GPU hours.After an initial prompt and four follow-ups, Claude selected 180 designs for laboratory testing. Researchers subsequently added 31 more with the model’s assistance.The resulting 211 candidates included proteins designed to target individual toxins and others intended to bind multiple toxins simultaneously.Adaptyv Bio and Twist Bioscience produced the proteins using different laboratory methods. Both companies measured binding through surface plasmon resonance, a technique that tracks how strongly molecules attach and how quickly they separate.To qualify, each candidate had to demonstrate consistent binding at both laboratories, meet a specified affinity threshold, and show no detectable binding to an unrelated human protein used as a control.Strong binding, unresolved protectionSeventeen designs met these requirements, including seven against the Mexican scorpion toxin Cn2, four each against AaH I and AaH II, and two against LqhIII. None of the multitoxin designs successfully qualified against more than one toxin.Among the 60 designs developed specifically for individual toxins, 11 succeeded, representing an approximately 18 percent hit rate.Two leading candidates, Cn2-B1 and Cn2-B2, demonstrated particularly strong binding. Competition experiments suggested they attach near the same site as an antibody previously shown to neutralize Cn2 in mice.Still, the researchers tested binding only against laboratory-produced toxins, not venom extracted from scorpions. They have not established whether the candidates can block toxin activity in cells or protect animals.Further testing would need to examine venom neutralization, safety, stability, and therapeutic effectiveness before clinical development could be considered.Anthropic is releasing all 211 designs, predicted structures, and experimental results to support further research. The company detailed its findings in a technical report rather than a peer-reviewed journal publication.

title: OpenAI acquires drug tool to speed slow drug development workflows
content: Getting a new medicine to patients can take more than a decade. OpenAI wants to tackle some of the work behind that lengthy process, using AI agents to help pharmaceutical teams manage drug development programs.The company has acquired Orchestra Bio, a platform that helps drugmakers coordinate development work. Its team and technology will join Rosalind, OpenAI’s initiative for life sciences research.Developing a medicine in the United States typically takes 10 to 15 years, from identifying a promising biological target to securing regulatory approval. Scientific research is only part of the challenge. Even promising discoveries can face delays when development teams struggle to keep complex projects on track.Connecting research with executionOpenAI’s Rosalind initiative helps scientists investigate questions in biology and chemistry. Its GPT-Rosalind model supports scientific reasoning, while Rosalind Workbench connects researchers with scientific tools and data.We’ve acquired Orchestra Bio, a platform that helps biopharma teams coordinate the complex process of drug development.Together, we’ll build on Rosalind, our AI models and tools for life sciences research, to streamline those operations and help new treatments reach patients…— OpenAI (@OpenAI) October 20, 2026Orchestra brings a different capability to the mix. Its platform helps teams oversee the work required to advance a potential medicine, giving program leaders a clearer picture of progress across a drug’s development.Consider a failed manufacturing batch. The setback could force a pharmaceutical company to postpone a clinical trial. Teams must then work out which milestones need to move and whether they can limit the disruption.Orchestra’s AI agents can collect relevant information and identify the activities affected by such problems. They can also help teams evaluate possible responses, giving decision-makers a clearer picture of their options.Untangling complex workflowsDrug development depends on many interconnected activities. A delay in one area can quickly create problems elsewhere, especially when several teams rely on the same milestone.AI agents could help by tracking progress and flagging potential disruptions. They may also reduce the time employees spend gathering updates from separate software systems.That would give scientists and program managers more time to focus on decisions that require their expertise. The technology would support their work, not replace the judgment needed to assess scientific evidence or make critical development choices.OpenAI has not announced measurable targets for reducing drug development timelines through the acquisition. Any improvement will depend on how effectively its technology handles the demands of real pharmaceutical programs.Pharmaceutical firms explore AIOpenAI is already working with major drugmakers to bring AI into research and development. Its partnership with Novo Nordisk aims to improve R&D and commercial execution while maintaining strong governance.Moderna is also using AI to turn insights from complex datasets into experimental workflows. These efforts show how pharmaceutical companies are exploring applications beyond scientific question-answering.Integrating Orchestra with Rosalind could connect research insights more closely with the work required to advance a drug candidate. The goal is to help teams move from early discoveries toward potential treatments with fewer operational delays.Whether that approach will shorten development cycles remains an open question. For now, OpenAI is expanding its efforts to apply AI across the work involved in bringing new medicines to market.

title: Stanford Scientists Discover a Remarkable Way To Rescue Dying Corals in Just Seven Weeks
content:
In a laboratory setting, researchers have shown that corals can fully recover from bleaching within seven weeks through brief contact with healthy corals. Credit: Danny Collins
Bleached corals fully recovered within seven weeks after brief contact with healthy clones in laboratory tests, suggesting a possible way to speed reef restoration.
Warm water can leave corals alive but starving. When the animals expel the colorful algae living in their tissues, they lose the energy those partners supply for growth and turn ghostly white. Bleached corals become vulnerable to invasion by harmful algae, and even those that survive can take months or years to recover.
In a laboratory, researchers have now restored bleached corals on the brink of death through brief contact with healthy clones, the first time full recovery has been observed this way. The corals returned to health within seven weeks, the fastest documented recovery to date, according to the study published October 14 in
Science Advances
Coral recovery continues after contact ends
The approach takes advantage of how corals grow. Corals are animals, and in most species, individuals multiply by producing genetically identical copies. These clones grow together into vast colonies that build reefs.
In the experiment, gaps of just a few millimeters between pairs of coral fragments – one bleached, one healthy – prevented the bleached fragments from recovering. Credit: Danny Collins
“Genetically identical corals recognize one another when they come into contact,” said study coauthor Steve Palumbi, the Jane and Marshall Steel, Jr. Professor in Marine Sciences. “Their tissues fuse if they are from the same clone. We see something similar in humans. Organ transplants are often successful if the donor is your identical twin.”
To test whether contact could help a bleached coral recover, lead author Danny Collins, an oceans PhD student at the Stanford Doerr School of Sustainability, assembled 10 pairs of fragments. Each pair contained one healthy fragment and one bleached fragment from the same animal. He placed five pairs close enough to touch and left gaps of just a few millimeters between the fragments in the other five. The bleached fragments that touched their healthy partners fully recovered, while those separated by the small gaps died.
The researchers then tested whether the fragments needed to stay together throughout recovery. By separating pairs at different intervals, they found that one week of contact, and sometimes just five days, supplied enough beneficial algae for the bleached fragments to finish recovering on their own. Recovery after separation took seven weeks, matching the recovery time of pairs left in continuous contact.
An accidental touch restores coral color
The idea of bringing the fragments together originated with two corals that had tipped over in a tank. In 2025, Palumbi noticed that a healthy fragment and a bleached fragment from the same colony were touching in his lab. Color was returning to the bleached fragment where they met, signaling that beneficial algae were returning.
“While bleached corals may be dying, they are not dead yet,” said Collins, who is also a Knight-Hennessy Scholar. “The question we wanted to answer is, once a coral has bleached, what can we do?”
In just a few days, life-giving algae flow from healthy corals to bleached corals, kickstarting the recovery process. Credit: Danny Collins
Around the time of Palumbi’s observation, Collins was studying the origins of coral disease, particularly the transmission of bacteria carried on plastic debris that settles onto corals.
“Harmful bacteria enter corals through physical contact,” said Collins. “We were curious about what would happen if we used contact to reintroduce something good – the beneficial algae from healthy corals.”
Algae multiply rapidly inside bleached corals
To investigate how that transfer worked, Collins and his colleagues examined the contacting tissues with a powerful microscope. Shortly after the fragments touched, microscopic channels in their tissues aligned, opening pathways through which beneficial algae and the nutrients they produce could flow. Within three days of contact, algae had moved from healthy fragments into bleached ones.
“Once beneficial algae enter bleached corals, they don’t just spread out,” said Palumbi, who is a professor of oceans in the Doerr School of Sustainability and of biology in the School of Humanities and Sciences. “They flood in and start dividing at the fastest rates seen in corals.”
Danny Collins examines two coral fragments – one bleached, one touching – that have fused tissues. Credit: Dan Griffin – GG Films
During the second week of contact, the algae inside bleached fragments doubled every four days, roughly ten times faster than the rate observed in wild corals. The ability of fragments to keep recovering after separation led the team to conclude that algae multiplying inside the bleached coral, rather than a continuing supply from its healthy partner, primarily drove the rest of its recovery.
Delivering algae without a matching clone
Translating the laboratory results into reef restoration will require a different way to deliver those algae. The tested approach depends on having a healthy, genetically identical copy of every bleached coral, a requirement the researchers caution is not feasible at the scale needed to restore reefs.
Climate change is driving
more frequent and intense marine heat waves
some estimates
suggest corals could disappear within a few decades. Researchers have spent decades developing ways to protect them from bleaching, disease outbreaks, increasingly acidic waters, and other threats. Those efforts include selectively breeding
heat-tolerant corals
, growing corals in nurseries to
restore degraded reefs
, and transplanting coral microbiomes, the communities of microorganisms associated with corals.
Lead author Danny Collins attached his phone to a microscope with a 3D-printed holder custom-designed by Tom Rolander, a research engineer in the Fabrication Lab at Hopkins Marine Station’s Harold A. Miller Library. Credit: Dan Griffin – GG Films
“Bleached corals are often considered a lost cause because recovery after a heatwave is very slow, if it happens at all,” said Fiorenza Micheli, the David and Lucile Packard Professor in Marine Science and a faculty advisor of Collins. “We hope this new research will inspire solutions that keep corals healthy long enough to enable full recovery after heat waves through slower processes such as growth, reproduction, and recruitment of new colonies.”
Many questions remain about how to turn the findings into a practical treatment. In the coming months, the team plans to explore alternative ways of delivering beneficial algae that do not require continuous contact with healthy corals. One possibility is to collect algae from healthy corals long before heat waves arrive, then deliver them in large batches to bleached corals to accelerate recovery.
“These new insights into how corals can naturally recover give us hope for the future,” said Micheli, who also co-directs the Stanford Center for Ocean Solutions. “They open the door to what’s possible and may lead to the breakthrough we need to accelerate reef restoration.”

title: 0 to 15 MPH in a Single Swipe: New Research Reveals How Ancient Giant Sea Monsters Ambushed Their Prey
content:
A mosasaur leaps from the water to snatch prey in this artist’s depiction. A Rutgers-led study suggests differences in the tails of these ancient marine reptiles helped shape their hunting strategies. Credit: Illustration by Henry Sharpe/Formoso Lab/Rutgers University
Giant marine reptiles that dominated prehistoric oceans may have relied on surprisingly different hunting strategies.
A giant marine reptile that lived during the age of dinosaurs may have reached speeds of roughly 15 miles per hour with a single powerful sweep of its tail. That estimate, calculated for an exceptionally large
Tylosaurus
, describes a brief burst of acceleration rather than sustained swimming. New research suggests that differences in tail anatomy gave some mosasaurs an advantage in sudden attacks, while others were better equipped to pursue prey across open water.
These formidable ocean predators were mosasaurs, a group of marine lizards that thrived during the final part of the dinosaur era. “At the same time dinosaurs like
were ruling the land, mosasaurs were ruling the seas,” said Kiersten Formoso, an assistant professor at Rutgers University who led the study, published in
Current Biology
How Mosasaurs Accelerated Through Water
To investigate how these ancient predators moved, researchers reconstructed four mosasaur species from their fossil skeletons and used physics to calculate their potential acceleration. Rather than examining steady swimming, the team focused on a sudden movement called a “slam-start.” During this maneuver, an animal bends its tail to one side before forcefully sweeping it through the water, propelling its body forward.
“It’s the tail itself pushing off the water,” Formoso explained, comparing the motion to a swimmer launching from the wall of a pool. Because muscles rarely survive fossilization, the researchers estimated the missing tail musculature using anatomical evidence from living lizards, including Komodo dragons. They then tested different assumptions about muscle strength, tail flexibility, and water resistance to evaluate how these factors affected acceleration.
Different Tails, Different Hunting Strategies
The simulations consistently showed that
Platecarpus
Tylosaurus
could accelerate more rapidly for their body size than
Mosasaurus
Plotosaurus
. Of the four species studied,
Platecarpus
achieved the fastest modeled lunges. Its advantage came primarily from a relatively long, flexible portion of the tail that could bend farther before delivering a powerful stroke. The extent of this bending influenced acceleration more strongly than any other variable the researchers examined.
These differences suggest that
Platecarpus
Tylosaurus
were particularly well suited to ambushing prey in shallow seas.
Mosasaurus
and especially
Plotosaurus
, by contrast, appear to have been better adapted for sustained pursuit in open water. “That doesn’t mean
Plotosaurus
was slow,” Formoso said. “Its tail was built for sustained, tuna-like swimming rather than sudden bursts.”
Reconstructing the Lives of Ancient Ocean Predators
The proposed hunting strategies are consistent with other fossil evidence, including tooth wear, estimates of bite force, and chemical analyses that provide clues about mosasaur ecology. The researchers also investigated exceptionally large individuals, including a
Mosasaurus
reconstructed from a New Jersey fossil preserved at the New Jersey State Museum in Trenton. Although the precise swimming speeds remain uncertain, the results provide what the researchers describe as the first numerical estimates of burst swimming performance for marine reptiles from the dinosaur era.
Formoso, who also advised the documentary series
Prehistoric Planet
on mosasaur movement, studies how animals descended from land-dwelling ancestors adapted to aquatic environments. Her team is making its modeling tools publicly available so other scientists can investigate the swimming abilities of extinct animals, including species without close living counterparts. The approach relies on physical principles that have remained unchanged for millions of years. “Physics is physics,” she said.
Reference: “Mosasaur tail morphology reveals burst swimming performance and ecological diversity” by Kiersten K. Formoso, Nicholas Hebdon, Frank E. Fish, Robert L. Cieri and Michael B. Habib, 7 October 2026,
Current Biology
DOI: 10.1016/j.cub.2026.09.036
Funding: U.S. National Science Foundation, Geological Society of America, Paleontological Society

title: Scientists Say a Simple Blood Test Could Reveal Depression
content:
Scientists have identified a potential biological marker for depression hidden in the aging patterns of certain white blood cells. Credit: Shutterstock
Scientists have discovered that aging immune cells may hold a hidden blood-based clue to detecting depression.
Scientists have discovered that the biological aging of certain white blood cells may provide an important clue to depression, potentially opening the door to a blood test that could help identify the condition.
The study found that measuring how quickly these immune cells age can help predict emotional and cognitive symptoms of depression, including hopelessness and loss of pleasure. Interestingly, the same biological markers were not associated with physical symptoms such as fatigue or changes in appetite.
Why Depression Is So Difficult to Detect
Doctors currently diagnose depression primarily by evaluating symptoms reported by patients. Although blood tests may help eliminate other possible medical explanations, there is still no established biological test that can reliably identify depression or detect its earliest signs.
Part of the challenge is that depression does not affect everyone in the same way. Some people develop physical (or somatic) symptoms, including exhaustion, reduced appetite, or agitation. Others experience changes in thinking and mood, such as persistent hopelessness or anhedonia, a condition characterized by an inability to experience pleasure or maintain interest in activities that were once enjoyable.
“Depression is not a one-size-fits-all disorder—it can look really different from person to person, which is why it’s so important to consider varied presentations and not just a clinical label,” said study author Nicole Beaulieu Perez, assistant professor at NYU Rory Meyers College of Nursing. “Our study reveals unique biological underpinnings of mental health that are often obscured by broad diagnostic categories.”
Why Researchers Studied Women With HIV
Depression occurs more frequently among people living with certain conditions that affect the immune system, including HIV. Several overlapping factors may contribute to this increased risk, such as ongoing inflammation, social stigma, and socioeconomic challenges.
Women living with HIV face particularly high rates of depression. When depression goes untreated or unrecognized, it can interfere with their ability to participate in medical care and consistently take antiretroviral medications, which are essential for managing HIV.
“For women with HIV who may be experiencing depression, we want to better understand what’s going on and catch it earlier so that it doesn’t harm their whole overall health,” said Perez.
To investigate possible biological connections between depression and HIV, the research team focused on accelerated biological aging. Previous studies have linked this process to both conditions.
Unlike chronological age, which simply counts the years since a person was born, biological age reflects changes occurring within the body over time. Researchers can estimate biological age using tools known as “epigenetic clocks,” which analyze chemical changes to DNA. These modifications can influence how genes function without altering the underlying genetic code.
Blood Samples Reveal a Surprising Depression Link
The researchers examined information from 440 participants in the Women’s Interagency HIV Study, including 261 women living with HIV and 179 women without the infection.
To evaluate depression, they used the Center for Epidemiologic Studies Depression Scale (CES-D), a standardized 20-item questionnaire designed to assess both physical and nonphysical symptoms.
Blood samples were then analyzed using two different epigenetic clocks. One estimated biological aging across multiple types of cells and tissues, while the other focused specifically on monocytes, a type of white blood cell involved in the body’s immune defenses.
Monocytes help the immune system respond to infections and other threats. They are especially important in HIV infection, and previous research has found elevated monocyte levels in people experiencing depression.
The results revealed a notable difference between the two aging measures.
Biological aging in monocytes was associated with nonphysical depression symptoms, particularly anhedonia, hopelessness, and feelings of failure. This relationship appeared in women both with and without HIV.
However, the same aging measure was not associated with physical symptoms of depression.
“This is particularly interesting because people with HIV often have physical symptoms like fatigue that are attributed to their chronic illness rather than a depression diagnosis. But this flips that on its head because we found that these measures are associated with mood and cognitive symptoms, not somatic symptoms,” said Perez.
The broader epigenetic clock, which measured aging across multiple cell and tissue types, showed no association with depression symptoms.
These differences suggest that examining biological aging in specific immune cells may reveal connections to mental health that are missed when researchers measure aging more generally.
Could a Blood Test Transform Depression Diagnosis?
Although the findings are promising, Perez emphasized that additional research is necessary before measurements of immune cell aging can become part of routine depression diagnosis or treatment.
The study identifies a potential biomarker, but it does not establish a clinically validated blood test for depression. Researchers will need to investigate the relationship further and determine how reliably these biological signals can identify depression across different populations.
Eventually, such a test could complement traditional mental health assessments, potentially helping clinicians recognize depression sooner and tailor treatment to individual patients.
One possible application would be using a person’s biological profile to help predict which antidepressant medication is most likely to be effective. This could reduce some of the uncertainty involved in finding appropriate treatment.
“I think about the adage, ‘What gets measured gets managed.’ An aspirational goal in mental health would be to combine subjective experience with objective biological testing,” said Perez. “Our findings bring us a step closer to this goal of precision mental health care, especially for high-risk populations, by providing a biological framework that could guide future diagnosis and treatment.”
Reference: “Monocyte epigenetic age acceleration is linked to non-somatic depressive symptoms in women with and without HIV” by Nicole Beaulieu Perez, Ke Xu, Yanxun Xu, Lang Lang, Kathryn Anastos, Maria L Alcaide, Mardge Cohen, Sadeep Shrestha, Andrew Edmonds, Jacquelyn Meyers, Seble Kassaye, Igho Ofotokun, Gypsyamber D’Souza, Bradley Aouizerat and Leah H Rubin, 11 May 2026,
The Journals of Gerontology: Series A
DOI: 10.1093/gerona/glag083
Additional study authors include Ke Xu of Yale University; Yanxun Xu, Lang Lang, Gypsyamber D’Souza, and Leah Rubin of Johns Hopkins University; Kathryn Anastos of Albert Einstein College of Medicine; Maria Alcaide of the University of Miami Miller School of Medicine; Mardge Cohen of Stroger Hospital of Cook County Health System; Sadeep Shrestha of the University of Alabama at Birmingham; Andrew Edmonds of UNC Chapel Hill; Jacquelyn Meyers of Downstate Health Sciences University; Seble Kassaye of Georgetown University; Igho Ofotokun of Emory University; and Bradley Aouizerat of NYU.

title: Late-Night Snacking Could Be Putting Your Liver at Risk
content:
Eating late at night may have an unexpected downside for your liver. Credit: Shutterstock
A study of nearly 200,000 people links late-night eating to up to 30% higher liver disease risk, suggesting that your last meal of the day could matter more than you think.
Eating late at night may have consequences beyond weight gain and poor sleep. A major study led by Oregon Health & Science University (OHSU) suggests that regularly eating after dinner or close to bedtime is associated with a higher risk of liver disease.
The findings, published in Clinical Gastroenterology and Hepatology, link late-night eating to two liver conditions: metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (fatty liver disease) and cirrhosis. For the study, late-night eating was defined as consuming food after dinner or after bedtime.
Earlier research has connected nighttime snacking with obesity and heart disease. This time, scientists wanted to determine whether the habit might also be associated with liver problems.
“A few studies have hinted at this idea, but this is among the first long-term analyses to explicitly draw the connection to fatty liver disease,” said lead author Robert Wilechansky, M.D., a hepatologist at OHSU who specializes in liver transplantation.
How Your Body Clock Affects Liver Health
Wilechansky became interested in the relationship between meal timing and liver health partly because of the health challenges faced by night shift workers. Working overnight can disrupt the body’s natural sleep-wake cycle, and these workers experience higher rates of obesity and heart disease.
Fatty liver disease affects as much as 30% of the U.S. population, making it an important public health concern. Wilechansky wanted to explore whether something as straightforward as adjusting meal times could help reduce the risk.
“We know the liver is very much in tune with the body’s circadian rhythms,” he said. “So we’re interested in changing the timing of eating in a way that could make a difference in health without changing the composition of what people eat.”
Late-Night Eating Linked to 20% to 30% Higher Liver Disease Risk
To investigate, the research team examined information from three major nationwide studies: the Nurses’ Health Study, the Nurses’ Health Study II, and the Health Professionals Follow-up Study.
Together, these datasets included self-reported dietary and lifestyle information from nearly 200,000 participants. Researchers categorized people according to their eating habits and examined how those patterns related to reports of fatty liver disease and cirrhosis.
The results revealed a notable association. Participants who reported eating late at night had rates of liver disease that were 20% to 30% higher than those who did not report the habit.
Although the findings raise concerns about nighttime eating, Wilechansky emphasized that most people with fatty liver disease do not progress to its most severe complications.
“It’s important to remember, of the people who developed fatty liver disease, only a small fraction develop serious forms of the condition like liver cirrhosis,” Wilechansky said. “Even so, the big take-away here is that confining your calorie intake to several hours before bedtime might be beneficial.”
Why Eating Before Bed May Disrupt Metabolism
The findings add to growing evidence that the body’s internal clock plays an important role in how it processes food. This biological timing system helps coordinate sleep, metabolism, and other essential functions throughout the day and night.
Andrew McHill, Ph.D., a study co-author, associate professor, and sleep and circadian physiologist at OHSU, explained that the timing of everyday activities can influence health in ways that researchers are continuing to uncover.
“We are seeing over and over again that the timing of behaviors, whether it’s sleep, eating, or exercise, really matters,” said co-author Andrew McHill, Ph.D., associate professor and sleep and circadian physiologist at OHSU. “For example, we have shown that eating during the night, when the internal biological clock is promoting sleep, reduces the ability of your body to metabolize foods as efficiently and can eventually lead to obesity, diabetes, and now poor liver health.”
Previous experiments involving animals have also shown that the liver is particularly vulnerable when eating schedules become misaligned with the body’s normal sleep cycle. These findings offer a possible explanation for the connection observed in the new human study.
Scientists Are Testing Whether Earlier Meals Can Protect the Liver
Despite the association, the researchers caution that the results do not establish that late-night eating directly causes liver disease. The analysis was observational and relied on participants’ own descriptions of their eating habits, which were collected using relatively broad definitions.
Additional research is needed to determine whether shifting meals to earlier hours can actually improve liver health.
Wilechansky is now working with an OHSU team that is recruiting participants for a new study. Rather than relying solely on previously collected self-reports, the researchers plan to monitor eating habits directly and investigate whether eating earlier produces measurable improvements in people with underlying fatty liver disease.
This next phase will help determine whether adjusting meal timing could become a practical way to support liver health without requiring major changes to the foods people consume.
“Our findings add to the growing body of literature linking late-evening eating patterns to adverse metabolic and liver outcomes,” the authors write.
Reference: “Late-Night Eating is Associated with MASLD and Cirrhosis: The Nurses’ Health Study and Health Professionals’ Follow-Up Study” by Robert M. Wilechansky, Kevin Casey, Andrew W. McHill, Andrew T. Chan and Tracey G. Simon, 10 October 2026,
Clinical Gastroenterology and Hepatology
DOI: 10.1016/j.cgh.2026.09.047
The research was supported by the American Association of the Study of Liver Diseases Foundation, award CTORA24-179910.

title: Scientists Discover a Potential Early Warning Sign of Alzheimer’s in Adults As Young as 45
content:
Alzheimer’s disease is a progressive neurological disorder that gradually damages memory, thinking, and behavior. It is the most common cause of dementia and is associated with the accumulation of abnormal proteins in the brain, including amyloid-beta and tau. Credit: Stock
Researchers have identified a potential early warning sign of Alzheimer’s disease in middle-aged adults experiencing subtle concerns about their memory and thinking.
Adults as young as 45 who expressed concerns about their memory or thinking had elevated levels of a blood biomarker associated with Alzheimer’s disease, even though brain scans showed no detectable structural changes. The findings from the University of Otago suggest that biological signals linked to Alzheimer’s may emerge long before conventional imaging can identify abnormalities.
Researchers analyzed data from the Dunedin Multidisciplinary Health and Development Study, focusing on a blood plasma biomarker called pTau181, which has been strongly associated with Alzheimer’s disease in older adults. At age 45, participants reported concerns about their cognitive health, completed detailed cognitive assessments, and underwent MRI scans. Their biological aging was also assessed using DunedinPACE.
Alzheimer’s-Related Changes May Begin Decades Earlier
Lead author Dr. Ashleigh Barrett-Young, from the University of Otago’s Department of Psychology, says the findings add to evidence that processes associated with Alzheimer’s may begin decades before clinical symptoms become apparent.
“This means there may be an important window for prevention, which remains one of the most promising approaches for Alzheimer’s disease,” she says.
Although higher pTau181 levels were associated with self-reported cognitive concerns, researchers found no detectable changes in brain structure. The results raise the possibility that subtle cognitive changes could emerge before they become measurable through standard assessments. However, further research is needed to determine whether these early signals predict subsequent cognitive decline.
“This highlights the need for careful research to understand how early changes relate to later outcomes.”
Blood Biomarkers Offer Promise, but Important Questions Remain
Blood tests that detect Alzheimer’s-related biomarkers could eventually make early identification more accessible. However, such tests are not yet available for routine clinical use in Aotearoa New Zealand, and scientists still need to establish what elevated pTau181 levels mean for otherwise healthy middle-aged adults.
“Understanding the earliest stages of disease development is essential for designing effective prevention and treatment strategies, even if clinical tools are still some way off,” Dr. Barrett-Young says.
“Importantly, biomarkers like pTau181 reflect risk, not certainty.”
An elevated reading does not establish that someone has Alzheimer’s disease or will develop it. Long-term follow-up will be necessary to determine how these blood measurements relate to future cognitive health.
A Long-Running Study Tracks the Biology of Aging
The research draws on the Dunedin Study, which has followed participants across decades to investigate how health and aging develop throughout life. With the age 52 assessment now complete, researchers have additional opportunities to examine how earlier biological measurements relate to changes in middle age and beyond.
Dunedin Study Director Professor Moana Theodore credits Dr. Barrett-Young’s leadership and the contributions of New Zealand researchers to international aging research.
“Following the recently completed and highly successful age 52 assessment, we are entering the next stage of the research with momentum,” she says.
“The University of Otago Dunedin Study continues to inform global aging policy by demonstrating aging as a lifelong process allowing for better targeting of preventative healthcare.”
Professor Theodore also emphasizes the commitment of participants, who continue to provide personal health information despite the uncertainty surrounding emerging biomarkers. Individual pTau181 results are not shared because the test remains a research tool and its long-term implications are not yet understood.
“They take part to support future generations, knowing that this biomarker is still at an early, research-only stage and that individual results are not shared because scientists do not yet understand the long-term outcomes.
“Many have seen first-hand the multiple ways dementia can affect families and hope that the information that they provide will be used to reduce disease and help others.”
Reference: “Plasma pTau181 is associated with subjective cognitive concerns but not objective cognitive decline or structural brain integrity measures in midlife” by Ashleigh Barrett-Young, Erin E. Cawston, Brigid Ryan, Wickliffe C. Abraham, Antony Ambler, Tim Anderson, Kirsten Cheyne, Elizabeth Goodin, Sean Hogan, Renate M. Houts, David Ireland, Annchen R. Knodt, Jesse Kokaua, Tracy R. title: 75,000-Year-Old Neanderthal Skeleton Reveals a Mysterious Spear Wound Aimed at the Heart
content:
View of the entrance to Shanidar Cave in Iraqi Kurdistan. Credit: Graeme Barker
A Neanderthal’s fatal wound points to a possible spear attack aimed at the heart, offering a rare glimpse of prehistoric violence.
A small, round hole in a Neanderthal’s shoulder blade suggests a wooden spear pierced the chest about 75,000 years ago. The remains, found in a cave in Iraqi Kurdistan, may preserve the earliest known evidence of lethal violence between individuals involving a wooden spear in the fossil record of the human lineage.
The individual, known as Shanidar A, was approximately 45 years old at death. A Cambridge-led team unearthed the remains in 2020 at Shanidar Cave. Alongside the shoulder blade, archaeologists recovered a mostly complete right hand, two left ribs, a fragment of a right rib, and seven teeth. Their findings are published in
Scientific Reports
The ventral (left) and dorsal (right) views of the Shanidar A scapula. Ventral is the front of the scapula, the side that faces the ribs (chest). Dorsal is the back of the scapula. Credit: Emma Pomeroy
A broken tooth suggests care
One of those teeth records an earlier injury that Shanidar A survived. An incisor at the front of the lower jaw had split lengthwise, leaving only half in place, while neighboring teeth had rotated inward. Substantial tartar, also called dental calculus, had accumulated along the broken tooth’s exposed root canal. That buildup suggests the tooth remained in the mouth for some time after what the researchers identify as major blunt-force trauma to the front of the face.
“Surviving a blow that splits a tooth in this fashion, then continuing to live and eat for a period of at least a year and maybe more, would have required care and support from other Neanderthals,” said Dr. Emma Pomeroy, the study’s lead author from Cambridge’s Department of Archaeology.
Pomeroy suggests that others may have provided soft food while Shanidar A recovered from the initial injury. Previous research on sediment from the cave indicates that people there were soaking plant foods before cooking them around the same period. “There’s no doubt that Shanidar A would have had difficulty communicating and been in absolute agony for a long period of time.”
Bone fragments trace a fatal strike
The shoulder blade preserves evidence of a different, apparently fatal injury. This broad, flat bone, called the scapula, is so thin in places that light can almost pass through it. Yet Shanidar A’s left scapula survived nearly intact beneath 7.5 meters, or about 25 feet, of rock and sediment.
“It’s extraordinary to have a perfectly preserved scapula from 75,000 years ago. These bones are so thin that you often don’t get complete scapulae from modern burials,” said Pomeroy. “We were able to lift it out in one piece from under almost eight meters of rock and sediment.”
The hole in the scapula and the fragments found embedded in the sediment below the perforation. Top left: Ventral view of the hole in the scapula, showing two refitting fragments. Top right: The linea muscularis, highlighted by the dashed line, indicates that the fragments are correctly refitted. Bottom: 3D rendering of the hole and fragments embedded in the sediment underneath the scapula in situ prior to conservation. Credit: Dr Emma Pomeroy
The exception was a circular hole 15 millimeters wide, roughly 0.6 inches across. Beveling around its edges is characteristic of an exit wound. The researchers reconstructed a strike that entered the left side of the chest from the front, passed through a lung and likely major arteries, and punched through the left shoulder blade, causing rapid death.
Tiny bone fragments displaced by the weapon helped establish its direction. Their positions suggest the spear entered from above and traveled downward. The team also fitted some fragments back into the hole, matching faint ridges where muscles had marked the bone.
The hole’s shape points to sharpened wood, the researchers argue, because a flint or stone spear tip would leave a flat or angular opening. The wound could therefore provide the first evidence that sharpened wooden spears were used in the prehistoric Middle East.
“Holes left by recreations of spears from this time are an excellent fit for the one we found in the Neanderthal scapula,” said Pomeroy, a fellow at Newnham College, Cambridge. “That early technology absolutely works for this wound.”
Various views of the mandibular left lateral incisor that had been spilt longitudinally. Views of the tooth, from left to right: top (chewing surface), bottom (root end). Middle: toward the front of the dental arch (mesial), toward the lips (labial), toward the back of the dental arch (distal), and toward the tongue (lingual). Credit: Emma Pomeroy
Wood usually decomposes, leaving few weapons from such distant periods available for comparison. Some survived in waterlogged conditions at Schöningen, Germany, where spears dating to around 200,000 years ago were discovered in the 1990s. Early Neanderthals were living in Europe at that time.
Made from carefully selected timber, the Schöningen spears had weight distributions suited to throwing, much like modern javelins. Some exceeded 2 meters, or about 6.6 feet, in length and were probably used to hunt large game. An even older example, the earliest known rounded wooden spear, is more than 400,000 years old. Only its pointed end survived, recovered from the shoreline at Clacton-on-Sea in the United Kingdom in 1911.
“What evidence we have suggests that Neanderthals and their ancestors developed woodworking and weapon-making skills many thousands of years before the death of Shanidar A. This package of capabilities could have spanned the full range of Neanderthal homelands, from Wales to Siberia,” said Pomeroy.
A hunting accident remains possible
Identifying the likely weapon does not establish why it struck Shanidar A. The researchers suspect the fatal thrust may have been an intentional “heart shot,” although a hunting accident remains possible.
“The position of the wound and the force required to push it right through the Neanderthal’s body bear the hallmarks of an intended kill shot directed towards the heart,” said Pomeroy.
Close-range hunting could also have put people in danger from one another’s weapons. As Pomeroy noted, “Animals such as mammoths may have been hunted up close with thrusting spears, so it’s easy to imagine lethal injuries.”
The left scapula of Shanidar A, photographed in the University of Cambridge’s Leverhulme Centre for Human Evolutionary Studies. Credit: University of Cambridge
The circumstances cannot be recovered, including whether modern humans might have been involved. The archaeologists consider violence between Neanderthals the most straightforward interpretation.
“All we can ever know about the end of this Neanderthal’s life is that it was violent, and came at the end of a wooden spear,” said Professor Graeme Barker, a fellow of St. John’s College, Cambridge, who leads the Shanidar Cave excavations.
“Evidence of systematic violence is extremely rare in deep prehistory. The vast majority comes from periods of settled farming communities thousands of years after hunter-gatherer societies like our Neanderthals.”
“The remains of Shanidar A reflect the dual nature of so much of what we recognize as human. On the one hand, we have evidence of a terribly violent end. On the other, this was clearly an individual who was cared for during their lifetime,” said Pomeroy.
Neanderthals returned to bury their dead
Shanidar, a vast cave in the foothills of Iraqi Kurdistan and one of the world’s best-known Neanderthal sites, has yielded other evidence of care. Another individual, found elsewhere in the cave and living thousands of years after Shanidar A, had a paralyzed arm, arthritis, deafness, and partial blindness. Their long survival despite those conditions has been interpreted as evidence that others cared for them.
Excavations led by Ralph Solecki in the 1950s uncovered ten individuals, including a “cluster” of four who occupied the same spot despite dying at different times. Their placement suggested that Neanderthals returned there to bury their dead.
Multiple images of one of the spears found at Schöningen, Lower Saxony, Germany, in 1995, which is believed to be around 2-300,000 years old. This is Schöningen Spear II, replicas of which have been tested as javelin-style throwing spears. Credit: Dirk Leder et al. (eds), Weapons, Tools and Technology (2026)
Together, these indications of social support and ritual surrounding death helped overturn the Victorian portrayal of Neanderthals as brutish and subhuman. Evidence of sophistication has continued to emerge through cave art and jewelry, while genetic analyses have revealed interbreeding between Neanderthals and modern humans.
“It is fascinating to have evidence for both compassion and violence amongst Neanderthals, our closest evolutionary cousins, embodied in this one individual,” said Barker.
Shanidar A is one of three further Neanderthals found in the burial cluster by the Cambridge-led team since 2015. The team now identifies five individuals, four adults and an infant, within a space just 1.5 meters long, 1 meter wide, and 1 meter deep, or about 5 by 3 by 3 feet.
The remains lie directly behind a large upright boulder, described as a “prominent marker,” with thin layers of sediment separating them. Shanidar A occupies the deepest position found so far and may have been the first individual laid there. The body rested on its back with the head facing east, matching the orientation of the body directly above it.
“The best explanation is intentional and symbolic funerary behavior,” said Pomeroy. “These Neanderthals returned to the same place to lay their dead to rest. Some were deposited before the earlier body had fully decomposed, so this was happening within years or decades.”
Reference: “Evidence for funerary behaviour and lethal trauma in a new Neanderthal individual from Shanidar Cave” by Emma Pomeroy, Christopher O. Hunt, Lucía López-Polín, Nohemi Sala, Ana Pantoja Pérez, James Holman, Jessica Twyman, Paul Bennett, Tim Reynolds, Ross Lane, Duncan Pirrie and Graeme Barker, 15 October 2026,
Scientific Reports
DOI: 10.1038/s41598-026-69193-z

title: NASA’s Roman Space Telescope Is Sharper Than Anyone Expected
content:
NASA’s Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope is already exceeding expectations after engineers made incredibly precise adjustments to sharpen its view of the universe. Credit: NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center
NASA’s Roman Space Telescope has achieved nearly 30% better optical performance than required, promising stunningly sharp views of the universe and its greatest mysteries.
NASA’s Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope is performing even better than scientists anticipated after engineers completed an extensive series of tests and precision adjustments. The work has sharpened the observatory’s focus and brought its primary instrument closer to regular scientific operations. Remarkably, the telescope’s Wide Field Instrument is now delivering optical performance nearly 30% better than predicted.
“All of Roman’s sweeping surveys will rely on the Wide Field Instrument,” said Dave Hickey, a Wide Field Instrument systems engineer at NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland. “Many of the mission’s primary goals, like studying dark matter and dark energy, wouldn’t be possible without it, so it’s both exciting and a huge relief to see that it’s working well!”
NASA Tests Roman’s Powerful Wide Field Instrument
After the Wide Field Instrument was
activated in September
, engineers began carefully examining its components to confirm that each worked properly on its own and as part of the complete system.
The first tests focused on the instrument’s
18 detectors, each roughly the size of a sticky note
, along with their associated electronics. Engineers then evaluated the element wheel, which holds filters and other optical components. These allow selected
wavelengths of light
to reach the detectors and can separate incoming light into its individual colors.
Next came the calibration system. Engineers activated its internal LEDs, which produce different colors of light and can be precisely adjusted in brightness through commands sent from Earth. By measuring how the detectors respond to varying light levels, the team can identify and compensate for small differences in sensitivity.
The team also examined the instrument’s alignment mechanism and moved it from the deliberately unfocused position used during launch to the position expected to provide the clearest images. Additional tests confirmed that the thermal control system could maintain the temperatures needed for the instrument’s components to operate correctly.
“Calibrating an instrument is like tuning a piano or guitar before a concert,” said Maxime Rizzo, a Wide Field Instrument systems engineer at NASA Goddard. “You adjust everything until it’s just how you want it and then leave the settings alone so it performs consistently while you use it.”
Roman’s Telescope Was Already Close to Perfect Alignment
While one group evaluated the Wide Field Instrument, another concentrated on refining the telescope’s optical alignment to produce the sharpest possible images.
“The telescope’s performance was excellent even before we began adjusting the alignment of all the mirrors and other optics, thanks to exceptional preparatory work done on the ground prior to launch,” said Matthew Bolcar, Roman’s optical systems lead at NASA Goddard. “All of the testing and modeling work done at Goddard and by contractors at L3Harris and BAE Space and Mission Systems left only small corrections for us to make to bring everything into near-perfect alignment.”
Achieving that level of accuracy is particularly challenging for a space telescope. Even with extensive preparation, engineers cannot perfectly predict how launch forces and the conditions of space will affect its delicate optical components. Roman
launched on August 30
“Our ground testing couldn’t exactly reproduce the environment Roman would experience in space, such as the absence of gravity,” Bolcar said. “And there are also slight differences in temperature variations and moisture content. Despite those challenges, the recent assessments showed that our ground testing was excellent, with both instruments either matching or exceeding the performance we had predicted.”
A Mirror Adjustment Smaller Than a Human Hair
To produce a clear image, light entering Roman must travel along a carefully controlled path, reflecting between mirrors and other optical components before reaching one of the telescope’s two instruments. Even extremely small alignment errors can affect how precisely that light is focused.
Fortunately, the telescope’s optics were already positioned so accurately that only tiny corrections were necessary.
“We moved the secondary mirror by about one-sixteenth of the diameter of a human hair,” said Alden Jurling, a senior optical engineer working on Roman at NASA Goddard. “This adjustment nudged the height of the secondary mirror above the primary. If we scale that height up to the height of the Empire State Building, the change in height is a little bit less than you would get by stacking a single U.S. penny on top of the tip of the tower.”
Despite its almost unimaginable smallness, that adjustment could significantly improve the scientific observations Roman will make.
Engineers first refined the focus of the Coronagraph Instrument, which had initially produced images that were slightly blurry. The problem was less severe than anticipated and proved relatively straightforward to fix. Following the correction, the instrument is now performing at the high level the team expected.
Work on the Coronagraph Instrument is continuing. Engineers will fine-tune its camera settings and identify the best configurations for its deformable mirrors before demonstrating its ability to block unwanted light in the coming weeks.
With the coronagraph’s focus corrected, the team returned to the Wide Field Instrument for additional optical adjustments.
NASA’s Roman Telescope Exceeds Image Quality Predictions
The results were better than expected. Roman’s Wide Field Instrument now has optical performance nearly 30% better than the mission team had predicted, meaning its future observations should be even sharper than originally anticipated.
Engineers had established an image quality requirement of approximately 90 nanometers RMS (Root Mean Square). This value describes the average scale of optical imperfections relative to an ideal wavefront. At 90 nanometers, the error is already extraordinarily small, measuring roughly 1,000 times less than the thickness of a human hair.
But Roman surpassed that demanding requirement. After the final corrections, the Wide Field Instrument achieved an optical error of just 63 nanometers RMS.
The improvement represents an important achievement for a telescope designed to conduct vast surveys of the universe. With its optics performing beyond expectations, Roman will be able to capture exceptionally detailed images as scientists investigate dark matter, dark energy, and other major cosmic mysteries.
“All of the images from Roman’s cosmic surveys will be even sharper than we expected,” Jurling said. “It’s a great outcome from years of careful modeling, precision metrology, and testing.”

title: 40 Years of Superconductor Science Just Got Turned Upside Down by a Stunning Discovery
content:
Superconductors are remarkable materials that can conduct electricity with zero resistance when cooled below a critical temperature. They hold enormous potential for revolutionizing energy transmission, medical imaging, powerful magnets, and quantum computing. Credit: stock
A material that carries electricity without resistance may be held back by its own structure, challenging 40 years of assumptions about copper-based superconductors.
A crystal that scientists thought had the same structure throughout is actually a patchwork of two subtly different arrangements of atoms. The boundaries between those regions are hundreds of times wider than expected, so broad that they behave almost like a structure in their own right rather than a simple dividing line.
The material belongs to a family called cuprates, copper-based superconductors that can carry electricity without resistance at unusually high temperatures for superconductivity, although those temperatures are still very cold. High-temperature superconductivity underpins research into future power grids, medical scanners, and quantum computers. Its promise also includes magnets far more powerful than those possible today.
X-rays reveal the crystal’s internal divisions
To examine the crystal’s interior, researchers in the University of Warwick’s Department of Chemistry worked with the European Synchrotron Radiation Facility (ESRF) in France. They used scanning 3D X-ray diffraction, a technique that works somewhat like a medical CT scan but maps the arrangement of atoms inside a crystal. This allowed the team to build a three-dimensional picture deep within the material for the first time, revealing structural differences throughout its bulk. The study was published in
Physical Review Letters
3D X-ray reconstruction revealing regions of different crystal structures in a 214 cuprate superconducting material. Dark regions have the expected structure, while lighter regions show a different structure. The boundary regions between them are approximately 150 nm wide. Credit: Professor Mark Senn / University of Warwick
A recent €150 million upgrade to the ESRF made the technique possible. The researchers see its reach extending beyond superconductors, allowing scientists to examine a wide range of materials in three dimensions at a previously inaccessible level of detail and investigate how their internal structures shape their behavior.
Crystal boundaries may hinder superconductivity
Within superconductivity research, the team suspects that this hidden structural complexity is common across the wider cuprate family. It may also occur in related materials being explored for superconductivity under extreme pressure.
Professor Mark Senn, of the University of Warwick’s Department of Chemistry, who led the study, said, “For 40 years, the working assumption has been that these materials are the same all the way through, and nearly all the theory is built on that picture. We’ve shown it doesn’t hold. The crystal is fundamentally patchworked and textured, with unusually wide boundary regions that likely work against superconductivity rather than just sitting alongside it.
“This might explain why some materials perform better than others and means some existing bulk measurements will need to be reinterpreted and future theoretical models built that incorporate this structural complexity.”
Reference: “Giant Domain Walls and Intrinsic Heterogeneity in 214 Cuprate Superconductors” by Evie Ladbrook, Jon P. Wright and Mark S. Senn, 17 September 2026,
Physical Review Letters
DOI: 10.1103/r62x-kt5j

title: Study Uncovers a Surprising New Way Deadly Brain Cancer Spreads
content:
Open microfluidic chip for studying glioblastoma invasion under high-viscosity conditions. The device uses a removable cap to control cell migration and a ring-shaped micropillar array to simulate confinement, revealing nuclear deformation and YAP activation. Long-term exposure to viscous fluid (7.1 cP) allows researchers to track changes in tumor cell movement, flexibility, and invasive behavior. Credit: Microsystems & Nanoengineering
Scientists have uncovered evidence that glioblastoma cells can retain a lasting mechanical memory of their surroundings.
Glioblastoma, one of the deadliest forms of brain cancer, spreads by sending tumor cells into surrounding healthy tissue. Along the way, those cells encounter an unusual physical challenge: fluid at the tumor’s invasive edge can be about eight times more viscous than fluid near its dying center.
New research suggests that prolonged exposure to this thicker environment may actually help glioblastoma cells invade. After spending a month in highly viscous fluid, laboratory-grown cancer cells became smaller, more deformable, and better able to squeeze through narrow spaces. Rather than simply slowing their movement, the increased resistance appeared to produce lasting changes in how the cells behaved.
How Thick Fluid Changes Brain Cancer Cells
Researchers from Chongqing General Hospital and Chongqing University in China investigated this effect using two human glioblastoma cell lines, U-251 and LN-229. They cultured the cells for one month in a medium with a viscosity of 7.1 centipoise, comparable to conditions near a glioblastoma’s invasive boundary.
Both cell lines adapted in ways that improved their ability to navigate confined spaces. Compared with cells grown under normal viscosity, the adapted cells traveled farther and faster through the researchers’ experimental device, despite the added resistance of the thicker fluid. Microscopic observations showed that they had also become smaller and more flexible, allowing them to pass through gaps that would otherwise restrict their movement.
The team also observed changes inside the cells as they squeezed through narrow passages. Their nuclei became visibly compressed, while a protein called YAP accumulated inside the nucleus. YAP helps cells respond to mechanical forces by influencing gene activity, making its movement into the nucleus a sign that physical stress was activating cellular signaling pathways.
A New Device Reveals Hidden Effects of Viscosity
Studying these changes required an experimental system that could separate the effects of fluid viscosity from other physical forces. Conventional closed microfluidic devices can introduce additional complications, including friction against channel walls, limited access to oxygen and nutrients, and difficulties maintaining cells for extended periods.
To overcome these limitations, the researchers developed an open microfluidic chip containing a two-layer membrane, a removable cap, and an array of microscopic pillars. The design allowed scientists to control when cell migration began, observe nuclear deformation in real time, and maintain cell cultures for up to one month.
The work was published in the journal
Microsystems & Nanoengineering
Different Cells Adapt Through Different Molecular Pathways
Although both glioblastoma cell lines developed similar physical characteristics, their underlying molecular responses differed sharply.
U-251 cells underwent changes resembling a mesenchymal transition, a process associated with increased cellular mobility and invasiveness. They showed increased activity in genes linked to tumor invasion, including
. LN-229 cells, however, demonstrated comparable changes in shape and movement without substantial lasting shifts in gene expression.
Protein analysis also showed that some viscosity-associated changes persisted after the cells were returned to normal viscosity. This suggests that prolonged mechanical exposure can leave a lasting biological imprint rather than producing only a temporary response. The different molecular reactions of the two cell lines indicate that glioblastoma cells may reach similar invasive states through different biological mechanisms.
Could Tumor Viscosity Become a Cancer Treatment Target?
The findings suggest that fluid viscosity may do more than physically impede tumor cells. Sustained exposure could help shape the characteristics that allow glioblastoma cells to migrate through surrounding tissue, potentially influencing how the disease spreads.
The open chip also offers a potential tool for investigating treatments under more realistic mechanical conditions. Because it supports long-term imaging, direct cell access, and standard laboratory culture methods, researchers could use it to test drugs targeting YAP signaling, the cellular skeleton, or other pathways involved in mechanical adaptation.
Reference: “Open micro-valley chip reveals long-term viscosity-induced glioblastoma cellular invasion states” by Haotian Jiang, Chao Xu, Cheng Zeng, Xun Liu, Lan Deng, Yi Jian, Chuan Shao, Gang Zhang, Yigang Shen, Yaxiaer Yalikun, Ming Li, Tao Tang and Nan Wu, 13 April 2026,
Microsystems & Nanoengineering
DOI: 10.1038/s41378-026-01241-0

title: Scientists May Have Solved a Billion-Year-Old Mystery About DNA’s Evolution
content:
Chemistry
A building block of DNA may have served as a molecular sunscreen, with laboratory tests suggesting thymine could have helped early genetic molecules survive by making UV damage easier to reverse. Credit: Stock
On an early Earth exposed to intense ultraviolet radiation, the evolution of DNA may have depended on an unexpected molecular advantage.
Early life on Earth faced intense ultraviolet (UV) radiation from the sun without the protection of an ozone layer. Yet DNA came to rely on thymine, a chemical building block that is more prone to UV damage than uracil, its counterpart in single-stranded RNA.
A study at
Texas A&M University
suggests that thymine may have helped early genetic molecules survive by directing that damage into a form that was easier to reverse. The findings, published in
Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
(PNAS), offer a possible explanation for why thymine replaced uracil as genetic systems evolved toward DNA.
Thymine favors more reversible UV damage
Dr. Peter Rentzepis, a professor in the university’s Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, and his research assistants, Keyvan Khosh Abady and Negar Karpourazar, compared thymine and uracil under controlled UV conditions designed to mimic the intense radiation environment of primordial Earth. They used biophotonics, a field that applies light-based methods to biological questions. Their tools included absorption, fluorescence, and Raman spectroscopy, which examine how molecules absorb, emit, or scatter light.
“We found that thymine tends to direct UV damage into a more reversible form, suggesting that early genetic molecules may have survived intense sunlight not by avoiding damage, but by controlling it and making it easier to self-repair,” said Khosh Abady. “In that sense, thymine may have acted as a molecular sunscreen, absorbing harmful UV energy and keeping the damage confined to the genetic bases rather than allowing it to harm more vulnerable parts of the molecule.”
Genetic ingredients from Earth or space
Rentzepis and his team plan to extend their investigation to an earlier stage in the origin-of-life process by examining the forces that brought thymine, uracil, and other components of early genetic systems together.
“We hope to explore whether life’s chemical building blocks formed and assembled entirely on Earth or whether some were delivered to our planet from elsewhere by meteorites and later incorporated into early genetic systems,” said Khosh Abady. “We are grateful to Texas A&M University and our research sponsors for supporting this work and enabling us to explore fundamental questions about life’s origins.”
Light signatures could help detect pathogens
The measurements also establish a new reference framework that could support research beyond molecular evolution. The team identified distinct spectral signatures, recognizable patterns in how the molecules interact with light, that may eventually have practical uses.
“The distinct spectral signatures we measured could support applications in faster, more sensitive pathogen detection and in monitoring whether UV disinfection has effectively inactivated microorganisms, particularly in water-treatment systems,” said Khosh Abady.
Reference: “UV photodamage pathways and the evolutionary selection of thymine over uracil in early genetic systems” by Keyvan Khosh Abady, Negar Karpourazar and Peter M. Rentzepis, 3 August 2026,
Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
DOI: 10.1073/pnas.2615278123
This study was supported by Air Force Office of Scientific Research Grant number FA9550-20-1-0139 and Texas A&M Engineering Experiment Station funds.

title: Scientists Discover a Hidden Electrical Signal in the Heart That Could Predict Sudden Death
content:
Sudden cardiac death occurs when the heart’s electrical system unexpectedly malfunctions, triggering a dangerous heart rhythm that prevents the heart from pumping blood effectively. It can strike without warning, even in seemingly healthy individuals, and is often fatal within minutes without immediate treatment. Credit: Stock
Researchers have discovered a previously unrecognized electrical signal in the heart that could help predict sudden cardiac death before it strikes.
Sudden cardiac death can strike without warning, killing people who appear healthy and have no known history of heart problems. For decades, doctors have struggled to identify who is most vulnerable, even though a potentially lifesaving treatment already exists. Now, researchers have discovered that clues to these fatal events may have been hiding in one of medicine’s most familiar diagnostic tests.
Scientists at the
University of California, Berkeley
developed an artificial intelligence system that detects subtle electrical patterns in routine electrocardiograms (EKGs) associated with an increased risk of sudden cardiac death. In a study published in
, the AI outperformed a standard clinical screening method, raising the possibility that doctors could identify more at-risk patients before their hearts suddenly stop.
AI Detects Hidden Warning Signs in Heart Recordings
To develop the system, researchers analyzed more than 440,000 EKGs collected over six years through Sweden’s health care system. By linking these recordings to death certificates, they trained an AI model to recognize electrical patterns associated with subsequent sudden cardiac death. The training data included recordings from healthy individuals, patients with known heart problems, and people who later died from cardiac causes.
The researchers then evaluated the algorithm using separate patient datasets from San Diego and Taipei, testing whether its predictions remained reliable across different populations. The model identified subtle variations in EKG waveforms that conventional clinical assessments often overlook. Although these patterns were associated with an increased risk of sudden cardiac death, the underlying physiological mechanism remains unknown.
A More Accurate Way to Identify High-Risk Patients
Doctors commonly assess sudden cardiac death risk by measuring how much blood the heart pumps out with each contraction. Known as the ejection fraction, this measurement helps determine whether a patient qualifies for an implantable cardioverter defibrillator, a device that monitors dangerous heart rhythms and delivers an electrical shock when necessary.
The AI system identified a group of patients with a 7% annual rate of sudden cardiac death. By comparison, patients classified as high risk using the conventional measure had an annual rate of 4.6%. Many individuals flagged by the AI would not have been considered high risk under existing clinical criteria, suggesting that routinely collected EKGs could help identify patients who might otherwise go undetected.
“Medical decisions are really hard, and I think that’s why AI is so exciting for me,” said Ziad Obermeyer, an associate professor at UC Berkeley’s School of Public Health and the study’s lead author. “We can not only make better decisions, but also start to understand what’s actually going on with these patients before their heart stops.”
Why Sudden Cardiac Death Is Difficult to Predict
More than 300,000 Americans die from sudden cardiac arrest each year. Unlike a heart attack, which occurs when blood flow to part of the heart becomes blocked, cardiac arrest involves a sudden failure of the electrical signals that coordinate the heartbeat. The heart can no longer pump blood effectively, and without immediate treatment, death can occur within minutes.
Although CPR and defibrillation can restore circulation in some cases, approximately 90% of people who experience cardiac arrest outside a hospital do not survive. Victims include older adults with established cardiovascular disease and seemingly healthy young athletes with no known history of heart problems.
Implantable defibrillators can prevent some of these deaths, but determining who needs one remains difficult. About two-thirds of devices implanted in patients considered high risk never have to deliver a shock. Meanwhile, many people who eventually suffer sudden cardiac death never undergo the specialized cardiac evaluations that might identify a problem.
“In some fraction of those people, we could have prevented those deaths if we had just known it in time,” Obermeyer said.
Moving From AI Predictions to Preventive Care
Obermeyer and his colleagues are now collaborating with health systems in Sweden, Taiwan, and the United States to apply the algorithm to hospital EKG databases. Patients identified as high risk could be contacted by clinicians and offered wearable monitors that continuously record their heart’s electrical activity.
These recordings could help researchers determine what physiological changes produce the patterns detected by AI. They may also provide additional evidence to guide decisions about implanting defibrillators. However, further research is needed to establish whether using the algorithm to guide treatment actually reduces deaths.
Building the system required nearly a decade of work to assemble the necessary medical data. Obermeyer said that obtaining large, detailed datasets remains one of the biggest obstacles to developing clinical AI tools.
“Good AI starts with good data,” he said. “Unfortunately, data like the ones we used for this study are incredibly hard to access. It’s a big part of why there’s so little clinical AI in use today.”
The researchers hope that studying the electrical abnormalities identified by the model will help explain what happens inside the heart before it suddenly stops. Such findings could eventually improve both risk prediction and understanding of the biological processes behind sudden cardiac death.
Obermeyer has also launched a
where people interested in assessing their own risk of sudden cardiac death can provide basic information and an email address. The research team may contact participants about EKG analysis once the AI tool becomes more widely available.

title: Panasonic to start mass-producing perovskite solar glass a year earlier, in April 2029
content:
Panasonic to start mass-producing perovskite solar glass a year earlier, in April 2029
Panasonic Holdings
has moved up the start of full-scale mass production of its glass-type perovskite solar cells by a year. Production will now begin in April 2029 at its mass-production technology base in Nagahama, Shiga Prefecture, instead of in fiscal 2030.
Earlier this month
, Panasonic was reported to be discussing an earlier date.
The cells are designed to turn windows and exterior walls into power sources. Panasonic says it uses proprietary materials, inkjet coating and laser processing, which give flexibility in size, transparency and design, along with glass-sealing technology for the durability that building materials require. Early-production models went on sale in September 2026 and are made at the company’s development base in Moriguchi, Osaka. Panasonic is installing them with customers to build up construction and operation know-how, and plans to establish mass-production techniques and accelerate market formation before Nagahama starts.
Panasonic cited technology progress, growing market expectations and government policy support for the decision. It also pointed to rising demand for decarbonization and renewable energy, and to limited roof space on urban buildings, which makes windows and walls attractive for generation. The company was selected in September 2025 for Japan’s NEDO Green Innovation Fund project and is developing mass-production and construction technology under it. It did not disclose capacity, investment or subsidy amounts.
Panasonic has been testing the technology in buildings. It
launched a BIPV field test with YKK AP in Osaka
in November 2025, and it first
launched power-generating windows with perovskite solar cells
in 2023.

title: 深谋智能带臂作业四足机器人“伏魔”中标国网电力-索比光伏网
content:
深谋在业内率先中标国网电力智能带电作业人形机器人项目，成为国内首个实现该场景落地交付的人形机器人企业，为此，深谋带电作业人形机器人“伏安”获《电力具身智能技术创新奖》和《电力具身智能创新应用案例奖》。
近日，深谋再次宣布，其智能带臂作业四足机器人“伏魔”中标国网电力《面向复杂环境的四足机器人》项目。
能源、电力、运输等高价值行业的复杂环境对具身智能设备提出非常高的技术要求，比如：电力隧道管廊是城市输配电网络的大动脉，因其封闭，潮湿，隐蔽，环境恶劣，一旦发生故障影响面极广，定期巡检十分必要。
旧式电缆隧道占比仍在60%以上，长期处于无电、无网及无固定在线监测条件运行状态，普遍存在空间狭窄、通风不畅、潮湿积水及结构不平整等复杂工况。旧式电缆隧道依靠人工巡检，运维人员携带照明、测温、气体检测及记录设备，劳动强度大、人员存在缺氧、中毒、滑倒、磕碰、触电及应急撤离困难等安全风险。目前的四足机器人巡检还有很多局限性，仅停留在视觉巡检各类仪表及示数等，不能有效使用工具开展作业；难以实现狭窄路径、落差较大地段、积水路段的通过性，不能在无电无网环境下工作等等，大大限制了四足机器人的巡检能力与效果。
在复杂空间环境智能作业对具身智能设备的严苛要求令人生畏，而凭借多年硬核技术积累，深谋在以下方面尽显竞争优势：
*四足机器人本体结构及其与机械臂、灵巧手的集成化设计
*机器人在狭窄空间、复杂地形与积水环境下的运动稳定与通行能力
*旧式电缆隧道无电、无网及弱光照条件下的环境感知定位与多源信息融合
*面向配网隧道场景的多模态数据基础采集与缺陷识别算法、动态视觉伺服算法
*抗电磁干扰灵巧手与复杂环境智能交互作业能力
*有效检测O₂/CO/CO₂/CH₄/H₂S等有害气体浓度（深谋独有的声表面波单芯片多通道无线无源传感器）、
*低照度、潮湿及水雾干扰等复杂环境条件下的图像质量增强与信息恢复
部分技术属业内首创，最终击败主流厂商，深谋自研四足机器人“伏魔”中标国网电力。
需要看到的是，四足机器人好像已经无处不在，而其实真正能够在能源、电力复杂环境中智能作业而非普通巡检的四足机器人却寥寥无几，是绝对的蓝海市场，具有巨大的商业价值。
真正满足高价值行业客户需求的具身智能产品，因为其技术复杂度带来的稀缺性，完全可以实现较高的价格，深谋认为代表未来产业的具身智能产品在商业化落地的初期本来就不应该只是廉价商品，企业如果做不到，不愿深耕为行业创造价值、高难度系数的技术和产品，只是跟风做寻常场景一般巡检，而这早已是僧多粥少的红海市场，最终只能靠不断降价把代表未来产业的具身智能做成廉价的硬件平台，而深谋的思路显然与之截然不同，且已经不断在电力等高价值行业率先破局。
当前具身智能行业现状存在这样的问题，一边是高价值行业对于真正能干事的具身智能产品巨大的刚性需求，另一边是部分资本热衷于套模型、拱虚火、订单“左手”倒“右手”，一些企业沉迷于跟风讲故事、做表演，拿不出真正满足行业需求的东西，却又一再感叹商业化落地难盈利难。
反观深谋，不盲从此一时彼一时的所谓“热点”，深耕硬核技术，直击行业痛点，接二连三地以高技术难度，不同形态的具身智能产品中标高价值行业，拿下真正的市场化商业化项目，一再刷新行业认知。

title: 一座车棚里的零碳密码！周云杰带你看懂海尔园区怎么“算碳账”-索比光伏网
content:
近日，海尔集团董事局主席、首席执行官周云杰在其个人社交媒体上发布视频，带网友打卡海尔零碳园区。
​视频从园区一座普通的车棚讲起：棚顶是光伏板，底下是充电桩，旁边连着储能柜，车棚背后其实是靠AI能源机器人智能调度的微电网场站，也是海尔新能源零碳园区系统的“最小单元”。
零碳园区，核心是算平两本账
去年12月，首批52个国家级零碳园区建设名单公布。海尔上合工业园冰箱互联工厂，是山东首批、青岛唯一省级零碳试点园区。
零碳园区难在哪？
周云杰概括其核心是统筹三件事：电从哪来、电往哪走、电什么时候用。
国内工业碳排放过半来自各类产业园区，工厂既要核算产线能耗、电价波动，还要算出口产品碳足迹。传统模式下，发电、储能、生产各管各的，碳账很难平衡。
周云杰打了个通俗比方：零碳不是不排碳，是把碳排放的账做平。就像家庭有两本账，一本记支出，是用能产生的碳；一本记收入，是风光发的绿电产生的绿证。两本账对得上，才算零碳。
源网荷储+AI，让每度电都算数
海尔的零碳全区方案就五个字：源、网、荷、储、AI。
整套体系依托海尔新能源 “纳晖” 能源互联网生态平台，打造会算账、懂调度的能源管家。系统还设置电芯、储能柜、平台三层安全防护，出现异常可分级研判，必要时自动断电。
当前，这套零碳方案已经走向海外，落户18个工业园区、服务超700家企业。
周云杰表示，真正的零碳园区，不是简单堆光伏设备，而是让每一度电都可管理、可交易、可增值。
