title: 推动煤电与新能源融合发展 拓展新能源开发消纳空间-索比光伏网
content:
近日，国家能源局印发《关于推动煤电与新能源融合发展的实施意见》(以下简称《意见》)。《意见》提出近区公用煤电机组协同送出消纳、公用热电联产煤电机组清洁供热、海上风电接入沿海公用煤电机组协同送出消纳、自备煤电机组打捆利用、煤电厂自身用能绿色替代五类场景模式，并明确了技术要求和配套政策机制。现围绕政策意义和导向、场景模式和技术要求、落实路径三个方面，谈几点认识和理解。
一、准确把握煤电与新能源融合发展的意义和政策导向
要准确理解融合发展对协同推进新能源消纳与煤电节能降碳的重要意义。《意见》将煤电节能降碳与新能源消纳统筹推进，支持新能源承担更多电量和热量供应，减少煤炭消耗和碳排放。煤电通过改造提升调节能力，为新能源腾让利用空间;新能源逐步替代部分燃煤发电和供热，进而带动煤电降碳。两者协同使存量煤电改造与新能源开发相互促进，将新能源消纳增量转化为实际减排成效。
要准确把握融合发展对引导新能源开发布局与调节能力相匹配的重要导向。《意见》明确，融合应在不降低煤电对电力系统支撑调节能力的前提下实施，新能源规模要与煤电改造升级提升的调节能力匹配。若开发规模超出实际消纳能力，风光集中出力时仍可能出现弃风弃光，影响项目经济性和降碳成效。因此，应结合煤电设施布局及改造条件，统筹不同季节、时段的调节能力和消纳条件，合理确定新能源规模及储能储热配置，提高实际利用水平。
要充分认识融合发展引导盘活存量设施、拓展新能源消纳空间的重要作用。《意见》将煤电送出线路、供热系统和厂区空间等纳入融合场景，有利于提高既有基础设施利用效率，减少重复建设，增强项目经济性。这与新能源集成融合发展所强调的多能互补、空间集约利用和协同运营理念一致，也为落实《新型电力系统建设“十五五”规划》中煤电向支撑调节性电源转型要求以及《可再生能源发展“十五五”规划》提升新能源系统友好性能、推进非电利用布局提供了具体路径。
二、深刻理解煤电与新能源融合发展的场景模式与技术要求
准确把握五类融合场景模式及其融合方式。《意见》提出了五类融合场景模式。一是新能源直接接入近区公用煤电机组实现协同送出消纳，支持煤电机组通过深度调峰改造进一步压减最小技术出力，为近区新能源接入腾让发电空间，鼓励配套改造建设储能储热系统，实现“低储高放”，并利用煤电送出线路协同送出。二是新能源直接接入近区公用热电联产煤电机组实现清洁供热，支持新能源与公用煤电机组供热系统协同运行，提升调峰顶峰能力等涉网性能，降低供热受阻比例，在北方民生采暖地区鼓励通过改造建设电制热、储热等电热协同系统，实现新能源替代煤电供热。三是海上风电直接接入沿海公用煤电机组实现协同送出消纳，面向送出路由紧张的沿海地区，统筹海上风电规划、登陆点选址、汇集站布局，通过煤电机组深度调峰改造和送出系统增容改造，实现海上风电登陆后依托沿海煤电机组及其送出系统协同运行送出。四是近区新能源接入自备煤电机组实现打捆利用，支持自备煤电通过深度调峰改造压减最小技术出力，“应融尽融”为近区新能源打捆利用腾让发电空间，近区新能源可通过公用电网或直接接入，实现对自备煤电机组的发电量和供热量替代。五是厂内或近区新能源直连煤电厂用能系统实现煤电自身用能绿色替代，支持充分利用厂区设施空间条件开发厂区内分布式新能源或近区新能源直接接入煤电厂用能系统，参与厂用电等自身用能环节，提升绿色用能替代水平。此外，《意见》对近区公用煤电机组协同送出消纳模式、海上风电协同送出消纳模式、自备煤电机组打捆利用模式，均提出鼓励碳排放较融合前降低5%以上，力争降低10%以上的要求。
系统落实融合发展的七方面技术要求。《意见》从改造力度、接网方式、接入线路、计量方式、涉网性能、技术研发和标准体系七个方面提出了明确要求。一是加大煤电节能降碳改造实施力度，现役煤电机组通过调节能力改造、增设储能储热系统、送出系统增容、建设厂区或近区新能源等方式，为新能源消纳利用腾挪空间。二是明确新能源接网方式，融合项目应与公用电网形成清晰的物理界面与责任界面，公平承担相关费用，新能源可选择直接接入煤电厂区内储能储热设施，也可选择接入厂内配电装置或送出系统第一接入点，形成统一整体后共用线路送出，原则上新能源场址边缘距离煤电厂址直线距离不超过100公里。三是优化新能源接入线路方案，系统梳理煤电厂接入条件和新能源接入线路走廊资源，优化路径方案，尽量减少与存量电网线路的交叉跨越。四是明确计量方式，融合项目应具备煤电与新能源独立电量计量条件，合理设置关口计量表，确保计量界面清晰、结果准确。五是确保涉网性能，融合项目的新能源应实现“可观、可测、可调、可控”，新能源和储能均应满足相关技术标准和安全要求，不应影响煤电厂涉网性能，并网运行后的应满足电力系统安全稳定各项相关标准要求。六是鼓励技术研发和应用，加强储能储热、宽温域熔盐等储热介质、超(特)高温热泵、电加热设备、协同运行平台等技术研发。七是加快标准体系建设，建立完善规划设计、投产验收、生产运行标准体系，健全协同运行和参与电力、绿证、碳交易等市场的标准规范，形成融合项目碳排放核算方法。
三、大力推动煤电与新能源融合发展落地实施
扎实做好资源普查与基础条件调查。充分利用全国风光资源普查试点已形成的技术方法和工作机制，以普查成果为科学依据，摸清煤电厂周边风光资源分布、可开发规模及出力特征，核查厂区和近区可利用空间，做到有的放矢。同步调查煤电调节能力及改造潜力、既有送出和供热设施条件，梳理周边电热负荷及用能特点，为场景选择和项目布局提供依据。
科学引导融合项目规划布局。各省能源主管部门要做好规划引导和统筹协调，拟开发项目企业要做好具体项目的深入论证，因地制宜确定适宜的融合场景、开发区域和项目规模，加强与电力、供热及国土空间规划衔接。统筹新能源建设、煤电改造及储能储热配置，衔接建设时序，综合评估消纳能力、供能保障和项目经济性，形成具备实施条件的项目储备。
积极推进融合项目技术和模式创新。面向五类场景模式，加强储能储热、宽温域熔盐等储热介质、超(特)高温热泵及协同运行平台等技术研发和集成应用，推进产学研用协同创新。结合新一代煤电升级专项行动，推动融合项目中的煤电机组提升深调、快调、高效调节能力;对照新型电力系统建设试点中系统友好型新能源电站的要求，推动融合项目中的新能源通过风光储智慧联合调控运行等方式提升系统友好性能，提升高峰时段置信出力水平;结合不同场景模式特点，探索设施共用、多能互补和协同运行的适宜模式，开展示范验证，结合实践完善相关标准，总结可复制的技术模式与运营经验。
用好用足配套政策工具和保障措施。《意见》从开发实施模式、市场交易、资金支持、组织实施四个方面明确了配套政策机制。创新融合项目开发实施模式，鼓励由同一主体统筹开发实施，或通过建立联合体实施运营，鼓励各地区因地制宜探索创新运营方式，合理体现融合项目环境价值。加大中央资金支持力度，对符合条件的融合项目予以资金补助，鼓励发电企业拓宽投融资渠道。各省级能源主管部门还应会同有关部门结合本地区实际制定细化政策举措，完善市场和价格机制，加强要素保障。(水电水利规划设计总院副院长

title: 供给交易双向发力 河北可再生能源建设跑出加速度-索比光伏网
content:
促进绿色发展全面转型，加快建设美丽河北。我省坚持开发与消纳并举，持续扩大绿电供给能力，多点拓展绿电应用场景，通过供需两端协同发力，加快构建安全可靠、绿色低碳的新型电力系统，为全省高质量发展注入源源不断的绿色动能。
在华能深泽100兆瓦风力发电项目现场，施工人员正在对风机塔筒进行吊装。项目建设16台塔筒高度为160米的风机，全部投产后，预计每年可提供清洁电能超2.2亿千瓦时，节约标煤6.6万吨。
华能上安电厂副总工 杜彦楼：目前三台风机已完成并网工作，剩余的各风电机组正在紧张地安装中，整个项目预计10月底完成全容量并网发电。项目在满发的情况下，每小时可发10万度电，能够满足12500户居民一天的用电量。
据介绍，该项目由华能上安电厂负责建设。华能上安电厂火电装机256万千瓦，是我省最大的火力发电厂。企业负责人介绍，面对能源转型的时代大潮，“十四五”初期，他们厂就开启了从单一火电领域向综合能源市场发展的绿色低碳转型之路。
华能上安电厂厂长 张广忱：过去的五年，我们新能源发展的速度非常快。截至目前，我们厂新能源装机容量达到了258万千瓦，已经超过了火电。
“十四五”时期，上安电厂建成了“北线张承、西线石保、沿海沧州”三大清洁能源基地，涵盖了“农光互补、渔光互补、山地风电、储能电站”等多种业态。目前，该厂共建设新能源项目25个，覆盖雄安新区、石家庄、张家口、承德、沧州、衡水、保定等多个地区。
华能上安电厂厂长 张广忱：到“十五五”末，全厂总装机容量要突破1000万千瓦，也就是新能源装机容量要达到火电的将近三倍。
上安电厂的新能源发展之路，正是我省推进新型能源强省建设、能源绿色转型的生动实践。截至2025年年底，我省可再生能源累计并网装机突破1.5亿千瓦，占全省电力总装机比重73.4%，远超“十四五”规划目标。
今年1-8月，全省可再生能源并网装机达16140.3万千瓦，同比增长15.8%。如何让绿电用得好?我省多点拓展绿电应用场景。在沧州市运河区工业园区，由华润集团打造的2.8兆瓦屋顶分布式光伏项目，发出的绿电就首先供给了园区内企业使用。
华润沧州市运河区工业园屋顶分布式光伏项目负责人 王泽涛：采用的是自发自用、余电上网的模式，按正常的天气，大约每天发1.4万度电，在满足工业园区内用电需求同时，多余的电还可以送至国家电网。
同样是在运河区，沧州市首个光储充智能超级充电站季屯充电站已经投入使用。作为绿电的消费和调节端，充电站上方光伏板自发绿电，在优先供给充电站自用的同时，多余电量可以存入配套的储能系统，在用电高峰反向释放给电网来平抑负荷压力，打通了“绿电生产-储能调节-绿色消费-反向馈网”全链条。
沧州市民：充电方便而且充电点也特别多，价格便宜、亲民，平常时候在这儿充电，二十块钱就可以充满了。
加快构建布局合理、服务高效的充换电服务体系，为绿色出行提供坚强电力保障。截至今年8月底，沧州地区充换电业务用电量达5.5亿千瓦时，同比增长88.88%。
沧州供电公司营销中心电力负荷控制员 杨小同：依托我们的用电信息采集系统，可以实时监测充电设施运行状态和配网负荷情况，精准研判充电需求热点区域，为充电设施选址布点、配网增容改造提供良好的数据支撑，全力保障充电设施用得上、充得快、服务好。
国网河北电力数据显示，河北南网绿电交易规模连续三年实现跨越式增长，截至8月21日，今年累计绿电交易量突破百亿千瓦时大关，标志着我省绿电交易进入到了规模化高质量发展新阶段。

title: 国家能源局：2026年1-9月全社会用电量同比增长3.9%-索比光伏网
content:
日前，国家能源局发布2026年109月电力数据显示，9月份全社会用电量8997亿千瓦时，同比增长1.2%。
从分产业用电看，第一产业用电量135亿千瓦时，同比增长4.1%。第二产业用电量5800亿千瓦时，同比增长1.7%;其中，工业用电量5751亿千瓦时，同比增长1.8%，高技术及装备制造业用电量1167亿千瓦时，同比增长4.6%。第三产业用电量1852亿千瓦时，同比增长4.9%;
其中，充换电服务业、互联网数据服务用电量分别为168亿、98亿千瓦时，增速分别达到57.0%、35.4%。城乡居民生活用电量1210亿千瓦时，同比下降6.0%，主要原因是受“沙德尔”台风等极端天气影响，9月上中旬华中、华东、南方等高负荷区域降温用电需求下降。
1～9月，全社会用电量累计80734亿千瓦时，同比增长3.9%。从分产业用电看，第一产业用电量1182亿千瓦时，同比增长3.4%。第二产业用电量51098亿千瓦时，同比增长4.1%;其中，工业用电量50632亿千瓦时，同比增长4.3%，高技术及装备制造业用电量9619亿千瓦时，同比增长8.7%。第三产业用电量16109亿千瓦时，同比增长6.8%;其中，充换电服务业、互联网数据服务用电量分别为1315亿、793亿千瓦时，增速分别达到55.4%、41.6%。城乡居民生活用电量12346亿千瓦时，同比下降0.3%。

title: 困在电力体系里的光伏：谁是敌人，谁是朋友？-索比光伏网
content:
紧跟党中央，跳出电力体系，拥抱新经济。
在我们集体躺平之前
近期许多人都有同样的感受，光伏人在“集体躺平”，大家都认为：近期一两年行业不会好，未来五年十年也看不到爆发点。
多做多错，不如躺平。
当遇到难以解决的问题的时候，不妨看看伟人面临困境时是如何破局的。
一百年前，毛泽东在《中国社会各阶级的分析》开篇问：“谁是我们的敌人？谁是我们的朋友？”
他说：“这是革命的首要问题。”
对今天的光伏行业来说，这也是首要问题：近五年间，我们至少有一半的努力，方向都是错的。
纵观人类历史，能源变革从来都不只改变能源行业本身，而是覆盖科技、经济、政治、民生等方方面面。
连科学家评定文明等级，都是以可掌握能源的多寡作为唯一标准。可以说能源约等于生产力。
我们光伏企业也都非常清楚，光伏在海外各国承担的都是什么职能：能源安全、拉动GDP、无电区供电……
但在中国，大部分光伏人寄望的出路，都只在电力体系，本质是要期望电网自发变革来适应新能源的发展。
认不清自身，认不清敌人，也认不清朋友。
怎么搞能源革命？
- 不要对电网心存幻想，光伏需要在电力体系之外，建立或融入新的发展体系。
- 紧紧拥抱新能源最坚实可靠的盟友——党中央。
作为一个行业观察者和记录者，我近五年看到党中央许多的政策与新能源的发展不谋而合，说明高层对未来中国的发展是有很明确规划的，所需的，是中国光伏企业提供一份系统而详细的“自荐信”。
为什么光伏要跳出电力体系
电网、部委、党中央所思所想
先说电网，不要心存幻想，电网不是新能源的盟友。
光伏和电网的关系，是在《可再生能源法》、“碳中和”目标推出后被“绑”在一起的，但当能源变革逐步走向深水区，双方必然会发生“冲突”。
电网欢迎大基地扩大管理规模（正面），与新能源共同承担绿电减排工作（中性），但对新能源的不稳定性带来的挑战与灵活特性削弱了电网的管理（负面）。
当新能源在新型电力系统中真正占主导时：
- 我们是否还需要电网？
- 电网是否会发生形态变化？
- 管理难度极具上升后，电网监管调度会更严格还是更开放？
新能源对电网中的改革进取者来说是创新、是机遇，而且未来为新型电力体系重构的新电网也可能更强大，但对大部分普通电网人员来说，新能源给电网带来的大多是负面的：增加工作量与削弱决策权。
能源局、工信部、发改委等主管部门，更多的是推动光伏产业自身的健康发展，或者是能源体系的建设，在这方面，它们不仅是坚实盟友，更是在产业发展初期起到了至关重要的推动作用。但它们受职能所限，对光伏产业的扶持也多仅限于能源领域。
所以在过去几年的“内卷”之中，各部委大多通过“高门槛”、“强约束”的方式，通过管理的方式让产业更健康（详细可参见我2024年初的报告），但难以解决最关键的“大市场”。
要真正摆脱“马尔萨斯陷阱”，避免恶性厮杀的同时，也避免极致僵化，只有把市场做大。
接下俩，只需很简单的逻辑推导就能得出：能真正让市场做大的是谁？
一直被我们忽略的最强力量。
接下来我们详细分析：为什么党中央是光伏的天然盟友，又为何光伏是党中央的最佳辅助。
一封“自荐信”：
从制造问题到成为答案
谈到解决行业内卷，几乎没有人想到借助党中央的力量：一是不敢想，二是光伏产业1500GW的产能，让国家解决销路，是不可能的。
一个行业亏损，不成为中央支持它的理由。
那我们能否换个思路呢？党中央天然是新能源最强的政治盟友，因为新能源是中国目前少数能够同时回答经济、政治、社会、国防和全球发展问题的关键行业。
中央与部委、电网和地方政府不同，它不只计算某一张资产负债表，而必须考虑中国未来十年、二十年的能源安全、经济增长、社会稳定、产业竞争和国际空间。
光伏必须在这个更大的价值体系中证明自己的价值，才有可能“下一步触及电网利益”的，否则电网利益边界就永远是光伏的天花板。
所以我们不是向党中央证明行业有多困难，而是证明新能源能够帮助国家解决什么。
我们来梳理一下党中央面临哪些挑战：
第一 新旧动能转换：把有效需求不足变成新的发展目标
中央经济工作会议把国内需求不足列为当前经济运行面临的困难。对此最常见的理解，是居民消费不足、企业投资意愿不足。
但更深一层的问题是：新的发展目标还没有形成。
中央政府很早就意识到新发展目标的重要性，早在2018年1月，国务院批复《山东新旧动能转换综合试验区建设总体方案》，山东成为首个国家级综合试验区。
新旧动能转换是发展经济学概念，指通过新模式、新业态、新技术、新材料新能源替代传统动能，推动经济增长方式向质量增长型、内涵增长型和知识密集型转变。其实质是增长向发展转换，核心机制包括价格机制向价值机制转换、经济规模向规模经济转换等，理论基础为对称平衡论。
看着很复杂，但核心就一句话：新发展目标。
我之前在《越努力，越失败：光伏内卷背后的集体行动困境与政府治理路径》中提到了马斯克提太空光伏目标让中国光伏估值涨了3000亿的例子，在中美“G2”新格局的背景下，中国在AI、芯片领域追赶的同时，也要学会如何把这些关键要素组合起来，形成新经济。
过去几十年，中国在许多领域主要承担跟随者和生产者角色。欧美提出产品、生活方式和市场规则，中国把它做出来，并且做得更快、更便宜。今天，中国在光伏、储能、电动汽车和部分智能制造领域已经走到全球前列。前面没有成熟答案可以照抄，继续等待别人提出需求，只会让领先的制造能力重新回到价格竞争。
这里存在一个极大的误区：全社会对新能源在新旧动能转换工作的定位，大多是“新酒装旧瓶”，对各种新要素很感兴趣，但对于新的模式、体系缺少整体规划。
讲这么多“新”字，如果还一味做“旧”的事，那和慈禧“马拉火车”一样荒唐。
而在组合新要素方面，没有比从新能源入手更合适的了。
历史上的能源变革，从来不只是替换一种燃料。煤炭和蒸汽机创造了工厂、铁路和现代工业城市；石油、电力和内燃机创造了汽车、航空、流水线生产和大众消费。新能源和智能制造真正可能创造的，也不只是更多绿电，而是一套新的生产和生活方式。
碳中和，也不是光伏的天花板。
我们应该围绕光伏清洁、便捷、低廉的特性思考：任何地区和场景，有足够便宜、稳定的电后，可以做什么？
可以为中国带来的新发展目标：1、增强居民电力消费改善生活体验，中国相比美国还有三倍的增长空间；2、无电场景电气化升级；3、新能源+智能制造与应用带来的新经济。
光伏、储能和智能制造可以共同推动零碳工厂、智能农业、数据中心、电动交通、工业热泵、海水淡化、绿色化工、冷链物流、分布式社区能源和新型城市基础设施。每一个新场景都会形成设备、工程、软件、金融、运维和服务需求。
用足够多的能源，转化为衣食住行；提出目标，唤醒企业的热情。
这就是新目标的意义。
第二 从增量中解决分配，用安全感解决中国式焦虑
中国面临收入差距、就业压力、人口老龄化和公共服务负担。如果只在既有财富中做剧烈切分，企业家、资本和人才会改变投资与资产安排；如果只等待增长自然惠及底层，新增财富又可能继续集中。
相对可行的道路，是一方面完善税收、社保和公共服务，另一方面创造新的、能够被公共制度分享的财富增量。
新能源加智能制造可能提供这部分增量，尤其是在西部。
但路径绝不是“在荒漠里铺满光伏板”这么简单。完整链条至少有七步：
第一，把西部的阳光、风、土地和区位转化为长期能源资产，而不是一次性土地收入。
第二，建设电网、储能、水资源和交通体系，把波动电力变成可以支撑生产的稳定能源。
第三，用低成本绿电吸引材料、绿色化工、算力、农产品加工、冷链、装备制造等真实负荷，而不是再复制一批光伏工厂。
第四，让当地劳动者进入建设、制造、运维和服务环节，获得工资和技能，而不是只在建设期提供临时劳动。
第五，让地方国企、村集体、公共基金或者居民通过合适机制持有部分能源与园区资产，获得长期收益，而不是只有开发商获得现金流。
第六，把新增税收和公共收益用于教育、医疗、养老、交通和住房，使能源收益变成居民可以感受到的公共服务。
第七，通过中央财政转移、生态补偿和全国统一市场，让资源地区、用能地区和全国居民合理分享收益。
这条链条如果能够成立，新能源创造的就不只是GDP，而是工资、资产收益、公共财政和社会保障的新来源。它可以帮助中国在迈向中等发达国家水平的过程中，把更多新增资源用于托举普通人尤其是低收入人群。
反过来，如果能源资产、并网资源、工业利润和数据权都集中在少数企业手中，西部只承担土地和生态成本，新能源同样会制造新的财富集中。新能源能够创造增量，但增量如何分配，仍然是政治选择和制度设计。
这些动作从，以光伏产业的视角来看，似乎非常遥远，但我要告诉你新疆正在给非常优厚的落户政策、营商政策呢？
第三 从输出产品走向输出新的现代化能力
中国只出口组件、逆变器和电池的模式，正在遭遇越来越多的关税、供应链审查、原产地规则和本地制造要求。越是全球领先，越不能长期依靠把产品从中国工厂运到全世界。
但世界并不缺需求。许多国家仍然缺少可靠电力、灌溉、冷链、工业园区、技术人员和现代制造能力。它们不是不想发展，而是旧式工业化高度依赖化石能源进口、巨额基础设施和长期资本，起点太高。
新能源和智能制造提供了另一条路径。
中国可以与当地共同建设光储微电网、零碳园区、农业加工、冷链、水处理、绿色化肥、数字基础设施和自动化生产线，再配套工程、融资、保险、培训、本地制造和长期运维。
这样输出的不是一批设备，而是让一个地区持续创造财富的能力。
而且这是人类历史上前所未有的在任何国家地区，无视地理位置、无视工业基础，快速部署现代化工业的能力。
这既能为中国制造创造新的全球需求，也能增强全球经济韧性。更重要的是，它为发展中国家提供了更加多元的工业化选择，减少其对单一能源、金融和技术体系的依赖。
我曾以为这些也只是我的超前构想，但近期有报道我们在南美已经用外贸收益租赁了数千平方公里土地，我们已经有企业开始在为非洲设计打造零碳工业园区。
我们现在所缺的，就是将其系统化、批量化，让新能源工业星星之火，迅速燎原。
第四 为国防和国家安全建立新的能源底盘
新能源对国家安全的意义，也不仅是减少石油和天然气进口。
光伏、储能、微电网和智能控制，可以提高边远地区、通信设施、医院、交通节点、工业基地和应急体系的独立供能能力。集中式电网和燃料运输一旦受到极端天气、灾害或者外部冲击，分布式能源可以为关键设施提供另一层保障。
新能源与智能装备结合，还会推动高可靠电池、功率器件、高效电机、能源管理、无人系统和复杂环境自主运行等军民两用能力。它降低的不只是燃料成本，更是国家对长距离补给、单一电网和外部能源的脆弱性。
我们应该思考：有电以后的新型国防是什么样子的？边关7X24小时的机器人与无人机巡逻，遍布海上丝绸之路的后勤补给，还是新型电力化作战体系？
进一步看，新能源还能连接粮食、水、算力和工业安全：电力可以支持灌溉、冷链、海水淡化、绿色化肥、数据中心和关键制造。现代国家安全早已不只是军队安全，而是能源、粮食、水、通信、工业和社会运行能否在冲击下继续维持。
同时在这种中西方对抗的背景下，发展新能源还有一层意义：通过“新能源+AI”带来的工业革命，“拉崩”资本主义制度。
随着新能源、通用AI、自动化的发展，现有的生产关系会落后于生产力。接触新能源后，我才有对“共产主义”的真正认知：当AI真正发展到取代99%的岗位时，美国这种资本主义国家如果不改善分配，绝大多数人，要么饿死，要么爆发革命。
或许数十年后，美国也会变成北欧那样的社会主义国家。
第五 帮助国民迈向中等发达国家生活
2035年，我们中国要达到中等发达国家水平，不只是人均GDP增加。它意味着普通人能够更稳定地获得舒适住房、清洁供暖和制冷、便捷交通、优质医疗教育、数字服务和更有尊严的老年生活。
这些生活都需要更多高质量能源。
如果仍然主要依靠化石能源，提高人均能源使用就会同时受到进口、价格、污染和碳排放约束。新能源提供了一条不同道路：在降低单位能源成本和环境代价的同时，扩大普通人的有效能源使用。
光伏最终的社会价值，不是让每个人看见更多组件，而是让农村家庭用得起取暖和制冷，让小企业承担得起机器和冷库，让医院、学校和养老设施拥有可靠供电，让普通人的生活不再因为能源成本和供应短缺被限制。
从这个意义上说，光伏之于未来中国，就不只是“管饱”的一种能源。它更接近粮食、电力、铁路和互联网，是决定全社会生产能力与生活上限的底层条件。
把我们的答案，变成与盟友的共识
现在可以重新回答：谁是我们的敌人，谁是我们的朋友？
电网不是敌人，但也不是可以依靠其自发意愿的天然盟友。国家发展改革委、国家能源局、工业和信息化部、国务院国资委等主管部门，是重要的制度力量，但它们只会支持符合国家目标的新能源，不会为行业利润负责。火电是可以通过容量和调节机制转化的伙伴。地方政府既可能成为发展新能源最积极的力量，也可能成为重复建设和风险外溢的制造者。金融机构、制造企业和开发商，同样会按照自己的收益与责任采取行动。
光伏最深厚的社会盟友，是所有需要更便宜、更可靠能源的人；最强的政治盟友，则是党中央推动中国式现代化、进一步全面深化改革和发展新质生产力的战略意志。
但党中央需要的不是一个等待托底的光伏行业，而是一种能够解决国家问题的新生产力。光伏行业也不能继续只说自己能发电、能减碳、能出口。它必须证明自己能够创造有效需求、改善分配、开发西部、升级工业、增强国防韧性、扩大普通人的发展权，并为全球提供新的现代化道路。
做到这一点，行业的表达方式就要彻底改变。
不要只向党中央报告行业有多困难。要把光伏放进中国未来的发展全局里，证明它如何帮助国家解决有效需求不足、社会分配、产业升级、区域发展、国家安全和全球合作。
光伏不是因为自己重要，就自然拥有朋友。
当它能够让中央实现国家目标，让地方获得长期发展，让电网获得合理回报，让火电完成角色转换，让企业和居民获得低成本能源，让更多国家拥有现代化能力，它才会形成真正强大的利益共同体。
这才是今天重新讨论“谁是我们的敌人，谁是我们的朋友”的意义。
光伏最不应该做的，是继续把自己当成一个等待被救的困难行业。我们的出路，不是让所有人来解决光伏的问题，而是把光伏变成他们正在寻找的答案。

title: New strategic role to support Wick Harbour development plans
content:
Highlands and Islands Enterprise (HIE) has announced £52,500 in funding
to support a new strategic role at Wick Harbour Authority (WHA).
According to the announcement, the position will help deliver the harbour's
master plan, develop outline business cases, strengthen organisational
capacity and identify new business opportunities.
The funding is intended to support the commercial operations of the harbour
and secure new sources of activity. The announcement specifically highlighted
opportunities in the offshore wind and wider renewable energy sectors.
Wick Harbour serves as the operations and maintenance base for the Beatrice
offshore wind farm
and also supports fishing and commercial cargo operations.
Claire Wilson, HIE's area manager for Caithness and Sutherland, said: “The
strategy manager will develop commercially viable projects and engage proactively
with potential customers and partners.”
“It will help WHA build on Wick’s established role in the renewables
supply chain, pursue new business and create wider benefits for local companies,
workers and communities.”
The new role is expected to support the harbour's long-term growth strategy
while helping to strengthen its position within Scotland's renewable energy
supply chain.

content:
The UK government announced on October 21 that the Jackdaw gas field has
been approved as part of its New Energy Wealth Fund initiative.
In the announcement, the government cited geopolitical tensions, including
recent events in the Middle East, as a source of global energy market instability
that has contributed to higher energy costs for consumers in the UK.
The government said development of the Jackdaw field will help strengthen
the country's energy security while supporting efforts to reduce energy
costs for households.
Following the announcement, Scottish Renewables said: “Today’s decision
must now be matched by a renewed drive to deliver our long-standing clean
energy ambitions.”
The organisation called on the UK and Scottish governments to address delays
in the consenting and grid connection processes, arguing that greater certainty
is needed to support investment in the renewable energy sector.
Scottish Renewables added that significant progress and investment have
already been made in renewable energy and said momentum should continue
through the development of both fixed-bottom and floating offshore wind
projects.

title: Ignitis seeks delay to Curonian Nord Offshore wind project
content:
Ignitis Group and Ignitis Renewables have submitted proposals to Lithuania’s
Ministries of Energy and Finance outlining alternative scenarios for the
future implementation of the Curonian
Nord offshore wind project.
The companies said the preferred option is to adjust the project’s implementation
schedule, allowing development to be paused and resumed when market, financing
or technological conditions become more favourable.
The proposal follows recommendations made by Lithuania’s National Audit
Office, which called for a data-driven assessment of the project’s future.
According to the companies, several issues require consideration, including
aligning permitting and development timelines with offshore wind project
requirements, linking financial commitments to the start of construction,
accelerating onshore infrastructure procedures and establishing offshore-specific
design and work organisation rules.
Ignitis Renewables is continuing preparatory activities and investments
required to obtain a construction permit in 2027.

title: Ofgem opens tender for Hornsea 3 transmission assets
content:
Ofgem has launched OFTO Tender Round 14 for the offshore transmission assets
connecting the Hornsea
3 offshore wind farm.
The milestone is expected to be the largest offshore transmission asset
tender round to date.
Officially launched on 21 October, the tender round will see investors
compete to own and operate the transmission assets for the 2.9 GW Hornsea
3 wind farm.
Hornsea 3 is currently one of the largest offshore wind projects under
construction in the UK and, once operational, is expected to generate enough
electricity to power more than 3.3 million UK homes.
According to the announcement, the successful bidders will receive a long-term,
inflation-linked revenue stream to support the operation, financing and
maintenance of the pre-built transmission assets.
Beatrice Filkin, Ofgem’s Director of Major Projects, said: “By running
a competitive process, Ofgem is helping attract the investment Britain
needs for a cleaner, more secure energy system while making sure consumers
get value for money.”

title: NKT expands Esposende power cable factory
content:
NKT has unveiled an expanded power cable factory in Esposende, Portugal,
strengthening its capabilities and capacity for medium and high-voltage
power cables.
The expansion comes two years after NKT acquired Portuguese power cable
manufacturer SolidAl back in June 2024.
“The new capacity and capabilities strengthen our ability to support our
customers as they expand and modernise their power grids,” said Carlos
Fernandez, executive vice president and head of Distribution at NKT.
The EUR 50 million investment included new production lines, equipment,
CCV capabilities and enhanced testing facilities. NKT has also added 150
employees at the site, increasing the total workforce to 580.
The expansion comes at a key time for the industry as renewable energy
deployment accelerates, increasing the need for more resilient and intelligent
electricity grids to support the transition.
“Producing clean energy is not enough. It must be transmitted safely,
distributed efficiently and delivered to households, businesses and communities.
Power cables are therefore essential infrastructure and critical to the
energy transition,” said Dr. João Esteves, Portugal's secretary of state
for the environment.

title: OpenAI, Anthropic Should Cap Compute for R&D, Say AI Safety Advocates
content: Ideas are flowing fast and furious on how AI labs can “pace” AI development so safeguards keep up with the technology’s smarts. Last week, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman laid out three scenarios he said have been considered in the industry, including merging all of the AI labs into a single entity to develop new AI safely or creating a global regulatory body like the International Atomic Energy Agency . In the background, a loose group of safety advocates and researchers have been pushing for AI companies to cap the amount of compute they put towards research and development, a limitation they argue would be particularly effective in slowing AI development. The researchers are proposing companies commit to dedicating at least some minimum share of their computational resources to safety or monitoring, and another minimum share to running AI for customers, otherwise known as inference. That would limit the share of compute that could be used to develop stronger AI capabilities through R&D, such as training new models. Limiting the availability of specialized AI chips to research would be a hard pill for the labs to swallow, however. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei in February named “raw compute” as the top factor that contributed to growth in AI capabilities, while Google DeepMind co-founder Demis Hassabis in April called compute the biggest bottleneck in AI, particularly because research experiments need so much. What’s more, the size of compute budgets can persuade top researchers to stay or bolt for a competing lab. OpenAI recruiters in past years have advertised greater access to computing resources to attract researchers from rival Google, for instance. But advocates for the proposal say the idea is worthwhile because it could buy more time for AI companies to put security and safety measures in place, helping prevent more incidents like the rogue agent hacks that have proliferated in past months. In the latest, OpenAI on Tuesday reported instances of its agents weakening their own monitoring systems meant to detect misalignment, or actions not in accord with human desires and values. “Compute allocation is specific, verifiable, and hard to game,” Thomas Larsen , a researcher at AI forecasting nonprofit AI Futures Project , told The Information. Larsen co-authored “ How to Pace The US Frontier ,” a framework of how to limit R&D compute, that the nonprofit published in August. The framework suggests labs could agree to spend 25% of their computing resources on safety, or making sure AI is aligned and won’t commit cyber crimes, 70% on customer inference at 70% and just 5% on R&D. That allocation to R&D would likely be far lower than companies’ current allocation. The proposal to limit R&D compute is still in the early days of gathering support, but some employees at AI companies are supportive of the proposal, an AI safety advocate who spoke to the employees said. OpenAI, Anthropic, Google DeepMind and SpaceXSI did not respond to requests for comment. Companies could limit R&D compute voluntarily by disclosing how they are using their compute, according to the AI Futures Project. Advocates of the proposal say the government or embedded evaluators, such as those working at Anthropic to assess its safety practices and risks, could enforce the caps. Advocates could also try to bring the proposal to lawmakers for potential AI legislation, building on existing state transparency and auditing bills and proposed bills like the FRONTIER Act , which establishes size-tiered safety obligations on models and would allow the government to restrict models in emergencies. The advocates for capping the resources used for R&D note that the labs have been addressing their compute plans as they publicize efforts to prevent more breaches. OpenAI in the last few months has shifted about 10% of its total computational resources towards alignment and safety work, we reported last week , though that proportion may have since changed. At Anthropic, “about 6% of AI R&D compute” was dedicated to safety work in July with “a separate, comparable amount” of compute going to safeguards preventing harmful responses, the company wrote in a September blog post . In fact, Anthropic said that creating a measure of compute usage for different purposes could inform actions such as safety research, or “limits on the share of compute going towards AI research agents.” However, it’s not guaranteed that definitions of categories such as “safety work” are comparable between AI companies, RAND Europe research leader Henri van Soest said. One of the goals of the proposal would be to slow down the process of recursive self-improvement, where AI companies use one generation of AI models to make their next generation more capable. Many companies, OpenAI and Meta included, have said their goals include automating research to stay ahead of the competition. Limiting how much compute companies could use for R&D would throw a wrench in that business strategy. In addition, researchers at AI labs feel immense pressure to continuously innovate because the capabilities of open models, particularly those from Chinese companies, are often able to catch up to the frontier labs within a number of months. For that reason, some policy researchers say they don’t expect to see support among politicians for a proposal like limiting R&D compute until the U.S. and China both agree to tap the brakes on AI development. Even if domestic AI companies want to slow down, “once the next improvement from China gets announced, there’s all kinds of political pressure to keep rushing forwards,” van Soest said. “I don’t think you could reasonably have a working pacing deal without an understanding with China.” Aalok Mehta , director of the nonprofit AI research institute Wadhwani AI Center and former responsible AI policy lead at Google, said he is skeptical the proposal would create much of a slowdown in the pace of AI capabilities growth. That’s because a decrease in compute allocated to R&D could encourage researchers to find ways to train models and conduct research more efficiently. “Chinese labs are compute constrained, and what that has led to is a lot of innovation in efficiency,” Mehta said. Here’s what else is going on… Big Numbers Anthropic signaled in a draft S-1 viewed by the Wall Street Journal that it could potentially spend $750 billion on compute in the next few years. The AI company had revenue of $16.3 billion and a net loss of over $80 billion in the first half of 2026. SpaceX reported $14.6 billion in third-quarter revenue on Tuesday, largely driven by growth in its renamed “Super Intelligence” business line, which generated $7.5 billion in revenue from Cursor , Grok Bot , and the company’s burgeoning neocloud business. Salesforce agreed to acquire Braze , a customer-engagement platform with AI-powered marketing tools, for approximately $5.66 billion. People on the Move Mike Clayville , the former Amazon Web Services enterprise sales chief who played a key role in expanding its business with Fortune 500 firms before departing for Stripe six years ago, is back at Amazon as a vice president. Meta Platforms ’ chief global affairs officer, Joel Kaplan , is set to leave the company next year, a Meta spokesperson said, after more than 15 years at the company in which he helped strengthen ties with Republicans including the Trump administration . A collection of giant insurance firms bought more than $740 million of CoreWeave debt connected to a cloud-computing contract with Meta Platforms in the second quarter, highlighting how insurance money and the AI infrastructure boom are becoming intertwined. Legora , an AI legal startup, raised a $550 million Series E round at an $8.8 billion post-money valuation led by Atreides Management . Neolix Technologies , which makes autonomous delivery vehicles, raised $400 million in a Series E funding round led by Boyu Capital. ASI , which builds AI software for critical infrastructure, raised $325 million in a Series C funding round at a $3 billion valuation, led by Spark Capital. Pigment , which makes AI-powered business-planning software, raised $250 million in a funding round at a $2.3 billion valuation, led by the Scaleup Europe Fund. Arda Industries , which builds AI software for manufacturing engineering, raised $160 million in a Series A funding round at a $1.5 billion valuation, led by Altimeter , Accel and Khosla Ventures. The Information first broke the news of the startup here . Reliable Robotics , which builds autonomous flight systems for aircraft, raised $115 million in new capital consisting of $90 million in equity led by Nimble Partners and $25 million in debt from Silicon Valley Bank. Nvidia is in talks to invest “hundreds of millions of dollars” directly into Firmus , an Australian AI cloud and data-center operator, after Firmus abruptly pulled its planned $5 billion IPO earlier this month. Different , which built an AI marketing system for B2B teams, raised $48 million in a seed funding round led by General Catalyst , with participation from Lightspeed Venture Partners . Baba , which uses AI to improve the Medicare experience, raised $40 million in a Series A funding round led by FirstMark Capital. Mach9 , which develops AI-powered computer-aided design software, raised a $34 million Series A funding round co-led by First Round Capital and Bessemer Venture Partners . Qualitate , which uses AI for primary market research, raised $25 million in a Series A funding round led by Insight Partners. AuxoAI , which deploys AI systems for large enterprises, raised $20.7 million in a Series A funding round led by NTTVC. Firefly , which builds an AI platform for physical safety, raised $20 million in a Series A funding round led by Definition Capital. Electric Plant Company , which built an AI model for plant health, raised $11.2 million in a seed funding round led by Onto Ventures and Climactic VC. Elon Musk said Tuesday SpaceX and Tesla have formed special committees to explore a potential merger . This is the first step toward what would be the largest mergers of all-time, bringing together Musk’s sprawling empire of electric cars, rocket launch, satellite and AI businesses. OpenAI is buying Orchestra Bio , a startup that builds AI agents to help biotech and pharmaceutical companies with drug development, the AI lab announced on Tuesday. Google announced on Tuesday that TorchTPU , its version of PyTorch , is now available open-source, a sign of how it’s trying to break Nvidia’s stranglehold on the AI industry by making it easier for developers to run AI models on TPUs . DeepSeek has open-sourced DeepInfer , the in-house framework for running its own models. The move reveals some of the technical secrets behind how the Chinese AI developer achieves high efficiency and low compute costs when running its models at scale. METR , an AI research nonprofit, reviewed Anthropic ’s internal August risk report and concluded they were not confident the report’s methodology would reliably identify risk of catastrophic harm from misalignment. Compute Labs , a startup founded on the vision of bringing more capital to the market for graphics processing units, has started a matchmaking service for companies looking to buy the chips and lenders willing to lend against them. title: Hackers Used Claude and Grok to Automate Attacks on Banks
content: A hacking group called CyberCartel used a web of AI agents powered by models from companies including Anthropic, SpaceX and Chinese lab Moonshot AI to automate cyberattacks against more than 400 Latin American financial targets, according to an investigation by the cybersecurity startup Straiker. The research, shared exclusively with The Information, is one of the first detailed reports of cybercriminals using AI models to successfully automate attacks that break into financial institutions. The AI agents used by CyberCartel, which has long targeted Latin American businesses and whose latest targets included banks and payment apps, appear to have stolen passwords and customer data and to have accessed people’s bank accounts autonomously with little human effort, the Straiker research shows. The findings indicate how AI is giving cybercriminals an edge against defenders, at least for now, as the models enable them to coordinate and carry out a large number of cyberattacks so rapidly that they overwhelm victims’ defenses. That’s a big reason so many companies are now pouring money into AI-powered defensive tools in an effort to level the playing field. “Offense is way ahead of defense right now, that’s just how it is,” said Straiker Chief Executive Ankur Shah, whose firm sells software for monitoring and securing AI agents. “Enterprises are just not ready.” After Straiker reported its findings to Anthropic last week, the AI giant investigated and quickly blocked the cybercriminals’ use of Claude, an Anthropic spokesperson said in a statement. The Information reviewed records Straiker obtained showing sensitive data stolen from specific financial institutions, but is not naming them here because Straiker is still in the process of notifying affected parties. Anthropic rattled the cybersecurity world this spring when it announced Mythos, its most sophisticated model, and warned that hackers could soon try to use models like it to overwhelm the defenses of banks and government agencies and wreak havoc. The CyberCartel campaign is the latest evidence that sophisticated cybercriminals have indeed started chaining together AI models that, even if they’re not as powerful as Mythos, can create systems that automatically find software vulnerabilities and carry out attacks. Hackers had already been using AI to speed up similar cyberattacks. Cybersecurity firm CrowdStrike reported earlier this month that it found evidence that the perpetrator of a recent hack of South Korean financial institutions that resulted in data leaks used an open-source Chinese AI agent and Chinese large language models. Straiker learned about CyberCartel’s AI-powered methods after the hacking group mistakenly leaked information about its internal operations. While security researchers say CyberCartel has been active since at least 2012, the new AI agents have dramatically ramped up the speed and effectiveness of its attacks in recent months, Straiker said. CyberCartel didn’t appear to need access to Anthropic’s Mythos for the attacks. Instead, they used AI agents powered by SpaceX’s Grok to mine the web for information about their targets, Straiker said. They also used four different AI agents powered by Anthropic’s Claude Opus and Sonnet models to deliberate over how best to carry out attacks, while another Claude model running in the AI coding app Cursor acted as the “commander” orchestrating the hacks. The findings are significant because they show in detail how cybercriminals are automating the type of attacks OpenAI and Anthropic have been warning about in broad terms, according to Ken Huang, an AI security consultant and adjunct professor at the University of San Francisco who reviewed Straiker’s research. They also show how low the barrier to entry is for carrying out sophisticated hacks now thanks to AI, he said. “Tokens and a harness are all you need,” Huang said. “It changes the primary bottleneck of an attack from human technical skill to API token budgets and compute.” In theory, all of those AI models are built with guardrails meant to prevent them from agreeing to carry out such cyberattacks. But CyberCartel sidestepped those constraints by telling the AI models that they were operating in harmless environments such as an academic test or a company’s internal tests of its own systems. If Claude refused to carry out a hack, CyberCartel’s code would direct smaller models like Moonshot’s Kimi to actually hack the victims; if Kimi models also refused, the system of AI agents would automatically revert to a more old-school type of hack involving deploying malware, Straiker found. Straiker said it shared its research with SpaceX and Anthropic and that both labs were working to prevent CyberCartel from accessing their models. Straiker said it was attempting to get in contact with Moonshot. SpaceX and Moonshot didn’t respond to requests for comment. While alarming, the rise in cyberattacks fully automated by AI is something defenders have been bracing for in recent months. Other firms say they’ve seen a rise in activity on the part of hackers who appear to be assisted by large language models. “We’re seeing an increase in automated probing of our environment. Automated attacks have been on the rise for 20-plus years and now LLMs are making it even easier,” said Scott Roberts, chief information security officer at enterprise software company UiPath. “We’re going to have to adjust on our security operations and detections side to adapt.”

title: SpaceX’s Musk Lauds Its Soaring Cloud Business and Possible Tesla Merger
content: SpaceX put on a bit of a show for shareholders today—and I’m not referring to the sizzle reel of rocket and space videos it showed on its earnings call. No, the big attention grabber was the update from CEO Elon Musk on the progress of SpaceX’s contemplated merger with Tesla and just how involved—or not involved he is in the whole affair. First though, it’s worth mentioning the other big highlight from the call: SpaceX’s booming AI—excuse me, SI—business, a category that includes the company’s X social media service, its Grok Bot agent platform and a cloud infrastructure service it has started to rent to outsiders like Anthropic. The segment is on fire. It saw its third-quarter revenue nearly triple to $7.56 billion, making it the largest business category at SpaceX. And if that wasn’t enough, the SI business swung to an operating profit of $431 million from a $1.26 billion loss in the second quarter. SpaceX shares jumped nearly 7% in after-hours trading following the report. SpaceX executives made it clear that the big story in its SI (superintelligence) segment is its cloud business. Musk told investors the company’s phone is ringing off the hook with demand from businesses that want to lease SpaceX’s AI compute. “We are hounded relentlessly by every hyperscaler and by dozens of smaller companies to rent more of our compute,” Musk said. “We could rent out our compute several times over if we said yes to everyone.” For his part, Bret Johnsen, SpaceX’s chief financial officer, described that demand as “extraordinary” and said at the prices it’s currently charging its cloud customers, SpaceX is “generating a payback in less than a year” on new data centers after it deploys them. Musk also addressed a question from an investor about his desire to unite SpaceX and Tesla. He said the respective companies have formed special committees to examine a merger, but because he’s CEO of both Tesla and SpaceX, he has needed to recuse himself from those discussions. Still, that didn’t stop him from telling everyone listening to the call that he thinks a merger is a grand idea. “I do think there’s a lot of merit to combining both companies,” he said. Musk also stated the obvious caveat: Any deal will still need shareholder approval, and there’s no guarantee they’ll bless it. “I think some people assume a SpaceX-Telsa merger is a certainty,” he said. “I think that would be overstating it.” Nonetheless, Musk’s shareholders tend to be very obedient to him. If the companies decide to move forward with a merger, stay tuned for Musk to start turning up his X megaphone and encouraging them to fall in line. Netflix’s Sad Trombone The other shoe just dropped at Netflix. Last than a week after announcing the layoffs of about 1,000 employees, or 6% of the company, Netflix reported its weakest quarterly revenue growth in three years—an 11.8% jump to $12.87 billion in revenue. For a figure lower than that, you have to go all the way back to the third quarter of 2023. It didn’t help that Netflix told investors revenue growth will get even worse in the fourth quarter, estimating 11.5% for that period. The company’s shares fell 5% in after-hours trading. The weak third-quarter revenue number wasn’t exactly a surprise; it was slightly better than the growth rate Netflix had told analysts to expect last quarter. But it’s obvious from the heads that have rolled at Netflix over the past week that the company’s CEOs, Ted Sarandos and Greg Peters, aren’t happy with the state of its business. The firings included Bela Bajaria, chief content officer, and David Lin, film chief, a sign that the company wants to reset its approach to movies and series. It's still a powerhouse in living rooms: The new season of “The Diplomat” is back on with a vengeance on my TV set. But Netflix feels like it’s looking for a new act. In Other News In a draft IPO prospectus, Anthropic disclosed a net loss of more than $80 billion for the first half of the year, reflecting its accounting for financing agreements, The Wall Street Journal reported . Around a fifth of its $16.3 billion in revenue for the period came from two customers. Elon Musk ordered the slowdown in a military version of Starlink in Ukraine, The Wall Street Journal reported . Salesforce agreed to buy customer engagement platform Braze for roughly $5.66 billion, including debt. Joel Kaplan, Meta Platforms’ chief global affairs officer, plans to leave the company after more than 15 years. title: Nvidia Moves to Back GPU Cloud Provider Firmus After Investors Balk at Its IPO
content: Nvidia is in talks to invest hundreds of millions of dollars in Australian AI cloud provider Firmus, which abruptly pulled its initial public offering early this month, according to people familiar with the talks. The discussion indicates that Nvidia is likely to continue backing a group of unproven firms known as neoclouds that is facing financial pressure after they stacked up on debt to purchase Nvidia graphics processing units for data centers. Nvidia has already put more than $170 billion on the line for such firms and other large customers, including credit guarantees to help them raise the debt, according to The Information’s analysis . Many of these neoclouds are unproven and need massive revenue growth to be able to pay down debt they’re borrowing to buy primarily Nvidia servers. That’s become a problem as interest rates have ticked up. Last week, shares of the biggest neocloud, CoreWeave , and its smaller public rivals fell around 20%. The concerns even hit bigger AI cloud providers like Oracle. It isn’t clear whether Nvidia’s continued financial support will allay investors’ concerns about the sector. At an event in Stockholm last week, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said CoreWeave, for one, wouldn’t require a further credit backstop from Nvidia. And CoreWeave’s CEO, in a note to staff, privately blamed smaller neoclouds like Firmus that have shorter track records for damaging the sector’s reputation. Firmus’ revenues are tiny in comparison to CoreWeave’s, so it arguably needs a lot more support. Firmus is trying to privately raise at least $2 billion in the wake of its failed IPO, in which it was reportedly seeking to raise $5 billion. Nvidia was poised to invest a material amount of capital in that deal, said a person with knowledge of it. The amount Nvidia would invest in the new capital raise could change, and the raise could still fall apart. Bloomberg earlier reported on the Firmus private round but Nvidia’s role hasn’t been reported. Neoclouds are critical to Nvidia because its biggest customers—namely, Google, Microsoft and Amazon—are making their own server chips to reduce their reliance on Nvidia’s. This summer, Nvidia even changed the way it reports its revenue in a way that further highlights neoclouds, which it began to support in earnest in 2023, when demand for GPUs skyrocketed. Whether Nvidia continues to support that ecosystem could make or break some neoclouds’ survival or spark a consolidation of the sector, which some executives in the field view as inevitable. Nvidia appears eager to prove the skeptics wrong by providing additional equity investments, chip allocations, credit support and customer leads to the neoclouds. A team at Nvidia, which Huang’s son-in-law Nico Caprez co-leads, has even begun helping neoclouds find sites with available power, which are hard to come by because it takes a long time to either source independent power or get connected to the electric grid, executives at Nvidia and neoclouds say. The seven-year-old Firmus sought to list its shares at a reported $30 billion valuation on the Australian stock exchange before pulling the offering, citing market volatility. Investors reportedly felt the valuation was too high and too speculative, based on Firmus’ revenues and its planned data center capacity. Firmus’ major investors include Blackstone, Coatue Management and Jane Street. Nvidia has participated in Firmus’ last three funding rounds. The company has raised more than $13 billion in total, including around $10 billion in debt. Firmus was one of the first participants in Nvidia’s new program to provide credit support to neoclouds in exchange for a cut of their cloud revenues. Nvidia agreed in June to backstop Firmus’ purchase of server racks containing at least 170,000 of its Rubin and Blackwell GPUs, to make it easier for the firm to raise debt. The server racks would cost an estimated $15 billion and are set to go into a data center in Batam, Indonesia built by Singaporean data center developer DayOne, which is also trying to go public. Neocloud executives say that despite the market turn against neoclouds, their counterparts at Nvidia have been positive in meetings and haven’t yet suggested brand-new types of financial arrangements to remedy the market jitters. However, Nvidia has already modified the way it provides credit support to some firms that must raise capital for new facilities. Some bigger neoclouds passed on Nvidia’s initial credit-support offer, which it made in exchange for a share of the neoclouds’ future revenues. Nvidia is now offering shorter-term, credit-support agreements in exchange for a smaller cut of revenues, according to one of those executives with knowledge of the shift.

title: Private Equity Firms Weighed $100 Billion-Plus Buyout of Microsoft’s Xbox
content: A group of private equity firms in recent months considered a potential buyout of Microsoft’s Xbox gaming unit that could have valued it between $100 billion and $150 billion, according to people familiar with the discussions. The short-lived discussions by the private firms were exploratory and didn’t turn into a negotiation with Microsoft, the people said. But they show the company could find buyers if its turnaround of the struggling gaming division falters. The identities of the PE firms couldn’t be confirmed. A Microsoft spokesperson said in a statement that “Xbox is not for sale,” and declined to comment further. Based on the unit’s revenue, the high end of the price those firms considered would have been roughly in line with the recent leveraged buyout of another gaming giant, Electronic Arts. The private equity firms’ interest happened around the time The Information reported in June that Microsoft had considered spinning out or restructuring the Xbox unit as a wholly owned subsidiary, which could make it easier to sell. Microsoft had also considered creating a joint venture with other partners. Since then, Xbox management under CEO Asha Sharma has focused on improving the unit’s operations and accelerating growth. The Xbox unit includes Activision Blizzard, a gaming publisher Microsoft acquired for $75 billion in 2023. The business, which employs about 14,000 , has suffered in recent years from razor-thin profit margins and declining sales, as its bet on acquiring a large number of studios didn’t generate as much new revenue as it had hoped. Xbox’s revenue fell 7% for the fiscal year ending in June, to $21.8 billion. Its accountability margin, which is similar to an adjusted profit margin, has fallen over the past year to just 3% as of June, the company disclosed earlier this year. Since taking over the unit this February, Sharma has tried to turn the business around. In July, she laid out a plan to cut 3,200 jobs, or around 20% of its staff, over the next year and invest more in franchises such as Halo and Minecraft, The Information has reported . Still, the unit is a relatively small part of Microsoft, about 7% of its total revenue, and the company is pouring capital into data centers and other AI investments, hurting its free cash flow. Few buyers would be able to raise $100 billion or more for a takeover of Xbox, making it more likely that any deal would involve several firms. A deal involving Xbox, if it ever materialized, would dwarf the largest leveraged buyout in history: Earlier this year, Silver Lake, the Saudi Arabia Public Investment Fund and Jared Kushner’s Affinity Partners took Electronic Arts private in a leveraged buyout that valued the gaming company at $55 billion, including debt. That was about seven times Electronics Arts’ annual revenue of around $7.5 billion in the 12 months ending in March, though unlike Xbox, Electronic Arts doesn’t have a hardware business weighing on its margins. While the games industry grew rapidly during Covid-19, it has since come under pressure as sales have stalled and the AI boom has driven up the price of the hardware needed to manufacture consoles. In one sign of rising costs, Xbox recently internally projected that a console set to ship in 2028 could cost consumers $1,200 to $1,800, Fortune reported Tuesday. The Xbox console business competes with Sony-owned PlayStation and Nintendo. Sony’s game and network services division, which operates PlayStation, reported around $29.8 billion in revenue in fiscal year 2025, roughly flat from the year prior, though sales of its console and games it develops fell.

title: Nvidia Has Put More Than $170 Billion on the Line for Neoclouds
content: Nvidia has become something of a central bank for companies expanding the market for its chips beyond tech giants, backstopping customers and demand. But as Nvidia-backed cloud firms come under pressure, the question is how much further it will go. The chipmaker has already disclosed as much as $164.5 billion in guarantees and other commitments to support new data centers, including agreements to pay landlords if tenants default on leases and promises to buy capacity, filings show, as of the company’s July quarter. That’s on top of more than $7 billion it has invested or agreed to invest directly in AI cloud providers. Those investments are part of Nvidia’s broader portfolio of equity stakes, valued at nearly $100 billion as of July, which also includes investments in data center developers like SB Energy and big AI labs including OpenAI and Anthropic. When it comes to AI cloud companies, Nvidia’s investments help seed their growth, providing capital to go toward project costs or purchases of graphics processing units that lenders typically won’t finance in full. Nvidia’s lease commitments and guarantees, meanwhile, can make it easier to finance new data centers or the Nvidia chips inside them. But equity markets are souring on AI cloud firms and their ambitious growth plans, with shares in CoreWeave, Nebius and Iren tumbling last week. Nvidia-backed companies including Firmus and Lambda have pulled or postponed initial public offering efforts, while SB Energy and Nscale made their IPO paperwork public last month but haven’t moved ahead. Meanwhile, financiers of some data center projects are getting jumpier . That all raises the prospect that Nvidia may have to go further to shore up confidence in the sector, despite its substantial existing commitments and growing demand among investors for protection on its own debt. Nvidia declined to comment. The Information reported on Tuesday that Nvidia is in talks for a fresh investment of hundreds of millions of dollars into Firmus following the abrupt cancellation of its IPO earlier this month. Nvidia says the financial risks it faces from supporting AI companies are manageable, with Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress saying on an August earnings call that its “risk is limited” in backing AI labs because it can redeploy its chips to other customers. And Nvidia’s commitments wouldn’t necessarily all come due at once if major cloud customers were to default. Still, stepping in if neoclouds struggle to find customers or secure financing could raise bigger questions about Nvidia’s growth prospects, especially as Google, Amazon and Microsoft invest more heavily in alternatives to Nvidia GPUs. Nvidia’s nonhyperscaler customers, including neoclouds and large enterprises, accounted for 45% of its data center revenue, or $40 billion, in its July quarter, more than double the number a year earlier.

title: The Download: introducing the Impossible issue
content:
The Download: introducing the Impossible issue
Plus: Elon Musk reportedly ordered the recent Starlink slowdown in Ukraine.
This is today's edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what's going on in the world of technology.
Introducing: the Impossible issue
We wanted our last print edition of 2026 to include a slate of stories that check in on impossible ideas. Why? Because it’s fun to dream about living on other planets or uploading our brains. But also because scientists and engineers who won’t give up on daring endeavors remind us what technology is supposed to do: make life better, safer, healthier, even more joyful.
That’s the ambition behind the stories in our new Impossible issue. We explore bold attempts to make synthetic blood, build cities on the moon, and attain cognitive immortality. We investigate AI’s ability to say no, a bionic eye that can restore sight, and high hopes for blended meat. Plus, we check in on six technologies that have been “coming soon” for years.
This issue is for the folks with the audacity to try, and refuse to let anyone—themselves included— tell them no. We hope you enjoy the ride.
Subscribe now to read the full print issue.
Astrolab’s upcoming rover will run the first LLMs on the moon
Large language models are set to go lunar. A computer capable of running AI software is one of the payloads aboard Astrolab’s FLIP lunar rover, which is slated to head to the moon as early as next month.
The mission will test whether LLMs can enable greater autonomy and real-time intelligent decision-making in the extreme lunar environment. But the moon will present formidable challenges, from extreme temperatures to intense cosmic radiation.
Find out how the lunar rover could change the future of space exploration.
—Tereza Pultarova
How to study a swiftly melting climate disaster
In Alaska’s Denali National Park, a 2013 lightning fire burned nearly 35,000 acres, stripping away the insulating layer that preserves permafrost. It’s given scientists a rare opportunity to study how fires reshape permafrost and carbon storage over time.
The work is providing critical clues into the complex mechanisms driving cascading climate feedback effects. As warming temperatures fuel fires, more permafrost thaws, releasing greenhouse-gas emissions that threaten to fuel more warming, fires and permafrost loss. Their observations are revealing worrisome signs about what lies ahead.
Discover what their fieldwork is revealing about a cascading climate disaster.
—James Temple
MIT Technology Review Narrated: the explosive claim that’s upended the AI world
“I think I have good news about the nature of neural networks.” With those simple words of optimism, Nick Cammarata, a researcher at AI startup Goodfire, kicked off a 26,000-word blog post that has knocked the industry on its head.
Cammarata claims that LLMs might be far easier to understand, and thus to monitor and control, than people previously thought. If true, it’s a huge deal. But not everyone is convinced.
MIT Technology Review spoke to Cammarata the day after his post blew up. He explained what he thinks researchers are getting wrong, what his work actually shows, and why skeptics aren’t ready to celebrate just yet.
This is our latest story to become an MIT Technology Review Narrated podcast, which we publish each week on Spotify and Apple Podcasts. Just navigate to MIT Technology Review Narrated on either platform, and follow us to get all our new content as it’s released.
The must-reads
I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology.
1 Elon Musk reportedly ordered the recent Starlink slowdown in Ukraine
The restrictions hampered drone strikes and air defences. (WSJ $)
+ The move sparked confusion in Washington over who authorised it. (CNBC)
+ Ukraine’s volunteer army is keeping Starlink alive. (MIT Technology Review)
2 An OpenAI model disabled its own safety checks—then lied about it
Two agents weakened the company’s safeguards during routine tasks. (CNBC)
+ They turned off systems designed to spot their misbehaviour. (FT $)
+ Here’s why AI agents lie to reach their goals. (MIT Technology Review)
3 SpaceX and Tesla have begun merger discussions
They’ve formed special committees to discuss a deal. (BBC)
+ Elon Musk, the CEO of both companies, said it’s “a good idea.” (Axios)
+ A merger could combine their AI and manufacturing plans. (Reuters $)
4 Global emissions have stalled, but warming is heading towards 2.8°C
The UN says the 1.5°C climate target is now out of reach. (Nature)
+ Current pledges would still bring warming to 2.1°C. (New Scientist $)
+ Climate tech companies offer rays of hope. (MIT Technology Review)
5 Ukraine says it’s carried out the world’s first drone evacuation
A heavy hexacopter flew a soldier to safety. (Ars Technica)
+ Ukraine has shared a video showing the evacuation. (CNBC)
+ A Russian satellite recently stalked a spacecraft believed to support Ukraine. (NYT $)
6 Meta has paused Muse sharing after private chats surfaced online
Researchers found 6,800 links exposing sensitive conversations. (Verge)
+ AI agents are not your "coworkers." (MIT Technology Review)
7 More than 1,000 mathematicians have pledged to shun AI companies
Some also vowed to avoid AI tools in their research. (New Scientist $)
8 AI is making it easy to clone almost any software
Viral tools promise easy copying, but often produce slop. (404 Media)
9 A computer program has finally outdone humans at cryptic crosswords
Its creator hopes to tackle the harder challenge of setting puzzles. (Guardian)
10 A newly-discovered particle could explain the origins of reality
In particular, it could reveal why matter survived the Big Bang. (404 Media)
Quote of the day
“I did not remove an enabled monitor from it.”
—GPT-6 Astra, an OpenAI coding agent, tells its user it hasn’t disabled a safeguard after doing exactly that, the company reveals in a new misalignment report.
One more thing
This giant microwave may change the future of war
US armed forces are hunting for a weapon that disables drones en masse—and they want it fast.
One solution focuses on microwaves: high-powered electronic devices that push out kilowatts of power to zap the circuits of a drone as if it were the tinfoil you forgot to take off your leftovers when you heated them up.
Defense tech startup Epirus may have the winning formula. The company has developed a cutting-edge, cost-efficient drone zapper that’s sparking the interest of the US military—and drones are just one of its targets. Peer into its crosshairs.
—Sam Dean
We can still have nice things
A place for comfort, fun, and distraction to brighten up your day. (Got any ideas? Drop me a line.)
+ Don’t feel guilty about enjoying a siesta; fish take naps during the day, too.
+ Every trade has its go-to tools. This site has built a fascinating register of them.
+ Wikipop spotlights what was most popular on Wikipedia yesterday, providing a daily snapshot of what the world is reading.
+ Meet the self-taught woodcarver who went from a broke young father to creating some of Disneyland’s most iconic attractions.

title: We can do impossible things
content:
I’d wager everyone has a rehearsed response to what’s absolutely one of the world’s worst interview questions: “What’s your biggest weakness?” Whenever I’ve gotten it, I take a slow—even pensive—breath and rattle off my line: “I say no to myself too much.”
I won’t lie. It’s a bit shameless—a definite humblebrag. I’m a systems thinker: When an idea pops up, I immediately spin up a feasibility assessment in my head. I run lists, plot timelines, and tally budget line items. Sometimes a rough Gantt chart starts to take shape. (I’m a gas at parties, as you can surely tell.)
My brain, throughout my 20-plus-year career as a science and tech journalist, has played host to a near ­constant tug-of-war between ambition and reality. Learning to find that balance is a big part of what’s helped me survive in this industry and, ultimately, led me here. This past spring, I had the great privilege of joining the incredible team of journalists behind
MIT Technology Review
to take the reins of the print magazine.
If you’ve been reading along with us for the last handful of issues, you may have noticed a few changes starting to materialize. We’ve brought back a regular roster of lists and infographics (both things that magazines do particularly well). But the biggest change is only just beginning to take shape, which is why Mat Honan, our editor in chief, asked me to hop in to introduce myself—and the issue you’re holding in your hands right now.
We’re giving ourselves permission to play around and experiment. To be a little … audacious.
Because, practical though I may be, I do still have plenty of ideas. It’s just that I sometimes need a reminder to stop blocking myself and
do the thing
. That’s the spirit driving this issue in particular.
We wanted to end 2026 with a slate of stories that check in on impossible ideas. Why? Because it’s frankly a lot of fun to dream about living on the moon or uploading our brains. Because losing sight of ambition is all too easy when it feels as if we’re playing whack-a-mole with the world’s problems. But also because the scientists and engineers who absolutely refuse to give up on even the most daring endeavors—like making synthetic blood or decoding animals’ speech—remind us what this whole technology thing is supposed to do to begin with.
It’s supposed to take cutting-edge research and development and apply it to make life better, safer, healthier, even more joyful. And when we eff up and make things worse (see: forever chemicals, traffic deaths, and AI that encourages potentially dangerous user behavior), we’re supposed to dig back in, assess the damage, and find ways to fix what we’ve broken. Even when unraveling the mess might itself seem impossible.
Right before I came to
MIT Technology Review,
I edited a newsletter about individual actions that can help address the climate crisis, which some would call—and have called—a fool’s errand, given the sheer scale of the problem. They might say it’s as implausible as an AI kill switch, practical nuclear fusion, or a superconductor that works at room temperature. But if I learned nothing else from three years spent finding ways for li’l old me (or li’l old you!) to chip away at one of humanity’s biggest existential threats, it’s that focusing on what we can’t do only makes the darkness darker.
So yeah, this one’s for the folks who have the audacity to try, and who refuse to let anyone—themselves included—tell them no.
I hope you enjoy the ride.

title: Nuclear-powered spaceships
content:
Are we there yet?
Read the rest of the package
Just before the Artemis II crew began its historic slingshot around the moon this past April, NASA announced plans to build Space Reactor-1 Freedom. SR-1, the first-ever nuclear-reactor-­powered interplanetary spacecraft, is meant to fly an uncrewed mission to Mars by the end of 2028, arriving in 2029. A successful mission would herald a new era of more efficient, potentially faster spaceflight—saving astronauts time and cutting their exposure to harmful cosmic radiation as they travel to Mars and beyond. “You wake up to that announcement, and it puts a big smile on your face,” says Simon Middleburgh, co-director of the Nuclear Futures Institute at Bangor University in Wales.
The sticking points
Running a nuclear reactor in space may sound like lunacy, but it’s not. The Soviet Union sent dozens of reactors into orbit, often to power spy satellites. And experts say there aren’t any major technical obstacles to making nuclear space propulsion happen. “I think it’s a very doable technology,” says Philip Metzger, a spaceflight engineering researcher at the Florida Space Institute.“I’m happy to see them finally doing this.”
Still, developing space propulsion using reactors has been slow going. The US has started—and terminated—
several programs
looking into it over the past 75 years. The latest casualty was DRACO, a collaboration between NASA and the Department of Defense, which
in 2025. The project was
canceled
because of high experimentation costs, an inability to compete with conventional rocket propulsion on price, and difficulty ensuring that ground tests could be performed safely and effectively. (You are creating an incredibly powerful nuclear reaction, after all.)
The progress
After much wavering, it now appears that nuclear-powered interplanetary travel is a $2 billion bet NASA is willing to make. The agency is pursuing an approach called nuclear electric propulsion, which uses the neutrons produced in a self-­sustaining, uranium-­atom-splitting reaction to create heat and ultimately electricity. The electricity is used to ionize a gas, which is blasted out of the spacecraft with the help of magnetic fields, generating thrust. The approach “is very low thrust, but very efficient,” says Sebastian Corbisiero, the US Department of Energy’s national technical director of space reactor programs. “So you can use it for a long period of time.”
What might such a rocket look like? A presentation by Steve Sinacore, program director of NASA’s SR-1 program, offers some clues. So far, the concept art makes the craft look like a colossal fletched arrow. The back will house the power-and-propulsion system, while the tip will hold a uranium-filled nuclear reactor with a capacity of at least 20 kilowatts. (For context, a
typical nuclear plant
on Earth is about 50,000 times more powerful.) The “fletches” on SR-1 are large fins that help cool the reactor by radiating heat into space.
Like many other pieces of space hardware, the reactor will need to be put through its paces on the ground before it’s cleared for the rough rocket trip to space. “Going through the launch safely is going to be a challenge,” says Middleburgh. “You are being shaken, rattled, and rolled.” For safety reasons, the reactor will be switched on around two days post-launch, when it’s comfortably far from Earth. Uranium isn’t tremendously dangerous by itself, but that can’t be said of the waste products that emerge when the reactor is running. If SR-1 works as planned, its journey to Mars will take about a year.
Will this novel form of space propulsion actually reach the Red Planet by 2029? It’s possible. NASA says the Idaho National Laboratory, which is building SR-1’s reactor, is making progress and is on target for a late-2028 launch. “Procurement of major components is underway, and integration work on the power and propulsion element is advancing steadily,” Sinacore told
MIT Technology Review
. The outlook will get even sunnier if the Artemis program, which aims to start laying the foundations for a base on the lunar south pole by the decade’s end, keeps to its own bold deadline.
“It’s an aggressive timeline,” says Lindsey Holmes, who is vice president of advanced projects at Analytical Mechanics Associates, an aerospace company in Virginia. She suspects the push is being driven partly by China’s and Russia’s own
deep-space nuclear ambitions
. The two countries have spoken about plans to place a reactor on the moon’s surface in the mid-2030s to power a jointly operated lunar base. Whether it flies or fails in space, SR-1’s development should help NASA put its own reactor on the moon; the technology involved in the two projects is broadly similar, given that the lunar surface, like space itself, is a vacuum. If an interplanetary nuclear-powered spacecraft works, a nuclear reactor on the moon should too.
Progress meter . . . . . . . . . . . . 6
Most of the technology for SR-1 already exists; it’s going to come down to piecing it all together and then seeing how it performs in space.

title: Exercise in a pill
content:
Are we there yet?
Read the rest of the package
We all know exercise is good for us. It builds muscle, strengthens bones, lowers blood pressure, and boosts mood. By deciphering how movement benefits the body, researchers hope to develop medicines that can offer some of the same perks—without the workout. The idea isn’t to replace exercise but to bring its upsides to people who struggle with frailty, disability, or chronic illness.
The sticking points
It will take a lot of experimentation to untangle the myriad pathways by which exercise promotes health. But IDing the cascade of hormones, enzymes, and other molecules related to physical activity is just the first step. Scientists need to figure out how to turn that knowledge into safe and effective drugs. That’s a tall order:
More than 90%
of treatments that enter human studies fail.
There are regulatory hurdles too. The FDA approves medications to treat diseases, not to enhance wellness, says Thomas Burris, a pharmacologist at the University of Florida whose work focuses on diseases that respond to exercise, like obesity, type 2 diabetes, and dementia.
The progress
There may never be a pill that delivers all the benefits of exercise, but research could lead to new medicines that mimic some aspects of working out. Scientists have already identified many important exercise-related signals and have even developed compounds to regulate them. (Some preliminary results have been so promising that doping authorities have proactively banned the compounds.)
Burris and his colleagues are focused on a receptor that’s always switched on, even without exercise. Working out appears to boost that receptor in muscle cells, which in turn helps bolster endurance over time. Burris’s lab has spent years
designing a drug
that cranks up the receptor’s activity directly, and mice treated with the drug ran longer and farther than mice that weren’t. They “become marathon mice without having to do any type of exercise,” Burris says. There are even indications—also in mice—that the compound mimics some of the cognitive benefits of exercise and could help treat heart failure. Burris founded a company called Pelagos to carry the work forward into a clinical trial.
Other workout-mimicking drugs have already entered human studies. In June, the biotech firm Cambrian Bio
reported
that its experimental drug ATX-304 boosted metabolism and reduced liver and belly fat in people with obesity and prediabetes
It activates a metabolic switch that helps cells sense when energy supplies dip and coordinates the production of more fuel—the same switch that helps us sustain long sessions jumping rope or swimming laps. Cambrian hopes it will help people lose weight without losing muscle, a common concern with GLP-1 medicines.
Progress meter ............ 5
Our understanding of how exercise benefits the body is still coming into focus, and drug development is prone to failure.

title: Interspecies communication
content:
Are we there yet?
Read the rest of the package
Humans are far from the only species with a gift for gab, and our furry, feathered, and finned friends could have a lot to tell us. Decoding how animals communicate with one another could offer a window into the inner lives of other species and help humans realize that “animals are sentient creatures who think, who have hopes and dreams of their own,” says Con Slobodchikoff, the founder of Zoolingua, a company working on dog-to-human speech.
The sticking points
Teasing all this out is complex. To decipher howls, squeaks, and clicks, researchers must match the creatures making sounds with what’s happening around them. Prairie dogs, for example,
utter a different series of yips
when a coyote approaches than when a hawk is nearby. It’s painstaking work, especially for difficult-to-­observe species, like deep-diving whales or subterranean mole rats.
There are other hurdles. Many animals communicate not just through sound but through visual cues, touch, pheromones, or a combination of signals, some of which might be difficult for us to perceive. And without a multispecies Rosetta stone, it’s hard to know if translations are accurate.
The progress
Over the past 50 years, a growing arsenal of devices has made it easier to observe the sophisticated ways animals communicate.
Hydrophones
at the bottom of the ocean can capture humpback whale song, and tiny wearable “
biologgers
” can record a bat’s every squeak.
In the last decade, advances in AI have leveled up our ability to make sense of it all. The technology can detect different calls, distinguish which sounds belong to which animal, and spot patterns. Researchers at the Earth Species Project (ESP), a nonprofit founded in 2018 to decode animal communication, recently used machine learning to
detect vocalizations of carrion crows
and determine which bird made which call.
They suspect that more advanced AI could translate critters’ chatter. Large language models like Claude and ChatGPT excel at finding relationships between words, explains Sara Keen, one of ESP’s behavioral ecologists. ESP hopes its own NatureLM—trained on human speech, music, and animal sounds—will be able to interpret the vocalizations of a variety of species.
That promise, however, is still theoretical. Yossi Yovel, a neuroecologist at Tel Aviv University, worries that these models will put too much emphasis on acoustic similarities and make mistakes—like lumping together similar sounds that have different meanings.
As for a two-way convo? It’s not clear when—or whether—that will happen. Still, “a lot of animals have an evolutionary structure that is similar enough that we should be able to understand what they’re saying,” Slobodchikoff says.
Progress meter ............ 4
Researchers have amassed heaps of data on animal communication, but they’re still trying to figure out how to decipher it all.

title: Cleaning up PFAS
content:
Are we there yet?
Read the rest of the package
Scrubbing Earth of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances—a.k.a. PFAS or forever chemicals—could eliminate a list of woes for people and planet. Used for decades in everything from nonstick pans to firefighting foams, PFAS have been linked to increased risks of
fertility
challenges,
developmental delays
reduced immune response
. They are known for a strong bond between carbon and fluorine, which the environment struggles to break down.
The sticking points
PFAS are everywhere: They spew from factories and slough off products and into water with normal use. Scientists have found them in everything from
human blood
Antarctic snow
2022 report
found that 89% of the US population had PFAS in excess of two nanograms per milliliter of blood plasma, a common threshold for potential adverse health effects, and 9% of the population had passed the riskier level of 20 nanograms per milliliter.
The PFAS monster is also a moving target. New compounds are still being created and used. There are more than 12,000 of them, and much of the cleanup research focuses on only a small handful.
The progress
Cleansing PFAS-contaminated soil is a project in its infancy, but it is possible to prevent more buildup by pulling the chemicals out of water systems. There are two ways to handle this: trap or destroy. Some scientists have found reverse osmosis—a process that pushes water through supertight filters—useful in
point-of-use cases, like water filters at kitchen sinks
Other techniques in the pipeline might be more suitable for large-scale removal—for example, at water treatment facilities. One, called
foam fractionation
, generates bubbles that capture PFAS. More approaches, like ensnaring the chemicals in nanothin layers of charged metal, are also under investigation.
Trapping, though, is imperfect. You’re left with PFAS-filled brine, which if not properly destroyed (an expensive and energy-sucking endeavor) can still end up in the environment.
Jack Huang, a professor of crop and soil sciences at the University of Georgia, is working on destruction. He’s testing a method called
electrochemical degradation
, which uses electrodes to break down the bonds that hold PFAS together. The product destroyed more than 90% of PFAS mass in tests and has already been
licensed by the engineering consulting firm AECOM
Ridding life of PFAS is also a policy challenge. There are alternatives; we just need the push to use them. And we’ve had success before: The EPA’s
2010/2015 PFOA Stewardship Program
has helped slash the release of water-repellent perfluorooctanoic acid by 95%. More recently, Minnesota, Maine, and New Mexico have passed bans on PFAS in products like cookware and dental floss.
Progress meter ............ 6
Scientists are making strides toward removing and destroying PFAS—but it’ll be all for naught if we don’t turn off the tap.

title: Solid-state batteries
content:
Are we there yet?
Read the rest of the package
The rise of the lithium-ion battery, which powers everything from the smallest personal electronics to gargantuan energy storage systems, has been nothing short of revolutionary. But as anyone who’s boarded a plane in the last decade could tell you, storing and pumping out energy by moving charged lithium ions through a liquid electrolyte soup has its drawbacks, not least that the batteries have a troubling tendency to catch fire. Enter the solid-state battery, which swaps liquid for a solid ceramic or polymer, creating power packs that charge faster, last longer, cram more energy into smaller spaces, and (crucially) run cooler. A new generation of companies aim to bring such batteries to market, and if their bets pan out, the tech could substantially ease the shift away from fossil fuels.
The sticking points
Solid-state batteries have been “just a few years away” for more than a decade now. In laboratories, the technology works. But there have been challenges. In designs that pair the solid electrolyte with a lithium-metal anode (the side of the battery that releases electrons into an electrical circuit), needlelike filaments called dendrites tend to grow during charging, and they eventually push through the electrolyte and short the cell. Solid electrolytes are
supposed
to physically block the formation of dendrites, but many of them crack as the treelike projections break through like roots in a concrete foundation.
Then there’s the problem of manufacturing at scale. Mass production requires large quantities of defect-free sheets of ceramic-like material to make the electrolytes as well as dry rooms for assembly, since those electrolytes have a tendency to react with water. Would-be manufacturers quote a range of potential prices for solid-state batteries, but most expect them to fall in line with lithium-ion packs sometime in the mid-2030s.
The progress
Nascent as the technology is, solid-state batteries have already seen
high-­profile missteps
. But one of America’s most advanced solid-state-battery companies says it’s closing in on being able to bring its product to market. The Bill Gates–backed QuantumScape launched in Silicon Valley in 2010 and built its battery around a class of ceramic materials that it says is compatible with lithium—meaning no dendrite formation. “We spent, then, like 10 years learning how to process it to satisfy all of the other requirements,” says Tim Holme, QuantumScape’s cofounder and chief technology officer. In 2025, the startup announced a proprietary, large-scale manufacturing method for quickly producing and heat-treating the ceramic electrolytes used in its batteries. “Nobody has ever done this in the field of ceramics before,” Holme claims. For 10,000 years, producing ceramics has involved slowly cooking the starting materials in an oven over the course of days. “We figured out a way to shorten that down to several minutes,” he says.
Plenty of other companies are pushing the tech forward as well. Toyota, the world’s biggest automaker,
launched
a research program on solid-state batteries way back in 2010. It’s now partnering with the global energy and petroleum company Idemitsu Kosan on a pilot plant, promising cars that can travel up to 745 miles after charging 10 minutes or less—a huge leap, if it works out. In China, CATL, the giant behind roughly 40% of the global battery market, is aggressively pursuing solid-state batteries too, pumping
nearly $2.6 billion
into a research program in 2024 alone. Mercedes, meanwhile, equipped one of its EQS sedans with solid-state batteries last fall; after driving nonstop for 750 miles, the car
still had some range
to spare.
Will the tech gain traction? Investing in vehicle batteries makes sense given the size of the potential market. But any little uptick in cost typically gets passed on to buyers, so the first solid-state EV batteries will inevitably be more expensive.
Grid storage buyers, who are working to meet the increasing demands posed by data centers, may also hesitate to purchase new technologies that still haven’t come down the cost curve. Then again, the promise of energy storage that lasts longer than lithium-­ion’s typical eight hours could make them easier to persuade.
Some companies are taking a page from a playbook employed by outfits pursuing fusion: Focus on near-term markets with better margins to help fund development and bring down costs. Solid-state firms including California-based Solid Energies and Arizona-headquartered Sion Power are looking at selling batteries to the aviation industry or the military. “Those are sectors that are less sensitive to cost, and they typically require lower volumes as well,” says Evelina Stoikou, head analyst for battery technologies and supply chains at the consultancy BloombergNEF. “It’s a good way to prove your concept, then go through and fund the pilot plant where you can make that and eventually scale up.”
Progress meter ............ 7
The technology works, the capital is there, and demand is not far behind. But as with anything in manufacturing, unknown unknowns remain.
